We hope the below detail adequately addresses questions raised by committee and supports the case for the value of exa-cel, and the severity of SCD, for patients, who have few other options. **2 Application of the non-reference discount rate Vertex maintains that exa-cel qualifies for the non-reference discount rate and demonstrates that each of three criteria are firmly met. Exa-cel provides an irreversible genetic edit that directly addresses the underlying cause of SCD, restoring patients to normal or near-normal health.** 

The overall objective of the 1.5% discount rate is to avoid penalising those treatments with high upfront (undiscounted) costs but where the QALY gain and cost savings accrue over a long time period and are subject to discounting.

## **Exagamglogene autotemcel for treating sickle cell disease [ID4016]** 

## **Draft guidance comments form** 

## **Consultation on the draft guidance document – deadline for comments** 5pm on 11 April 2024. Please submit via NICE Docs. 

SCD has significant negative emotional, social and quality-of-life (QoL) effects on patients, but also their families on a daily basis. As described in the ACD (S3.1), ‘ _They [patient experts] noted that they could not remember a day without pain, whether that be mild, moderate, or severe_ ’. The ACD also reports the findings of the 2019 Sickle Cell World Assessment Survey, in which 76% of respondents reported having to reduce their working hours, and 58% having to stop work entirely (4). This daily impact of SCD was characterised by clinical experts in the ACD, who explained that vaso-occlusion happens constantly, even if a patient is not experiencing a crisis. In view of this, the committee concluded that SCD is a debilitating and life-limiting condition. This conclusion is supportive of qualification for non-reference criterion #1. 

Furthermore, it is stated in Section 3.8 of the ACD that ‘ _Clinical experts commented that the life expectancy for people with SCD with recurrent VOCs is in the fifth decade of life_ ’. When exploring how best to define ‘severe’ SCD during an advisory board conducted in the UK, advisers were in agreement that any other disease with a median life expectancy in the 40s would be classed as severe as a whole (5). The severity of SCD, seen in both the substantial reduction in life expectancy, and impact on quality of life, is supported by clinical experts, the body of evidence detailed below, and the committee deliberations, as detailed in the ACD. 

The committee asked for additional data on mortality and QoL, which we provide below to further demonstrate the severity of SCD, and substantial impact on daily living. 

## **Early mortality** 

Patients with SCD are affected by a myriad of complications and associated chronic multi-organ comorbidities, which results in a reduction in life expectancy by several decades relative to the general population. 

There is extensive recent literature (including studies from the UK) that consistently demonstrates that SCD patients have a significantly reduced life expectancy which is further reduced for patients with severe SCD/recurrent VOCs. These figures are consistent across cultures and over time with a lack of significant improvement over the last few decades even if optimal treatment is available (6). We summarise this data in Table 1, before providing additional detail.

## **Exagamglogene autotemcel for treating sickle cell disease [ID4016]** 

## **Draft guidance comments form** 

## **Consultation on the draft guidance document – deadline for comments** 5pm on 11 April 2024. Please submit via NICE Docs. 

Udeze et al (2023) observed a mean age at death of 40 years in a UK severe SCD population (n= 1,117), defined as at least 2 VOCs per year for 2 consecutive years, followed retrospectively between 2008 – 2018 (7). 

In another UK SCD cohort followed from 2009-2018, Piel et al (2021) observed a mean age at death of 39.7 years for those with four or more hospital admissions due to sickle cell crises over the two base years (n=1,171) (8). Notably, in this study the mortality rate for the five-year period of 2014 – 2018 (3.2%) was actually higher than that observed between 2009 – 2013 (2.2%), with the number of deaths increasing over time, from 36 in 2009 to 69 in 2018. 

Brousse _et al._ (2023) had similar findings with an observed mean age of death of 44 for severe SCD patients between 2012-2018 in France (n=4,270) (9). In this study, severity was defined by 2 vasoocclusive events in the year preceding index or 4 VOEs in the 2 years preceding index for 3,855 of the 4,270 patients, with the definition for the remainder relating to hydroxyurea and transfusion use. _Increased mortality in all patients with SCD regardless of severity_ In a recent analysis of data from the southeast London sickle cell gene bank cohort, Di Mauro _et al._ (2023) observed an average age at death of 41.5 years for HbSS (all severities) male SCD patients (n=692) (10). Brousse et al (2023) had an observed median age at death of 58 years in the total (unselected for severity) SCD patient cohort (n = 2,619) and Piel et al showed a mean age of death of 46.7 in the total patient cohort (9). Similarly, Jiao et al showed a mean age of death of 52.6 years in the total SCD population (11). The SMRs applied in the economic model and accepted by committee were sourced from Desai et al (2020) (12). Between the period of 2000 – 2013, Desai et al observed a cumulative incidence of mortality of 27.3% in 19–35-year-old patients with SCD in a US Medicaid population (n=44,033), (of which 11,064 were 19-35 years), demonstrating the impact of SCD on survival in even young patients. In those >35 years of age, the cumulative incidence of mortality was substantial, at 45.4%. In this study, higher VOC burden in the preceding year was associated with a considerably increased risk of mortality: 2-4 VOC vs <2 VOC HR 1.62. 

In response to the EAG’s critique that the Desai mortality rates were obtained from a younger cohort, the SMRs from Desai were stratified by age band. Furthermore, there was no age limit restriction in the eligibility criteria of the Desai study. The reason that there was a lack of older patients in Desai was simply because there were none: the majority had died. The fact that both the US Institute for Clinical and Economic Review (ICER) and the present NICE committee favoured use of the Desai et al. paper to inform mortality estimates for exa-cel provides further support for the Desai mortality estimates and the substantial reduction in life expectancy seen in all patients with SCD (13). 

In summary, it is clear from the weight of the literature that life expectancy for SCD patients is reduced by many decades compared to the UK general population (median age at death of 81.8 years for males and 85.5 years for females in 2020 (14)), with this reduction even more pronounced in severe SCD patients, as demonstrated by a mean age at death of 40.2 years in a UK population.

## **Exagamglogene autotemcel for treating sickle cell disease [ID4016]** 

## **Draft guidance comments form** 

## **Consultation on the draft guidance document – deadline for comments** 5pm on 11 April 2024. Please submit via NICE Docs. 

_‘describing the actual pain I feel is a real challenge – I can say that it feels like being stabbed everywhere repeatedly or having all your bones broken, but the words just don’t do the pain justice’ –_ Patient expert, ACM1 slides Multi-organ damage, co-morbidities and complications 

As described consistently in the clinical literature and summarised in the NHS Commissioning Policy, severe SCD is associated with a very significant rate of morbidity and mortality (2, 15-17). The toll of SCD on the patient is considerable. Frequent severe and unpredictable acute pain episodes which often need hospital admission but may be managed at home prevent school and work attendance and cause disruption of normal life for the patient and their family. Patients experience high rates of acute complications including stroke, infection, acute chest syndrome, acute renal failure, respiratory failure. As their disease progresses patients will also experience high rates of chronic organ impairment and reduction in organ function (eg brain, lungs, kidney, heart, spleen, eyes) and high levels of chronic pain. These complications, both acute and chronic, inevitably worsen with age and are not stopped by current therapies (6). 

For example, in a 10-year cohort analysis of 9,503 patients with SCD in the UK, using Health Episode Statistics (HES) data, Piel _et al_ (2021) examined co-morbidities commonly associated with SCD and 10- year mortality rates compared with the general population (8). The most common acute co-morbidity recorded was acute chest syndrome, which occurred at least once in 53.9% of the most severe SCD patient group. High prevalence of eleven other co-morbidities (including osteonecrosis, sepsis, renal disease, cardiovascular disease and priapism) were also reported in this study. The mean number of co-morbidities per patient over the 10-year study period was 2.5, for severe patients, with 63.2% of patients having two or more co-morbidities. 

Substantial impact of SCD on QoL further adds to the severity of the disease There is robust and extensive evidence showing the impact of SCD on QoL confirming the severity of this condition. SCD patients have an inherited condition and have experienced symptoms since early childhood. Whilst it is clear that baseline EQ-5D in CLIMB SCD-121 is well below age-adjusted population norms, the likely adaptation to their condition and associated underestimation of the burden on QoL means that their experience may not be fully captured by EQ-5D. This is further discussed in the section on utility values in the model (Section 9). 

The ACD states that the committee expected the QoL difference between the SCD population and the general population to be greater than stated by the company ‘if a condition caused people to have a severely impaired life’. We refute the committee’s perspective that the data from the trial indicates the population is not severe. 

CLIMB SCD-121 EQ-5D data We believe that first, the difference in QoL between patients at baseline in the trial and the age adjusted general population norm is significant and does show a severely impaired quality of life. The baseline EQ-5D value in the trial is 0.81, which compares with the UK population norm for an adult aged 18-24 of 0.93, providing us with a difference of 0.12 (18). The minimal clinically important difference (MCID) for EQ-5D is 0.08, so a reduction of 0.12 relative to general population is significant and clinically meaningful. However, the reduction of 0.12 is not representative of the majority of SCD patients and we agree with the committee that this may be because the EQ-5D only partially captures the impairment of QoL in SCD, as evidenced through a more granular view of the CLIMB SCD-121 EQ-5D data:

## **Exagamglogene autotemcel for treating sickle cell disease [ID4016]** 

## **Draft guidance comments form** 

## **Consultation on the draft guidance document – deadline for comments** 5pm on 11 April 2024. Please submit via NICE Docs. 

Figure 1 depicts the distribution of EQ-5D scores in the d120 FAS. Two contrasting observations can be made from the histogram: firstly, while 0.81 represents the mean of the CLIMB SCD-121 cohort, a proportion of patients had extremely low EQ-5D index scores; the minimum EQ-5D value at baseline at d120 in the FAS (n=31) was 0.2 and approximately one fifth of patients had scores less than 0.55. Secondly, the mean of 0.81 represents a value highly skewed by a significant proportion of patients with an EQ-5D utility at full health (over of patients in the PES and over of patients in the FAS). When estimating the baseline value for those patients in the FAS and PES not reporting perfect health the mean EQ-5D was and , respectively. These two contrasting observations support the evidence that patients with SCD have a severely reduced QoL compared with the UK general population, but also that the EQ-5D may not adequately capture the impact of SCD in a significant proportion of patients: the idea that people with perfect health would be willing to trade that for a burdensome transplantation with an experimental therapy clearly lacks face validity. 

**Figure 1: Histogram of EQ-5D-5L UK Index Scores for all patients at baseline in CLIMB SCD121 FAS (N=30)** 

**==> picture [415 x 298] intentionally omitted <==**

The severity of SCD is further evident when one considers that this lower utility value of 0.81, relative to the age-adjusted general population at baseline, is captured at the point at which exa-cel would be administered before patients go on to develop additional significant complications that characterise their condition. The applicability of this value is evident based on the results presented in Table 8. When using a baseline value of 0.81, the predicted baseline net health state utility (0.71) in the model aligns with the observed baseline utility value reported by patients ≥18 and ≤35 with baseline utility < 1. 

It is also clear that their QoL would continue to deteriorate as they grow older and live with multiple comorbidities. This effect on QoL has been accurately captured in the updated Vertex economic model

It is evidently clear from published literature and from patients’ experiences (as illustrated in the APPG No One’s Listening report) that SCD severely affects patients’ life (22). Multiple studies in various populations all consistently show a reduction of QoL in SCD, and patients with severe SCD (characterised by frequent VOCs) have a more marked reduction in QOL, which, as already demonstrated, is also associated with a further reduction in life expectancy. 

A systematic review in 2012 by Panepinto and Bonner found 39 studies of HRQOL in SCD and concluded that adults and children have significantly impaired HRQoL that is comparable to or worse than other chronic diseases (23). The included studies looked at a variety of QoL measures, most commonly SF-36 or PedsQL. Most studies showed that pain has a negative impact on QoL. For example, a large study based on the US Co-operative Study of SCD (Dampier et al 2011) looked at 1180 patients (median age 28 years) (24). All individual SF-36 scores were significantly decreased compared to the general US population and the occurrence of VOCs progressively decreased SF-36 scores. 

A 2012 UK study measured HRQoL in 510 patients (mean age 28.9 years) using EQ-5D on admission with VOC to the day unit or hospital and repeating this measurement on discharge and at one week post discharge (19). It showed utility values of 0.39 on admission, increasing to 0.65 at discharge and 0.75 one week later. Health scores derived from EQ-5D showed a negative association with pain, with patients reporting EQ-5D well below general population level even after recovery from VOC. A further study from the same lead author (Anie et al 2002) included 96 patients (mean age 30.1 years) and showed a significant reduction in all domains of SF-36 compared with the general population (25). 

Similar findings were shown by Shafrin et al (2021), who enrolled a population of 301 patients (average age 30.1 years) performing EQ-5D twice, once when experiencing a VOC and once when not experiencing a VOC. Results showed a reduced HRQoL at baseline (0.738) reducing further to 0.311 during a VOC, with disease severity strongly predicting worse self-reported HRQoL (26). 

A further study by Drahos _et al_ (2023) looked at 142 adults from US and Europe and compared various PRO measures in patients who had or had not experienced a recent VOC (within one week). The overall mean EQ-5D-5L health utility US index score among participants with SCD (0.59 [SD: 0.27])

Further evidence of the impact of SCD on patient reported outcomes has been shown by the SWAY survey (2,145 patients), where a substantial proportion of patients reported that SCD caused a high negative impact on emotions (60%) and school achievement (51%) and a reduction in work hours (53%) (4). The significant burden of complications patients experience has a huge impact on overall health, which translates into a reduction of many decades in life expectancy, as already detailed. Severity of SCD is also demonstrated by considering the resource use associated with severe SCD and the complications patients experience (7, 9). For example, patients with severe SCD in the UK require 22.17 hospital visits per year compared with 2.63 visits per year in matched controls, and receive 31.06 outpatient prescriptions compared with 7.58 in the matched population (28). 

In summary, SCD has a substantial, daily impact on QoL, with worries about their condition worsening, lack of understanding from doctors, and fear of dying all posing a substantial burden on patients (Figure 2). This burden is particularly pronounced for patients experiencing recurrent VOCs, the patient population that would be eligible for treatment with exa-cel.

_them, knowing I no longer have to leave them to go to the hospital. I now work full time and I contribute to my household and my community. “_ Clear long-term benefits of exa-cel demonstrated in CLIMB SCD-121 The data from CLIMB SCD-121 demonstrates the substantial, transformational and consistent benefit of exa-cel for SCD patients. At baseline, these patients (PES, d120, n=29) were experiencing a mean 3.9 VOCs per year, 2.7 hospitalisations per year, and a mean of 17.4 inpatient hospitalisation days for severe VOCs per year. Following treatment with exa-cel, 96.6% of patients achieved 12 months free of VOCs, with 100% achieving 12 months free of hospitalisation, with patients VOC-free for up to 43.6 months at the time of the d120 data cut (29). 

Furthermore, we note that 27/29 patients in the PES, (follow-up of 17.8 - 48.1 months after exa-cel infusion) remain VOC free, a substantially clinically meaningful improvement from the rates reported at baseline. 

Pain 

As discussed at the previous committee meeting, a small number of patients do experience acute pain after exa-cel infusion. As discussed, these events are not VOCs, and do not represent treatment failure or lack of response to exa-cel. It is important to remember that the VOC definition as per CLIMB SCD121 protocol was ‘acute pain needing attendance at hospital for opiates/iv NSAIDs, ACS, splenic sequestration or priapism’ (29). This broad definition of acute pain will inevitably include patients who are experiencing acute pain not related to vaso-occlusion. Post-transplant acute pain events (which would be classified as VOCs if trial criteria were used) are observed in the post allo-transplant context, even in patients with 100% chimerism (i.e. only non-sickle red cells). This is more marked in patients with a history of chronic pain and hyperalgesia. Among patients with SCD who undergo HSCT, 1 in 5 patients continue to experience acute pain events during the 12 months post-HSCT period (30). We go into further detail on post-HSCT findings in the relevant sub-section. 

Of the small number of patients who experienced these acute pain events after exa-cel, none needed hospitalisation (29). There were no episodes of ACS (which is the leading cause of death, responsible for up to 25% of SCD-related deaths) and no priapism or splenic sequestration. When the clinical details of the patients who experienced acute pain post exa-cel are reviewed in detail, it becomes apparent that they all had chronic pain and had reasons other than vaso-occlusion for their pain. This point is substantiated in the section relating to benefits being sustained over a very long period. Other benefits of exa-cel 

While VOCs have been used as a primary endpoint in the study, they do not capture the systemic impact that exa-cel mechanism of action has on the pathophysiology of SCD. The rapid and consistent increase in fetal haemoglobin (HbF) not only prevents vaso-occlusion but also reduces haemolysis and resolves anaemia and consequently will remove the risk of acute and long-term complications of haemolysis. This is substantiated by the CLIMB SCD-121 clinical results showing a rapid and persistent resolution of anaemia (mean Hb >13.0g/dl from month 12) and reduction in haemolysis: Results presented at ASH 2023 showed that: 

1. **Lactate dehydrogenase:** mean levels normalised by Month 9 and were sustained at normal levels thereafter. Elevated LDH as a haemolytic marker has been independently associated with increased morbidity and mortality in SCD (31, 32) 2. **Haptoglobin:** all patients had increases in haptoglobin to detectable levels after Month 6, which sustained over time, consistent with resolution of intravascular haemolysis. 3. **Absolute reticulocyte count:** mean improvement from elevated levels at baseline, with reduction maintained over time, consistent with improvement in haemolysis post exa-cel

All of these improvements were durable, with data for 30 patients at month 24, and range of follow-up in the PES from 17.8 months to 48.1 months (29). This normalisation of haemolysis, while shown via surrogate markers, demonstrate the profound effect of exa-cel on addressing the underlying pathophysiology of SCD. Development of new complications is prevented. Existing complications will be halted or reversed by - prevention of vaso occlusion and maintenance of high HbF. As described in the CS, exa-cel’s mechanism of action results in an increase in HbF levels. Increases in HbF level ameliorate the clinical manifestation of SCD. Support for this comes from the experience of patients with hereditary persistence of fetal haemoglobin (HPFH), a naturally occurring variation that causes continued persistence of HbF into adulthood (33, 34). Patients with compound heterozygosity for SCD and HPFH experience little or no SCD symptoms, leading to a normal life expectancy, and this is particularly true for those who maintain HbF levels above 20% (34-36). In CLIMB SCD-121, a mean HbF % of 40% was achieved by Month 6, and maintained at this level thereafter, well above the level shown to result in little or no SCD symptoms. Exa-cel therefore has a positive impact on all aspects of SCD: reversing anaemia, haemolysis and vaso-occlusion and stopping crisis due to vasoocclusion (VOCs). A key factor in eligibility for treatment with exa-cel is the individual patients’ fitness to safely undergo myeloablative conditioning with busulfan. As such, while patients treated with exa-cel in CLIMB SCD121 had severe SCD (i.e. were experiencing recurrent VOCs at baseline), they will not have developed significant, irreversible, complications as this would render them ineligible for myeloablative conditioning. In the real-world patients will be treated in the ‘clinical window’ after they have developed severe, recurrent VOC but before they have developed severe organ damage, ensuring they are able to return to near-normality after exa-cel treatment. Furthermore, all cases will require approval by the National Haemoglobinopathy Panel which will confirm that all patients meet the eligibility criteria set out in the SmPC including fitness to undergo conditioning. Furthermore, there is evidence from treatment with hydroxycarbamide and transfusion that increasing the HbF and reducing the red cells ability to sickle reduces the development of complications and reverses the severity of complications (37, 38). In addition the contrast between asymptomatic patients with co-inheritance of HbS and genes that cause pancellular increases in HbF (HPFH) and symptomatic patients suggest that, if it were possible to induce high HbF levels in most sickle erythrocytes and if this could be done before organ damage occurs, one might expect the disease to be cured (36). Therefore, the literature supports the view that the sustained high levels of HbF will prevent the development of any new disease-related complications, and halt or reverse the progression of any existing disease-related complications. Post-HSCT outcomes in SCD support the return to full or near-full health The substantial body of evidence gathered in HSCT, the other curative therapy for SCD, indicates that once the sickle phenotype is reversed, there is no recurrent haemolysis, and therefore no further disease-related complications occur. - Precedent supports exa cel qualifying for this criterion 

We also note precedent from HST15, where ‘ _the committee was uncertain about whether most of the people who would have onasemonogene abeparvovec would be considered to have a ‘normal or near normal-health’. But believed that a proportion might’,_ with this consideration supporting an ultimate decision to apply the non-reference discount rate in HST15. 

_3.  The benefits are likely to be sustained over a very long period_ 

As a CRISPR technology, there is no biological plausibility that exa-cel’s genetic edit will not be permanent. There is no known mechanism by which an edited haematopoietic stem cell (HSC) could convert back to a wild-type sequence. Edits to HSCs are permanent and durable. Support for this comes from the latest data from CLIMB SCD-121. The stable proportion of alleles with the intended genetic modification (allelic editing) in peripheral blood and in the CD34+ cells of the bone marrow over time are indicative of the durable engraftment of edited long-term HSCs and reflect the permanent nature of the intended edit (29). 

Acute pain events may occur infrequently after allo-SCT and have been reported at low event rates even in subjects with high donor chimerism, who have no cells capable of sickling as all haematopoiesis has been replaced by donor cells (41-43). The interpretation of pain events after HSCT for SCD is complicated, because post-HSCT pain in patients with SCD can be related to factors that may not represent VOC events. Pain events can be due to consequences of pre-existing disease such as exacerbation of chronic pain (e.g., related to pre-existing avascular necrosis), allodynia (pain elicited by normally innocuous, low threshold stimuli) and hyperalgesia (enhanced pain response to noxious stimuli) exacerbated by chronic opiate use. 

Clinical experts have stated the reasons for the acute pain events seen after exa-cel in a small number of patients is likely to be similar (5). These events were predominantly in the first year following treatment with exa-cel. Pain, and acute pain events are complex, multifactorial issues in SCD. There is no evidence of microvascular occlusion-related VOC. All the VOCs observed are in patients with chronic pain, and so are not expected to be related to additional VOC complications. 

As explained by the clinical expert at committee ‘ _if fetal haemoglobin is maintained at around 40% across every red blood cell, this would be expected to stop the process of vaso-occlusion, but it would not necessarily stop all acute pain events, which may fall under the definition of VOC_ ’. **==> picture [429 x 193] intentionally omitted <==**

It is clear from this that despite experiencing acute pain events, exa-cel is providing a durable, stable, benefit, that allow rapid recovery from complications relating to co-morbidities, that would otherwise not be possible in patients with SCD. 

Clinical expert feedback obtained as part of this appraisal further supports the expected long-term benefits of exa-cel. It was agreed that clinical experts would like to observe stable HbF levels for at least another 12 months (24 months in total) with at least 10 patients to be confident that exa-cel is providing a sustained treatment effect (5). With additional data available since those discussions, at the D120 data cut there are a total of 15 patients with 24 months of data, with a mean HbF % of 42.2% in those patients, satisfying the required threshold for clinical experts to believe that exa-cel is providing a sustained benefit. 

Vertex robustly defend the duration of follow-up in CLIMB SCD-121 as suitable for decision-making - supported by the aforementioned regulatory approvals - and note the overwhelming efficacy of exacel, with 29 of 30 patients in the PES achieving VF12. However, to address remaining uncertainty, Vertex re-iterates a commitment to working in partnership with NICE, as we are currently doing in TDT, to agree a managed access agreement that meets the committee’s requirements. 

## Conclusion – non-reference discount rate 

In conclusion, 

- SCD has a substantial, daily impact on patients’ & caregivers’ QoL, and age at death for severe SCD patients is in the 40s, constituting a reduction of several decades relative to the general population. 

- Treatment with exa-cel has a transformational impact on outcomes, with no new complications related to SCD expected, and current complications likely to be halted or even reversed, as supported by evidence from HSCT in SCD. 

- Genetic editing with exa-cel results in a permanent and durable effect, supported by stable HbF %, and allelic editing in patients.

The EAG has only provided a table with hard coded percentage values in their model, which it claims estimates the “ _cumulative lifetime incidence_ [i.e., prevalence]” of “ _chronic complications over the course of the model or equivalent_ .” To follow the logic of the EAG’s argument, this suggests that peak point prevalence in the modelled SoC population is expected at roughly 43.5 years of age (i.e., mean survival, calculated as baseline age plus the predicted mean additional life years of SoC patients, which is 22.36 based on the EAG’s statements). However, in the EAG’s model, peak point prevalence of chronic complications in the SoC cohort occurs at roughly 25-27 years of age (see Figure 3 – note the OS line in the graph is the overall survival of the SoC cohort over time). This contrasts with Brousse et al., who demonstrated that the rate of development of chronic complications continued to increase past age 40 (see Table 3 in Brousse et al.). The predicted peak point prevalence of chronic complications in the EAG’s model is thus clinically unrealistic. **The EAG’s approach to calculating withdrawal prior to treatment with exa-cel is overly complex and double-counts the costs and outcomes of withdrawal prior to treatment with exa-cel** 

Vertex maintains its position 

and, therefore, that the cost uplift applied by Vertex appropriately captures the expected risks of withdrawal within the UK target population. Nonetheless, Vertex recognises the committee’s preferred assumption regarding this issue and has thus maintained model functionality to consider the additional costs and health outcomes of treatment withdrawal by means of a scenario. The scenario is implemented using the same approach used by the York EAG for the TDT model, with costs and outcomes weighted in a secondary table of results. 

Vertex does however note concern with the EAG’s approach to calculating the economic outcomes associated with patients who do not go on to receive exa-cel. The approach taken by the EAG seems to imply that patients only withdraw from the procedure for two reasons: inadequate apheresis or low manufacturing yield. The proportions of these patients are then used to inflate the costs of exa-cel and reduce its efficacy. Withdrawal prior to receiving exa-cel and exa-cel’s actual efficacy ought to be modelled as separate issues. This is discussed in in detail in Point 6 of this document. In addition to the fact that the methodology used by the EAG to estimate these proportions is highly ambiguous, Vertex considers the EAG’s interpretation of the reasons for treatment withdrawal as most critical.

## **Exagamglogene autotemcel for treating sickle cell disease [ID4016]** 

## **Draft guidance comments form** 

## **Consultation on the draft guidance document – deadline for comments** 5pm on 11 April 2024. Please submit via NICE Docs. 

Modelling outcomes of patients who do not receive exa-cel infusion 

The reasons that a patient may proceed to cell collection but not to exa-cel infusion are related to the nature of SCD rather than the treatment they received. Many were clinical trial related, and all are likely to be seen less outside of the clinical trial context. The proportion of patients not proceeding to treatment following their initial apheresis is higher in this patient population, compared to others, such as those patients undergoing CAR-T. This is partly due to the nature of their condition, as patients with SCD have challenges with collecting adequate stem cells during apheresis, and experience discrimination in the healthcare system. Depriving patients of treatment with exa-cel because of the characteristics of their disease would be adding to the already significant and systemic health inequalities experienced by this patient group (48). 

Some of the reasons for withdrawal were clinical trial related due to the experimental nature of the treatment such as withdrawing consent, and this is unlikely to be the case now that exa-cel is no longer an investigational therapy and is approved by regulators. In CLIMB SCD-121, 6 patients discontinued due to inadequate cell collection following apheresis (not adverse event related) which is related to the nature of sickle-cell disease (29). Several SCD related problems make collecting adequate cells more challenging, due to factors including chronic haemolysis, inflammation and hydroxyurea use which is myelosuppressive and toxic to stem cells. In addition, granulocyte colony stimulating factor (G-CSF), the most commonly used mobilising agent can induce severe SCD complications and is therefore not used in SCD patients making cell-collection even more challenging (49). 

It is therefore not equitable or reasonable to include the outcomes of the patients who do not receive exa-cel infusion in the exa-cel arm of the model, as this artificially dilutes the demonstrated efficacy of the therapy and may result in preventing approval of a much-needed therapy for this underserved population. 

## Modelling costs of patients who do not receive exa-cel infusion 

Via the commercial discussions with NHS England and the treatment centres, 

It 

would be unreasonable for the committee not to take a pragmatic approach to considering the exclusion of treatment effects for those patients that withdraw before infusion, thereby widening health inequity in this population. 

The pre-treatment cost of patients who withdraw during pre-transplant is accounted for via a cost uplift in the model. Specifically, the pre-transplant costs of patients who withdraw are added to the pre-transplant costs in the first cycle of the model. This cost uplift adds an additional to the pre-transplant costs in the exa-cel arm of the model. 

We strongly believe that our proposed approach of removing the outcomes of patients who do not receive exa-cel infusion from the exa-cel arm of the model, as well as the steps we have taken to reduce financial risk for the NHS, should be considered and accepted by committee. 

In addition, there is considerable uncertainty about whether the proportion of patients who have cell collection, but do not go on to exa-cel treatment would be the same in clinical practice as in CLIMB SCD-121 (29). Along with increasing knowledge and expertise in apheresis, and support that will be provided to centres the risk of withdrawal prior to receiving exa-cel will be reduced in clinical practice. In recognition of this uncertainty, we present a scenario where of patients withdraw during the mobilisation period (i.e. do not incur exa-cel treatment costs for patients who do not

|**7**||**Definition of baseline VOCs**<br>**Vertex strongly believes that all VOCs that require healthcare attendance should be**<br>**accounted for in the model. All VOCs are related to SCD complications, and result in a**<br>**reduction in QoL. Further, issues with VOCs definitions in baseline vs follow up periods are**<br>**alleviated by the new model structure.**<br>VOCs cause ischaemic tissue damage and inflammation, resulting in debilitating pain often requiring<br>healthcare resource utilisation, and are directly linked to end-organ damage, direct healthcare costs<br>and early mortality. There is no biological difference between a VOC requiring in-patient<br>hospitalisation, and a VOC requiring attendance in a day unit or emergency department. The<br>decision to admit to hospital will depend on local resources (e.g. whether a day unit is available),<br>patient factors (social support, caregiver responsibilities), patient prior experience and patient and<br>clinician preference. Therefore, the impact of VOCs on complications, mortality, quality of life and<br>disease burden applies to all hospital attendances. VOCs requiring hospital attendance, not just<br>those related to in-patient hospitalisation have an impact on quality of life, healthcare resource<br>utilisation and long-term outcomes and should be included in the economic model. As described in<br>our response to the non-reference discount rate issue, SCD has a substantial, and daily, impact on<br>patients, with patient experts struggling to remember a day without pain.<br>Hospitalisation is related to multiple factors<br>Whether a patient is admitted to hospital is due to many factors, for example if day units are available<br>patients will prefer to use these to avoid hospital in-patient stays and where specialist services are<br>not available, patients may be admitted to hospital unnecessarily.<br>The “No-One’s Listening” report highlighted that many patients avoid being admitted to hospital due<br>to fear of substandard care, and prefer not to be admitted to hospital following attendance at an<br>accident and emergency department (22). ## **Figure 5: Relationship between VOCs and requirement for hospitalisation** 

**==> picture [363 x 266] intentionally omitted <==**

The SWAY study found that patients reporting a higher number of VOCs (irrespective of whether these required hospitalisation) in the 12 months prior to survey completion were significantly more likely to report a high impact of SCD on all aspects of daily life, schooling, and emotional wellbeing (4). 

In summary patients with severe SCD suffer from VOCs, that often do not end up with in-patient hospitalisation, for a number of reasons including distrust of the healthcare system., All VOCs that require healthcare attendance impact a patient in terms of both QoL and disease-related complications and impose a significant disease burden. Therefore, all VOCs should be accounted for in the economic model. 

## **The updated model estimates mortality and complications independent of VOC rate** 

The committee noted inconsistencies in the baseline definition of VOCs. Vertex believe that these issues are now addressed based on several changes in the model and from perusing the sources of the data used to estimate mortality and complications. 

The discrepancy between the definition of the model baseline VOC and the calculation of mortality and complications is alleviated since mortality and complications are modelled independently of VOC rate in the updated model. Moreover, all data used to model mortality and complications aligns with the VOC definition applied in the model and CLIMB SCD-121.

Finally, the EAG made adjustments to the patient denominators in Brousse to adjust for presence of patients who had received curative therapies. Again, this incorporates strong assumptions regarding the relative follow-up times of patients in the Brousse cohort who did versus did not receive curative treatment. The impact of these adjustments is unclear. 

Despite these limitations, Vertex presents the committee’s preferred approach as a co-base case, using Brousse, for calculating chronic complications in our updated. This is primarily because the rate of complications is derived from the more severe cohort in Brousse and thus should generate similar results to those when using VOCs as a predictor. However, Vertex present data on complications from Udeze et al (2023) as a preferred co-base case. These data provide an alternative and more complete source for the relevant population, based on UK data, and should therefore be considered by committee. 

**Vertex acknowledges the committee’s preference to model complications unconditional on VOC rates** Notwithstanding the aforementioned reservations, Vertex understands that the committee would prefer to model complication rates independent of VOC frequency. Therefore, Vertex has adapted the version of the model submitted at technical engagement to calculate complication rates unconditional on VOC frequency. Vertex has implemented these changes using a different approach to the EAG, due to the calculation issues identified by Vertex in the model version shared by the EAG previously (discussed in detail in Point 4 of this response document and the Appendix). We have tabulated the point prevalence of chronic complications at 22.36 follow-up years based on the rates predicted by Brousse et al. compared to the EAG model and the updated Vertex model, as per Equation 2, in Table 5. We discuss the strengths of preferring Udeze et al (2023) and present a comparison of the expected chronic complications over time, between the updated Vertex model and the amended EAG model. **Vertex present Udeze et al (2023) as a preferred co-base case** As noted above, Vertex has added an additional co-base case as our preferred source for modelling complications, using complication data from Udeze et al (2023) (7). Vertex believes that this source is more robust than Brousse for several reasons. Firstly, Brousse et al. does not report data for six of the complications applied in the model. In contrast, Udeze et al (2023) report data for all complications applied in the model. Secondly, incidence of complications in Udeze et al. is reported as an incidence rate per 100 person-years, and it is thus not reliant on strong assumptions regarding duration of follow-up. However, this is required when using data from Brousse et al. because average duration of follow-up is not reported. Lastly, the definition and study criteria of a patient’s VOC rate in Udeze et al (2023) aligns with CLIMB SCD-121, thus alleviating point 3.10 in ACD. In Table 6 we compare the prevalence observed in patients from Udeze et al (2023) at baseline, indexed according to ages 12-35 and >36, with the predicted period prevalence of our updated model and the EAG model. The predicted period prevalence is calculated in each model as an average within two age groups. For the predicted period prevalence in ages 12-35, we take the average prevalence in the model from baseline age to age 35. For the predicted period prevalence in ages >36, we take the average prevalence in the model from ages >35 to age 86. We use a maximum age of 86 to align with the maximum age observed in the severe SCD cohort from Udeze et al (2023). 

Vertex reiterates that, given the evidence presented in Table 6, the corrections, applied by Vertex in the updated model, lead to more valid predictions that follow clinical reality more closely.

## **Utility of SoC patients at baseline and evolution over time** 

**As requested by the committee, Vertex provides a longitudinal view of how the net utility of SoC patients in the model changes over time, to ensure it is clear that patients experience a severe impact on their quality of life, especially as they grow older. Vertex has also implemented additional scenarios to evaluate the uncertainty related to baseline utility. We also include additional post-hoc analysis of the trial utility data, indicating significant ceiling effects in the baseline HRQoL trial data.** 

At the point when patients receive exa-cel they will have relatively fewer complications; however, it is clear from the literature that without treatment, their QoL would continue to deteriorate as they grow older and accumulate further co-morbidities. The overwhelming body of evidence looking at all PROs from multiple studies in SCD including EQ-5D shows that SCD has a significant negative impact on quality of life. Therefore, the committee requested additional information on utility values over time in the SoC arm in the model. 

As patients in the SoC arm age in the model, they develop comorbidities which results in added disutility to the baseline SoC utility value. Vertex provides a longitudinal view of how the net utility of SoC patients evolves over time in Table 7. Although the baseline utility starts at 0.81 for the cohort of CLIMB SCD-121 patients (29), this decreases substantially over time because of the comorbidities incurred and the associated utility decrements. Vertex emphasises that the predicted utility values

## **Exagamglogene autotemcel for treating sickle cell disease [ID4016]** 

## **Draft guidance comments form** 

## **Consultation on the draft guidance document – deadline for comments** 5pm on 11 April 2024. Please submit via NICE Docs. 

The committee has raised concerns about using the 0.11 mean change from baseline value and the resulting 0.92 utility value following exa-cel treatment in the model. The committee prefers using a health state utility value of 0.88 in the model for the exa-cel ‘functionally cured’ population. **The committee’s preferred utility value following exa-cel treatment does not reflect the QoL gains associated with functional cure in severe SCD populations** 

As shown in Table 3, exa-cel resulted in improvements above the minimal clinically important difference, across all QoL measures, irrespective of whether these measured general QoL (EQ-5D), pain (NRS Pain Scale), or SCD-specific QoL (ASCQ-Me). The magnitude of post-treatment gains in QoL observed in the 24-month follow-up period for patients treated with exa-cel is supported by similar observations in several studies, presented in Jiao et al (2022) (56). For instance, in patients who received HSCT, Jiao et al. (2022) report significant gains in utility, especially when patients do not experience post-treatment related complications, such as graft failure or GVHD (56). O’Brien et al (2009) reports a baseline utility of 0.70 for severe SCD patients pre-HSCT (20). Post-HSCT, these patients without graft-failure report an average utility value of 0.95. Vertex would like to highlight that, similarly, no patients in CLIMB SCD-121 experienced graft failure or GVHD (29). Due to the evidence found in the supporting literature, and the utility gain of reported in the post-hoc subgroup utility analysis, Vertex believe that using a utility gain value 0.11 is, in fact, conservative. However, because the committee has noted uncertainty in the model’s baseline utility value for severe SCD patients (already addressed in Point 9) and the utility value following treatment with exa-cel, we provide additional scenarios to address these concerns. 

**Post-hoc analysis of trial utility data indicates a significant ceiling effect present in CLIMB SCD-121 baseline utility values** Post-hoc analysis of the utility data also shows that there are significant ceiling effects in the baseline utility values of several patients, with of patients in the PES having EQ-5D scores greater than one at baseline. As explained in Point 2, we believe that this is because the EQ-5D fails to fully capture the QoL impact of SCD, as it is unrealistic for someone to be willing to trade off perfect health for a burdensome transplant with an experimental treatment. To alleviate these ceiling effects, Vertex has conducted a post-hoc subgroup analysis of the CLIMB SCD-121 utility data (55), to derive an alternative utility gain value post-treatment with exa-cel. This analysis excludes patients with a utility score of 1 at baseline, aged ≥18 and ≤35 years at screening. A comparison of the base case and the post-hoc utility value scenario are shown in Table 9. Given the results of the post-hoc analysis, Vertex believes that using a utility gain of 0.11 post-treatment with exa-cel is, in fact, conversative. Again, Vertex strongly emphasise that the committee’s preferred utility value following exa-cel treatment does not reflect the QoL gains associated with functional cure in severe SCD populations. 

The post-hoc subgroup analysis shows a consistent gain of , at month 24 in the subgroup of patients who did not have a perfect utility score of 1 at baseline. This gain is largely consistent throughout the follow-up period. From baseline (n = 15), at month 12 (n = 15), patients reported an average utility gain of without any patients lost to follow-up. Patients only ever experience a lower utility gain ) at month 3 of follow-up. The utility gain reported at month 24 is also not affected by sample bias, since only 2 patients are lost to follow-up throughout the follow-up period. The scenario results, using the alternative post-hoc utility value of , are provided in Table 11.

The expected cumulative incidences of chronic complications for severe SCD patients are relatively high, even when these estimates are derived from the rates found in Brousse et al (2023) (which is the EAG’s preferred source) (9). Therefore, to further expand on the issues found in the EAG’s calculations for chronic complications, we perform supplementary external validation by comparing the expected lifetime prevalence of chronic complications of severe SCD patients based on the rates found in Brousse et al (2023) to the predicted total cumulative incidence of the EAG’s and updated Vertex’s models respectively. 

To perform this comparison, we extrapolate the rates from Brousse et al (2023) over a 79-year horizon. We use the Brousse et al (2023) rates as calculated by the EAG. The 7-year rates were transformed to a year-period probability and then extrapolated using the standard equation 𝑝𝑡 = 1 − 𝑒[𝑟𝑡] where 𝑡 is the modelled time horizon, i.e., 79 years. As per Equation 1, Vertex assumes that the EAG’s incidence term is simply 𝑐ycl𝑒 𝑖ncidenc𝑒𝑡 . This is a reasonable assumption since we are only removing the mortality adjustment from the EAG’s equation in order to

Overall, the EAG’s modelled cumulative incidence of chronic complications when unadjusted for mortality deviates significantly from the expected lifetime prevalence estimated from rates found in the Brousse et al (2023) (also unadjusted for mortality). The EAG’s calculations are also clearly unreliable since total cumulative incidence can exceed 100%. Even when the EAG’s approach is adjusted for mortality, the cumulative incidence for Avascular necrosis exceeds 100%. When assuming a fixed population (i.e., a population with a constant population size over time), it is intuitive to recognise that incidence of a chronic complication ought to tend towards 0 as the prevalence of the chronic complication tends to increase. In other words, if there is 100% prevalence of a chronic disease within a fixed population, there should be no new incidence once the point of 100% prevalence is reached. Hence, over time, total cumulative incidence should be bounded at a maximum of 100%. 

The key issue with the EAG’s calculations for chronic complications is that the interaction between incidence and point prevalence is not appropriately counted before being adjusted for mortality. The EAG’s function used to calculate the proportion of alive SOC patients with chronic complications is shown in Equation 1.

Using the approach illustrated in Equation 2, the function is able to separate the proportion of patients who are still at risk of developing the chronic complication from the proportion of patients who have already developed the chronic complication. The per cycle point prevalence is then applied to the proportion of patients who are alive in each model cycle, i.e., the per cycle point prevalence is adjusted for natural or primary disease mortality. This is a standard approach to modelling chronic complications assumed to not contribute to any excess mortality from secondary disease (thus aligning with the committee’s preferred assumption, that complications do not directly contribute to the model’s mortality). 

## **Vertex has added an alternative approach to including the health outcomes and costs of treatment withdrawal** 

Vertex’s scenario to include the health outcomes of treatment withdrawal is implemented via a simple decision tree. It uses the QALY outcomes of both SoC and exa-cel modelled cohorts and the costs pre-treatment red blood cell transfusions (RBCTs) and pre- and post-mobilisation. 

To include the health outcomes of withdrawal, the total QALYs of the SoC cohort is weighted by the proportion of patients who withdrawal in the exa-cel cohort. Then, the total QALYs of the exa-cel arm are weighted by the proportion of patients who did not withdrawal. The sum of these weighted QALYs is then used as the total reweighted QALYs for all exa-cel patients. The sum of total costs of the SoC cohort, costs of pre-mobilisation, mobilisation, and pre-treatment RBCTs is weighted by the proportion of patients who withdrawal. The total costs of the exa-cel cohort are then reweighted by the proportion of patients who did not withdrawal. The sum of these two weighted costs is then used as the total reweighted costs for all exa-cel patients. 

The model does have the functionality to also include the associated with exa-cel in addition to the costs of premobilisation, mobilisation, and pre-treatment RBCTs, and the health outcomes of withdrawal. In this scenario, the decision tree is as described in the preceding paragraph, but also includes the cost of exa-cel in the total costs reweighting. 

To calculate the costs of withdrawal including the cost of exa-cel, the sum of total costs of the SoC cohort, costs of pre-mobilisation, mobilisation, pre-treatment RBCTs, and the cost of exa-cel is weighted by the proportion of patients who withdrawal. The total costs of the exa-cel cohort are then weighted by the proportion of patients who did not withdrawal. The sum of these two weighted costs is then used as the total reweighted costs for all exa-cel patients. QALY outcomes are reweighted as described in the preceding paragraphs. 

## **Vertex has also identified a minor input error in the latest EAG model version** 

Vertex identified an input error in the `Cost inputs` sheet. Specifically, the plerixafor cost per unit was incorrectly changed to £4,881. The correct value, which was inputted in the technical engagement model version, is £4,880. Albeit a very small difference, this did have a minor effect on the ICER.

## _**B.3.8 Managed access proposal – updated following ACM1**_ 

Vertex proposes that a managed access agreement within the Innovative Medicines Fund would be appropriate for exa-cel given the highly innovative nature of the therapy, its potential to address unmet need and significant clinical benefits (see sections see sections B.2.1, B.3.6 and B.3.12.1), and following the NICE committee’s request for data collection. 

The uncertainties described in Table 53 could be addressed through a period of managed access. At present, the main source of clinical evidence is the index CLIMB SCD-121 study in SCD patients; it is anticipated that supportive long-term data will primarily come from the corresponding long-term extension study for consenting patients treated with exa-cel (CLIMB-131), and a post-authorisation safety study (PASS) utilising the European Society for Blood and Marrow Transplantation (EBMT) registry. UK sites are included within the PASS protocol. 

The post-committee meeting outputs and subsequent discussions with the NICE Managed Access team have recognised the evidence uncertainties already captured in our proposal that can be fully or partially resolved through managed access. Vertex has now updated the managed access proposal in order to address additional uncertainties highlighted by the committee; namely around treatment withdrawal pre-infusion, generalisability of the trial population age to the UK, health-related quality of life (HRQoL) and disease complications for current standard of care. Additionally, Vertex has also proposed data collection under a managed access agreement for the maximum 5 year period to ensure an optimally sized cohort with a total of 8-10 years’ follow-up (from commencement of CLIMB-131), to provide robust assurances of treatment durability for healthcare providers and payers. 

The non-reference discount rate is a major driver of cost-effectiveness, and for this to be accepted at the end of the MAA period durability of effect and ability to return patients to a near-normal health state would apply. Following the first committee meeting, clinical experts stated that if data were collected out to 3 years post-infusion showing sustained, increased levels of Hb, HbF and F-cells (demonstrating pancellular distribution of HbF), 



<!-- page 48 -->

then the risk of relapse would be negligible. Therefore, we propose this is the most important outcome to consider when ensuring future cost-effectiveness. 

A summary of all stated uncertainties, with proposed data sources, is shown in Table 53.

## _**B.3.8.1. Proposed Data Sources to gather evidence for Managed Access Agreement**_ 

It is anticipated that the CLIMB SCD-121 and CLIMB-131 studies will fulfil most of the data gap requirements, with the latter as the main source of supportive long-term outcomes data, and further gaps to be filled with data from the PASS EBMT registry. 

## _**CLIMB-131**_ 

CLIMB-131 is an ongoing, multi-site, open-label, rollover study designed to evaluate the long-term safety and efficacy of exa-cel in patients who received exa-cel in a parent study (CLIMB SCD-121 for SCD) for a total follow-up of 15 years after exa-cel infusion. Consenting patients who completed or discontinued the parent study after exa-cel infusion were asked to participate. Applicable regulatory guidelines on follow-up of patients administered with gene therapy products (EMEA/CHMP/GTWP/60436/2007 and FDA Guidance for Industry on Gene Therapy Clinical Trials – Observing Subjects for Delayed Adverse Events) were used to define the 15-year follow-up period. 

Data from this trial will be reported periodically, as per timelines indicated in Table 54.

## _**PASS utilising EBMT registry**_ 

The EBMT was established in the 1970s and is an established data source on allo-SCT or cellular infusion therapy procedures. The EBMT registry currently receives data from approximately 80% of European transplant centres and is the principal source of transplant data to conduct retrospective clinical studies, epidemiological trends, and feasibility studies to design prospective clinical studies, in the field of oncology. In more recent years, the EBMT registry has been qualified by the European Medical Agency (EMA) as a suitable platform for collection of data for post-authorisation studies (160). 



<!-- page 52 -->

The EBMT registry is the proposed data source in UK, France, Germany, and Italy for Vertex’s regulatory mandated PASS in which exa-cel treated patients will be followed for a maximum period of 15 years. As part of the PASS, similar data will also be collected for patients in the United States via the Center for International Blood and Marrow Transplant Research (CIBMTR) Registry. Vertex considers that the EBMT registry would be a relevant data source to gather evidence on effectiveness and safety of exa-cel in the realworld setting, given its primary data collection capabilities and availability of secondary data to support long-term follow-up studies. Study variables to be collected for the PASS are presented in Table 55. The PASS protocol synopsis has also been provided to NICE.

## _**Other potential sources**_ 

Data on treatment withdrawals pre-infusion will be available from Vertex Connects™, a secure order management portal used to facilitate steps throughout the exa-cel order management process for authorised treatment centre (ATC) staff. The system will track all the constituent actions required for each step of the order process following patient identification and evaluation: pre-mobilisation; mobilisation & collection of cells; drug product manufacturing and quality; conditioning, administration and engraftment. Anonymised metrics on pre-infusion patient withdrawals will be available via aggregate summary reports. 

Vertex is currently exploring the feasibility of conducting a literature review to derive data inputs for current standard of care in SCD. Our main evidence submission presented data from an observational, retrospective database study we conducted to understand the clinical and economic burden of SCD in UK patients with characteristics similar to those eligible to receive exa-cel. The data collection period for this study could be extended to capture contemporary data on VOC burden, disease complication rates and mortality. Vertex can provide the study protocol to inform consideration of the feasibility of this approach. 

## _**B.3.8.2. Data Collection**_ 

Long-term data on the UK patients treated with exa-cel following MHRA approval will be collected by EBMT for the PASS. Data will be collected on SCD patients ≥12 years of age and treated with exa-cel at any of the ATCs in the UK. Vertex acknowledges that the number of exa-cel treated patients from the UK included in the PASS will depend on commercial uptake, and availability of patients’ informed consent to share their data for research purposes. The PASS will enrol a minimum of 100 exa-cel SCD patients overall. All consenting global patients, taking into account sample size considerations, will be entered into the study for approximately the first 3 years post-approval and will be followed for 15 years. Long-term data on consenting exa-cel treated patients will also be collected 



<!-- page 54 -->

from CLIMB-131, a rollover follow-up extension of the pivotal trials in TDT and SCD patients.

EBMT will facilitate retrospective data collection for Vertex using standard existing registry forms such as Med-A and Med-B, and prospective data collection using a study-specific reporting form (Med-C) developed for the Vertex PASS in collaboration with EBMT investigators. Vertex anticipates that, based on expert opinion, a timeline of approximately 3 years’ data collection following recommendation into the IMF would be sufficient to address uncertainties stated by NICE. Clinical experts, when consulted, have indicated that sustained increases in Hb, HbF and F-cells (demonstrating pancellular distribution of HbF) after 3 years of exa-cel treatment, with sustained engraftment plus improved iron status, will mean patients are likely to maintain a VOC-free status and, in turn, less likely to encounter further disease complications and subsequent organ damage. With mean duration of follow-up of 22.4 months as of June 2023 for patients who have already transitioned to the CLIMB-131 follow-up study, the proposed 3 years of data collection in the managed access agreement would include data for most patients in CLIMB SCD-121 



<!-- page 59 -->

beyond 5 years post exa-cel infusion, for a total of 8-10 years of follow-up in this group of patients.

## _**B.3.8.3. Additional considerations that may impact feasibility of data collection**_ 

**Informed consent** – Lack of patient consent to give access to their data after treatment with exa-cel. 

**Follow up** – Patients will be routinely followed up by the transplant centres (as part of the transplant clinic for year 1 and the long-term effects monitoring clinics thereafter). These clinics are resourced for data collection for EBMT and this will be part of their routine care. Patients will also be followed up by their haemoglobinopathy team with respect to long term sickle cell complications. Haemoglobinopathy patients represent a non-malignant population, and therefore may perceive less of a clinical imperative to adhere to followup visits when compared with patients with a malignant disease. It will be essential that patients are well informed about the need for long term follow-up to ensure they attend the long-term effects monitoring clinics at the transplant centre. 

**Socioeconomic status** – Patients in England with SCD are disproportionately represented in ethnic minority groups and lower socioeconomic communities; thus, potential increased fluidity in population movement may also challenge adherence to follow-up. 

In order to mitigate these considerations, Vertex will produce supportive educational materials for patients that fully detail the treatment process and explain the importance of compliance with data collection in the post-treatment period.

## **Draft guidance comments form** 

**Consultation on the draft guidance document – deadline for comments** 5pm on 11 April 2024. Please submit via NICE Docs. 

received to this consultation, and from a survey jointly conducted by Anthony Nolan and the Sickle Cell Society from 13/12/2023 to 11/01/2024, during which we received 60 complete responses from patients and carers/family members. 

**Key message: Sickle cell is a lifelong and progressive condition. It is therefore very difficult to objectively measure QoL and compare it to healthy individuals. Sickle cell patients should not be penalised for this.** 

- 85% of people responding to our survey were either diagnosed through newborn screening, or in early childhood. 

- People living with severe sickle cell have never had what would be considered by most a “normal” life, having only known what it is like to live with regular pain crises, having to manage their illness as best they can with very limited treatment options at every stage of life. 

- We welcome the committee’s willingness to further consider the limitations of the EQ-5D score in this context. 

**Key message: People with sickle cell who would be eligible for exa-cel have a severely impacted life. We believe the criteria for the non-reference case discount rate has been met.** 

   - 82% of people responding to our survey said that sickle cell has either a negative impact or very negative impact on their quality of life. Sickle cell has a negative or very negative impact on their emotional health and wellbeing (79%), work and education (76%), and family and social life (70%). 

   - • Nearly half (46%) of people who responded to our survey had experienced over 8 crises in the last two years, and a further 36% had experienced 2-7 crises in the last two years. This is despite the vast majority being on a current standard of care treatment (67% on hydroxyurea, 52% on blood transfusions, 30% on “other” treatments). 

   - Crises are debilitating and disruptive, often requiring emergency inpatient treatment that interferes with daily life – in the last two years, a third of respondents had received emergency care 4 or more times due to a sickle cell crisis, an additional third of respondents had received emergency care at least 2 or 3 times. 

- In their own words, this is how living with sickle cell has impacted people’s lives: 

- Impact on family and social life 

_“The impact is wide ranging. As a result of SCD, I have kidney failure and am a transplant patient. I am now unable to work due to ill health. I have frequent breathlessness and fatigue periods and limited mobility and stamina. My whole family has to bear my limitations in mind which causes them worry and anxiety whenever I am unwell.”_

## **Exagamglogene autotemcel for treating sickle cell disease [ID4016]** 

## **Draft guidance comments form** 

## **Consultation on the draft guidance document – deadline for comments** 5pm on 11 April 2024. Please submit via NICE Docs. 

The impact of Sickle Cell Disease on the Black community is absolutely staggering. In England, Black people are over 80 times more likely to have Sickle Cell Disease compared to White people. Furthermore, the mortality rate for Sickle Cell patients in the UK is alarmingly high, with an estimated 1 in 16 individuals with Sickle Cell Disease dying before the age of 18. 

In my capacity as the Co-Founder and Chief Executive of the ACLT (African Caribbean Leukaemia Trust) and Chair of the NBTA (National BAME Transplant Alliance), I communicate with many Sickle Cell patients who struggle physically and mentally on a day-to-day basis living with the fear of an unplanned Sickle Crisis which occurs suddenly when under stress from infection, fever, and dehydration and can result in severe brain damage or a potential fatal outcome. 

The above statistics and narrative highlight the urgent need for effective treatments like the CRISPR gene editing therapy called Exa-cel (brand name Casvegy) to be made available to the Sickle Cell patients who can receive a stem cell transplant but have no matching donor and who predominantly are from the Black community. The NICE decision sadly mirrors the daily health inequalities faced by the African and Caribbean communities in the UK, which are well-documented such as Black people being more likely to experience poverty, discrimination, and barriers to accessing quality & healthcare across many well documented disorders. 

Sickle Cell Disease has been prominent in the UK for approx. a century and heavily concentrated since the arrival of the Windrush Generation. However, there has historically been (and continues today) highly unacceptable variation in healthcare service provision and lowering in standards of care towards these patients especially in light of the severe NHS funding costs in recent years. The standard and access of treatment options are extremely limited for Sickle Cell patients in comparison to other inherited conditions such as Cystic Fibrosis. 

The above facts are backed up by a report by the NHS Race and Health Observatory that found that Black people in the UK have a life expectancy that is up to four years shorter than their White counterparts. Furthermore, Black people are more likely to experience poor health outcomes across a range of conditions, including Sickle Cell Disease. 

This new CRISPR gene therapy offers a revolutionary approach to treating Sickle Cell Disease by addressing the root cause of the condition. By modifying the patient’s own stem cells to produce healthy foetal red blood cells, gene therapy has the potential to alleviate the painful symptoms and complications associated with Sickle Cell Disease. The recent US trials of Exa-cel (brand name Casvegy) show that over 94% of patients have not had a Sickle Cell crisis within 12 months shows the true efficacy of this CRISPR gene edit therapy. 

This innovative treatment can greatly improve the quality of life for those affected and reduce the financial burden on the National Health Service system in the long run, due to lower primary care costs (hospital admissions, blood transfusions, blood exchanges, pain relief, etc.) in comparison to other health disorders which have far fewer affected patients. It is crucial that NICE reconsiders its decision and ensures that gene editing therapy remains available to Sickle Cell patients in the UK, particularly those from the African and

I write to you as a mother, a sickle cell patient, a sister, daughter, aunty, friend, a sickle cell advocate and recently published author, who desperately asks for the reconsideration of this decision. The latter two titles have came with a self-proclaimed huge responsibility and determination to raise awareness, for this life threatening and altering condition that I continue- as well as many others- to suffer with on a daily basis. 

As a sickle cell sufferer with the SC type, it’s commonly thought to be ‘less severe or considered ‘milder’ than those suffering with sickle cell SS. 

I can personally assure you that there is nothing ‘mild’ about my condition. The amount of pain and suffering this condition brings is indescribable. In fact my condition deteriorated so bad post pregnancy, I developed a widespread ‘bone death’ condition called avascular necrosis. Which meant I required bilateral double hip replacements a year after my son was delivered by emergency c-section, which was considered to be bought on by a sickle cell crisis. 

My son was also born with abnormalities, which then meant he had his own additional care needs - a ventilated tracheostomy. Becoming a first time mum and then developing a degenerative bone death condition met with the most excruciating vilest pain, is an experience that no person should ever have to be faced with at all, especially soon after entering motherhood. 

On top of enduring this nightmare with my poorly baby in tow, I wasn’t believed by the health care system when I noticed soon after the right hip replacement was carried out, that it was done incorrectly. Subsequently, I was left for four years and three months to suffer until it was finally revised. Before this eventually happened, my quality of life was so poor, I literally felt suicidal had it not been for my son I would have surely went through with ending it all as the pain was truly unbearable. Either that or I even envisioned cutting my leg off to excuse me from the pain! Nothing I did or took helped ease the pain. I’d routinely dose my hip and leg in deep heat, take several baths as and when I could, sleep with hot water bottles in between my legs at night (which affected my skin). Sleep with various pillows. I could barely walk. I suffered immensely. Before I had each side of my hip replaced, I’d go either temporarily blind in the opposite eye and/or experience floaters with shadows. 

I struggled to care for my son, couldn’t walk let alone run after him. I couldn't sit crossed legs and join in the stay and play groups I still was determined to take him to so he didn’t miss out. As well as both sides of my hips being affected, I also have the same condition bilaterally in my shoulders. I am currently awaiting shoulder replacements. The pain is awful. Even something as simple as putting the seat belt on in the car is a painful experience, never mind ‘simply’ lifting my arm. Sickle cell suffers are living in agony in silence, we are not believed, our pain is often disregarded, or often assumed to be drug seekers even when we do try and seek some relief for the pain. 

It was really disheartening to learn about the treatment currently not being made available on the NHS, as this would have been literally life saving for people like me who are suffering with this dreadful condition. Sickle cell anaemia is the fastest growing genetic - condition in England, we deserve to have the opportunity of a decent quality of life just

## **Exagamglogene autotemcel for treating sickle cell disease [ID4016]** 

## **Draft guidance comments form** 

## **Consultation on the draft guidance document – deadline for comments** 5pm on 11 April 2024. Please submit via NICE Docs. 

This decision is a devastating blow to our community, which has long faced significant health inequalities, especially when it comes to sickle cell disease. Sickle cell disease is a genetic blood disease that predominantly affects individuals of African and Caribbean descent. In the UK, it is estimated that 1 in every 2,000 babies born are affected by sickle cell disease, with the majority being of Black African or Black Caribbean heritage. This chronic condition causes immense pain, organ damage, and a significantly reduced life expectancy. Shockingly, the average life expectancy for someone with sickle cell disease in the UK is just 40-60 years, compared to the national average of 81 years. The impact of sickle cell disease on the Black community is staggering. In England, Black people are over 80 times more likely to have sickle cell disease compared to White people. Furthermore, the mortality rate for sickle cell patients in the UK is alarmingly high, with an estimated 1 in 16 individuals with sickle cell disease dying before the age of 18. These statistics highlight the urgent need for effective treatments like the CRISPR gene editing therapy to be made available to the African and Caribbean community. The health inequalities faced by the African and Caribbean community in the UK are welldocumented. Black people are more likely to experience poverty, discrimination, and barriers to accessing quality healthcare. A report by the NHS Race and Health Observatory found that Black people in the UK have a life expectancy that is up to four years shorter than their White counterparts. Furthermore, Black people are more likely to experience poor health outcomes across a range of conditions, including sickle cell disease. Gene therapy offers a revolutionary approach to treating sickle cell disease by addressing the root cause of the condition. By modifying the patient’s own stem cells to produce healthy red blood cells, gene therapy has the potential to alleviate the painful symptoms and complications associated with sickle cell disease. This innovative treatment can greatly improve the quality of life for those affected and reduce the burden on the healthcare system in the long run. It is crucial that NICE reconsiders its decision and ensures that gene editing therapy remains available to sickle cell patients in the UK, particularly those from the African and Caribbean community who are disproportionately affected by this condition. Denying access to this potentially transformative treatment would be a significant setback in the fight against health inequalities and would leave our community without hope for a better future. Moreover, the decision to stop the availability of gene editing therapy for sickle cell patients sends a troubling message about the priorities of our healthcare system. It suggests that the lives and well-being of those affected by this condition, who are predominantly from the African and Caribbean community, are not valued as highly as they should be. This is unacceptable and goes against the principles of equality and fairness that should underpin our society. I urge NICE to reverse its decision and work towards making gene therapy for sickle cell disease more widely accessible. The African and Caribbean community in the UK deserves the same opportunities for improved health outcomes as any other group. By investing in and supporting this innovative treatment, we can take a significant step towards addressing the glaring health inequalities that have persisted for far too long.
