The fact that pharmaceutical companies are willing to invest millions in research for medication but not thousands for proper training and education speaks volumes to the sickle cell community. Sickle cell receives low and unfair equity as opposed to cystic fibrosis that receives up to 9 times more funding and education. The exposure to racism and discrimination is directly linked to poor health management as you realise, we are the sole authors of our care and health. 

•The impact of sickle cell on life expectancy and risk of mortality: The risk of mortality is extremely high in the sickle cell community because of the exposure to systemic racism, discrimination and ignorance. Because of the lack of equity and funding that goes into sickle cell patients, we are more exposed to premature deaths when we visit Accident & Emergency department. The lack of resources and education given at university stage for medical students perpetuates the ignorance shown in hospital. Our life expectancy has direct links to being exposed to sickle cell abuse and poor treatment. If that is combined with inadequate funding, that then becomes the perfect cocktail for a shortened life expectancy and a high rate of mortality.

## **Exagamglogene autotemcel for treating sickle cell disease [ID4016]** 

## **Draft guidance comments form** 

**Consultation on the draft guidance document – deadline for comments** 5pm on 11 April 2024. Please submit via NICE Docs. 

I carry the sickle cell trait and have sadly lost friends prematurely because of the disease. I am in the process of writing a book for children and young people to raise awareness about the devastating chronic condition because many of our children are suffering and isolated because of it. Sickle cell disease is a genetic blood disease that predominantly affects individuals of African and Caribbean descent. It causes immense pain, organ damage, and a significantly reduced life expectancy. Some children and young people do not reach their full potential at school because of the condition and may struggle to make friends. In the UK, it is estimated that 1 in every 2,000 babies born are affected by sickle cell disease, with the majority being of Black African or Black Caribbean heritage. Black people are more likely to experience poverty, discrimination, and barriers to accessing quality healthcare and the impact of sickle cell disease on our community is staggering. A report by the NHS Race and Health Observatory found that Black people in the UK have a life expectancy that is up to four years shorter than their White counterparts. Furthermore, the mortality rate for sickle cell patients in the UK is alarmingly high, with an estimated 1 in 16 individuals with sickle cell disease dying before the age of eighteen. These statistics highlight the urgent need for effective treatments like the CRISPR gene editing therapy to be made available to the African and Caribbean community. Gene therapy offers a revolutionary approach to treating sickle cell disease by addressing the root cause of the condition. By modifying the patient’s own stem cells to produce healthy red blood cells, gene therapy has the potential to alleviate the painful symptoms and complications associated with sickle cell disease. This innovative treatment can greatly improve the quality of life for those affected and reduce the burden on the healthcare system in the long run. The African and Caribbean community in the UK deserves the same opportunities for improved health outcomes as any other group. Accordingly, I urge NICE to reverse its decision and work towards making gene therapy more widely accessible and available to sickle cell patients in the UK. I thank you in anticipation of your assistance. Yours sincerely, 6.43 Dear NICE, As an employee in a job role that supports the African and Caribbean community, I am writing to express my deep concern and disappointment regarding the recent decision by the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) to potentially stop the availability of gene therapy for sickle cell patients in the United Kingdom. This decision is a devastating blow to our community, which has long faced significant health inequalities, especially when it comes to sickle cell disease.

## **Exagamglogene autotemcel for treating sickle cell disease [ID4016]** 

## **Draft guidance comments form** 

## **Consultation on the draft guidance document – deadline for comments** 5pm on 11 April 2024. Please submit via NICE Docs. 

Sickle cell disease is a genetic blood disease that predominantly affects individuals of African and Caribbean descent. In the UK, it is estimated that 1 in every 2,000 babies born are affected by sickle cell disease, with the majority being of Black African or Black Caribbean heritage. This chronic condition causes immense pain, organ damage, and a significantly reduced life expectancy. Shockingly, the average life expectancy for someone with sickle cell disease in the UK is just 40-60 years, compared to the national average of 81 years. The impact of sickle cell disease on the Black community is staggering. In England, Black people are over 80 times more likely to have sickle cell disease compared to White people. Furthermore, the mortality rate for sickle cell patients in the UK is alarmingly high, with an estimated 1 in 16 individuals with sickle cell disease dying before the age of 18. These statistics highlight the urgent need for effective treatments like the CRISPR gene editing therapy to be made available to the African and Caribbean community. The health inequalities faced by the African and Caribbean community in the UK are welldocumented. Black people are more likely to experience poverty, discrimination, and barriers to accessing quality healthcare. A report by the NHS Race and Health Observatory found that Black people in the UK have a life expectancy that is up to four years shorter than their White counterparts. Furthermore, Black people are more likely to experience poor health outcomes across a range of conditions, including sickle cell disease. Gene therapy offers a revolutionary approach to treating sickle cell disease by addressing the root cause of the condition. By modifying the patient’s own stem cells to produce healthy red blood cells, gene therapy has the potential to alleviate the painful symptoms and complications associated with sickle cell disease. This innovative treatment can greatly improve the quality of life for those affected and reduce the burden on the healthcare system in the long run. It is crucial that NICE reconsiders its decision and ensures that gene editing therapy remains available to sickle cell patients in the UK, particularly those from the African and Caribbean community who are disproportionately affected by this condition. Denying access to this potentially transformative treatment would be a significant setback in the fight against health inequalities and would leave our community without hope for a better future.

## **Exagamglogene autotemcel for treating sickle cell disease [ID4016]** 

## **Draft guidance comments form** 

**Consultation on the draft guidance document – deadline for comments** 5pm on 11 April 2024. Please submit via NICE Docs. 

I am writing to as a member of the African and Caribbean community. More importantly, I am writing as a parent of a SCD patient. I want to express my deep concern and disappointment regarding the recent decision by the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) to potentially stop the availability of gene therapy for sickle cell patients in the United Kingdom. This decision is a devastating blow to our community, which has long faced significant health inequalities, especially when it comes to sickle cell disease. Sickle cell disease is a genetic blood disease that predominantly affects individuals of African and Caribbean descent. In the UK, it is estimated that 1 in every 2,000 babies born are affected by sickle cell disease, with the majority being of Black African or Black Caribbean heritage. This chronic condition causes immense pain, organ damage, and a significantly reduced life expectancy. Shockingly, the average life expectancy for someone with sickle cell disease in the UK is just 40-60 years, compared to the national average of 81 years. The impact of sickle cell disease on the Black community is staggering. In England, Black people are over 80 times more likely to have sickle cell disease compared to White people. Furthermore, the mortality rate for sickle cell patients in the UK is alarmingly high, with an estimated 1 in 16 individuals with sickle cell disease dying before the age of 18. These statistics highlight the urgent need for effective treatments like the CRISPR gene editing therapy to be made available to the African and Caribbean community. The health inequalities faced by the African and Caribbean community in the UK are welldocumented. Black people are more likely to experience poverty, discrimination, and barriers to accessing quality healthcare. A report by the NHS Race and Health Observatory found that Black people in the UK have a life expectancy that is up to four years shorter than their White counterparts. Furthermore, Black people are more likely to experience poor health outcomes across a range of conditions, including sickle cell disease. Gene therapy offers a revolutionary approach to treating sickle cell disease by addressing the root cause of the condition. By modifying the patient’s own stem cells to produce healthy red blood cells, gene therapy has the potential to alleviate the painful symptoms and complications associated with sickle cell disease.

## **Draft guidance comments form** 

**Consultation on the draft guidance document – deadline for comments** 5pm on 11 April 2024. Please submit via NICE Docs. 

and even walking to school (which is a 10-minute walk from her home) poses a daily challenge – she often asks, "why me?" and feels helpless to her condition. Vivica uses the aid of a wheelchair when she is having a crisis or is recovering from a crisis. Those with sickle cell are also susceptible to developing hyperhaemolysis, as my sister did, which poses an additional and life-threatening health challenge. 

For those living with sickle cell, the prognosis is that health will often deteriorate. While drugs such as hydroxycarbamide and penicillin do alleviate some of the symptoms of sickle cell, those will sickle cell will continue to have a life-threatening crises and hospitalizations, which studies show, and I have observed from those around me, increases with age. 

One of the reasons NICE has cited for not recommending gene therapy to the NHS for sickle cell is on the grounds of finance. In response, I urge NICE to reconsider their approach. Firstly, the severity of sickle cell, which is a life-threatening disorder with very few treatments outweighs the cost of gene therapy which research shows has been very effective in treating sickle cell – the FDA in the US last December approved two new gene therapies to treat sickle cell disease which has already cured patients living with the condition (1). My sister is amongst approximately 15,000 people who live with sickle cell in the UK and sickle cell is the most common genetic disorder worldwide and, in the UK, – there are currently very limited and often ineffective treatments for sickle cell – most people rely on hydroxycarbamide, penicillin and folic acid for relief. Comparably, cystic fibrosis affects approximately 10,500 people and there are various treatment options for cystic fibrosis. Gene therapy cures sickle cell and my sister's life is worth saving. She has plans to become an architect and a disability advocate, but her condition means that her health will severely limit what she can do – access to gene therapy for my sister and other's who have sickle cell will provide a very necessary lifeline, she would be less dependent on medication, the NHS on financial support from the government and she would be able to stand on her own two feet. 

Further, NICE have accepted using gene therapy for young children living with metachromatic leukodystrophy (2). This is fantastic progress and last year, the first baby received life saving gene therapy on the NHS. I urge NICE to extend this lifeline to those living with sickle cell. While metachromatic leukodystrophy and sickle cell are different conditions, its effects in shortening and reducing quality of life is comparable. If NICE's position is that people should be treated equally and the commission should focus its resources on saving lives, it is imperative to extend the same service to those living with sickle cell. 

I urge you to consider the severity of sickle cell and the positive effects that gene therapy will have on not only sickle cell patients, but on the black community who are the largest community in the UK impacted by sickle cell. My sister dreams of a future where she is pain free and where she can spend months at a time without being in excruciating pain and visiting hospital. Please consider that the benefits of treating sickle cell outweighs its associated costs.

Some thoughts on the hesitancy over offering gene editing treatment for sickle cell disorder by a retired senior research fellow, 50yrs in the field. 

Sickle cell disorder is one of the most common serious hereditary disorders in the world and the first to have a molecular cause identified[1,2] .  It is a life-long condition arising from a single base change in DNA causing a single amino acid change in the beta globin part of the red blood cell protein called haemoglobin, changing it from the usual haemoglobin A to one called haemoglobin S. Haemoglobin is the predominant protein within red blood cells and is responsible for carrying oxygen from the lungs to the tissues (each haemoglobin molecule can carry 4 oxygen molecules) and for transporting carbon dioxide back. 

The 200-300 million or so haemoglobin A molecules within each red blood cell are designed through evolution to remain independent of one another at all times and at all stages of oxygenation.  However, this is not the case for haemoglobin S.  As a result of its amino acid change on its surface, at high enough concentrations and after it has released its oxygen to the tissues, deoxygenated haemoglobin S is able to self-assemble into filaments and fibres that change the shape of the cell to a rigid elongated form called a ‘sickle cell’[3] .  Remarkably, on reoxygenation the haemoglobin S goes back into solution, and many of the red blood cells regain their usual shape. However, the red blood cell may be damaged, may remain distorted and may become more likely to stick to the blood vessel wall. _All_ these factors contribute to a tendency for the sickled cells to periodically block blood vessels supplying oxygen to tissues, causing inflammation and pain.  These events, known as veno-occlusive crises, are the hallmark of sickle cell disorder.  Damaged red blood cells are removed rapidly from the circulation (on average red blood cells of someone with sickle cell anaemia last about 20 days in the circulation instead of the usual 100 days) and severe anaemia also results. 

Beginning in infancy, sickling of the red blood cells within blood vessels can cause bouts of the most severe pain imaginable, and may lead to tissue and organ damage in any system of the body ultimately causing organ failures and various disabilities.  Disease severity and actual physical outcomes, both acute and chronic, remain so unpredictable that this is an extraordinarily difficult condition for a person diagnosed with sickle cell disorder to confront.  Life-threatening drops in haemoglobin level, episodic acute pain, chronic pain, spleen enlargement, spleen atrophy, sepsis, kidney damage, kidney failure, pulmonary damage, pulmonary embolism, pulmonary hypertension, transient ischaemic attacks, strokes, liver fibrosis, liver failure, priapism, gallstones, enlarged heart, heart failure, joint pain, repeated joint replacements, visual disturbance, blindness, hearing loss, painful leg ulcers – we can go on – occurring earlier, sometimes much earlier, in a person’s life than might be expected.  Nevertheless, the number of complications an individual may suffer varies.  A few are pretty universal, for instance: splenic atrophy leading to infection susceptibility, some kidney damage causing increased need to urinate (bed-wetting in infancy for instance) and risk of dehydration, and acute events of severe pain necessitating alleviation with powerful painkillers. Some people have few additional complications for reasons not yet understood, and, paradoxically, many who are more seriously affected look quite well most of the time.  An added challenge arises from the fact that most people in the UK with sickle cell disorder are of African, Caribbean, Middle Eastern and Asian Indian heritage and experience varying degrees of racial stereotyping, insult and abuse.  It is little wonder that people with sickle cell disorders often express feelings of sadness, isolation, frustration, uncertainty, fear, worry, lack of self-confidence, sometimes even despair. Schooling, further education and employment requires extraordinary persistence by, and additional cost to, the individual and family in order to cope with disruption caused by routine and emergency hospital visits while striving to fulfil personal ambitions and obligations to others.  Sickle cell disorder is often also called ‘sickle cell disease’, despite the term being disliked by many of those affected, in order to emphasise its severity, so often underestimated and misunderstood, when arguing for necessary resources to provide appropriate treatment and care. 



<!-- page 153 -->

Sickle cell disorder is an extraordinarily complex and unpredictable disorder to treat, with very few generally-available, effective therapies despite repeated publicised ‘breakthroughs’ and promises of ‘a cure’.  It is actually a group of disorders that range in severity both within and across the groups.  Even the best therapies available are not universally-effective and those that extend life may not improve its quality.  Important indicators of therapeutic success, e.g. increased Hb, may sometimes be more incidental due to homeostatic mechanism than truly preventative of complications, and may even herald a worsening of other symptoms, e.g. painful crises. 

The combination of (i) antenatal screening in order to target pregnancy choices available to parents whose baby is at risk of having a sickle cell disorder, (ii) neonatal screening to diagnose those affected early enough to offer prophylactic information, counselling and therapies, (iii) a network of specialist clinical centres linked both to local voluntary agencies and to expert clinical evaluation thereby available to all, (iv) use of the drug hydroxycarbamide and (v) improvements in delivery of regular blood transfusion for those who need it, has saved money through diminishing the projected increase in the number of births of babies with sickle cell disorder and by improving the health of and support available to many of those affected.   Nevertheless, mortality and comorbidity in the UK (England at least) remains high in the 14-15%[4] patients who are most severelyaffected which is projected to require a considerable increase in treatment resources over time. Besides the need to continue to work on effective and equitable service delivery[5] , more effective therapies are still required. 

The only curative therapies available are stem cell transplantation and gene therapy.  While stem cell transplantation is available only to the small proportion of people with sickle cell disorder who have a matched donor, this restriction does not apply to the gene-editing therapy proposed here.  Furthermore, some of the complications associated with stem cell transplantation will not occur with the gene-editing therapy (graft versus host disease for instance), the high cost of which will surely be driven down with experience of its use.  Of course, there is a need for great caution, for detailed face to face explanation with an experienced practitioner of risks to an individual wishing to undergo this therapy, and for detailed long-term follow up of such a novel therapy. Wider education of health professionals throughout the clinical network and of the general public about different types of gene therapy, and their associated risks, must continue.  Nevertheless, to have a potential curative treatment available to all who are severely affected by symptoms resistant to current therapies, rather than to the few, seems the right thing to do.  It gives hope that promises of therapeutic improvements were not empty ones and, through increasing participation and knowledge, may encourage more people with sickle cell disorder to have faith in the value of their much-needed participation in clinical research. 

Sickle cell disorder was the first serious hereditary disorder to have a molecular cause identified.  That discovery and its further study has led to advances in understanding the biochemistry and pathophysiology of many other clinical conditions.  People with sickle cell disorder should be at the heart of these developments.

3. Diggs LW & Bibbs J (1939) THE ERYTHROCYTE IN SICKLE CELL ANEMIA. Journal of the American Medical Association 110: 695-701. 

4. Piel FB, Jobanputra M, Gallagher M, Weber J, Laird SG, McGahan M. Some thoughts on the hesitancy over offering gene-editing treatment for sickle cell disorder from a retired Senior Research Fellow, 50yrs in the field. 

Sickle cell disorder (also called sickle cell disease) is an extraordinarily complex and unpredictable disorder to treat, with very few generally-available, effective therapies despite repeated well-publicised ‘breakthroughs’ and promises of ‘a cure’.  Even the best therapies available are not universally-effective and those that extend life may not improve its quality. 

The establishment in the UK of antenatal screening, neonatal screening, a network of specialist clinical centres linked both to local voluntary agencies and to expert clinical evaluation, use of the drug hydroxycarbamide and improvements in delivery and safety of regular blood transfusion for those who need it, has saved money through diminishing the projected increase in the number of births of babies with sickle cell disorder and by improving markedly the health of those affected.  Nevertheless, in 2021, Piel et al. reported[1] that mortality and co-morbidity in England remains high in the 14-15% patients who are most severely-affected and is likely to require a considerable increase in treatment resources over time.  Besides the need to work on effective and equitable quality service delivery[2] , more effective therapies are still required. 

The only curative therapies available are stem cell transplantation and gene therapy. While stem cell transplantation is available only to the small proportion of people with sickle cell disorder who have a matched donor, this restriction does not apply to the gene-editing therapy proposed here.  Furthermore, some of the complications associated with stem cell transplantation will not occur with the gene-editing therapy, the high cost of which, one would imagine, will be driven down with experience of its use. 

Of course, there is a need for great caution, for detailed face to face explanation with an experienced practitioner of risks to an individual wishing to undergo this therapy, and for detailed long-term follow up of such a novel therapy.  Also, wider education of health professionals throughout the clinical network and the general public about the different types of gene therapy, and their associated risks, must continue.  Nevertheless, to have a potential curative treatment available to all who are severely affected by symptoms resistant to current therapies, rather than to the few, seems the right thing to do.  It gives hope that promises of therapeutic improvements were not empty ones and, through increasing participation and knowledge, may encourage more people with sickle cell disorder to have faith in the value of their much-needed participation in clinical research. 

Sickle cell disorder was the first serious hereditary disorder to have a molecular cause identified[3] .  That discovery and its further study has led to advances in understanding the biochemistry and pathophysiology of many other clinical conditions.  People with sickle cell disorder should be at the heart of these developments.

## **Response to NICE Exagamglogene genen therapy for treatmet of sickle cell disease from British Society for Haematology General Haematology Guidelines Task Force** 

## **We feel strongly that the NICE appraisees have misjudged the severity of sickle cell disease (SCD).** 

SCD is a severe condition and patients die prematurely, including many moderately-severely affected individuals dying in their 30s and 40s, even those who have received best currently available treatment such as long-term red cell exchange transfusion and hydroxycarbamide treatment. 

The medical literature provides clear evidence for a reduced life expectancy, a severely impaired quality of life, and accumulation of complications and co-morbidities with age. 

Regarding the use of the EQ 5D quality of life assessment, it is not reasonable to imply that the baseline EQ-5D of 0.81 (1 is perfect health) from the trial is the measure of quality of life for all patients with severe SCD for their whole lifetime. 

Firstly, the EQ 5 the over estimates quality of life in long-term conditions such as sickle cell disease and this has been demonstrated in the literature. EQ-5D, while it is the preferred QoL measure for NICE, does not fully capture the experience of patients with severe SCD due to ceiling effects. EQ-5D has to be taken as a highly conservative representation of QoL. Looking at other measures such as ASQ-ME, FACT-BMT, Pain NRS are more validated measures of quality of life assessment in sickle cell disease. 

Secondly, quality of life deteriorates significantly with age in sickle cell disease and therefore an assessment at the start of this trial is not reflective of the quality of life in 5, 10 or even 20 years’ time for the patients. 

Patients entering the exa-cel trial necessarily had to meet the trial entry criteria, and therefore were unlikely to have accumulated significant irreversible complications despite being necessarily a severe population with frequent VOCs. They would have gone on to develop multiple complications and have a much lower QoL in the future had they not been treated with gene therapy. It is not reasonable to assume the 0.81 stays constant for patients over their lifetimes. 

## **Exa-cel has the potential to return patients to near normal health.** 

Because of the trial inclusion criteria, patients included in the trial have not accumulated significant irreversible complications prior to treatment with exa-cel, but did experience frequent VOCs which are indicative of severe disease which is likely to lead to multiple complications and poorer QoL over time. 

By treating these severe patients before the majority of irreversible complications have established, exa-cel has the potential to return patients to near normal health, life expectancy and quality of life, and prevent future complications. 

This is extrapolated from evidence from patients receiving sibling matched HSCT which shows prevention and reversibility of complications and improved long-term survival. Unlike sibling matched HSCT, Exa-cel would not lead to GVHD or graft rejection. 

Pan-cellularity of haemoglobin F following exa-cel treatment is likely to prevent further complications and potentially lead to some reversibility of pre-existing complications. 



<!-- page 169 -->

## **The benefits are likely to be sustained over a very long period** 

There is no biological plausibility that the genetic edit will not be permanent. Genetic edits to haematopoietic stem cells with CRISPR technology are permanent and durable. 

This is supported by data from CLIMB 121 in which the proportion of alleles with intended genetic modification (allelic editing) was stable over time. 

Acute pain can happen infrequently within the first year after allo-SCT. This can be due to exacerbation of chronic pain, allodynia and hyperalgesia. The reasons for acute pain events seen after exa-cel in a small number of patients are likely to be similar. These do not represent lack of effect of exa-cel. 

Fetal haemoglobin is maintained at around 40% in a pancellular distribution. This would be expected to prevent the process of vaso-occlusion. It would also prevent progression of existing organ damage and development of new organ damage. This is evidenced by outcomes in compound hereditary persistence of fetal haemoglobin (HbS+HPFH) in which affected individuals do not suffer the pain and organ complications seen in sickle cell disease and have normal life expectancy.

<!-- page 184 -->

## **Has all of the relevant evidence been taken into account?** 

Please see responses to subsequent questions. 

## **Are the recommendations sound and a suitable basis for guidance to the NHS?** 

I believe the recommendations fail to take into account the severity of sickle cell disease. I was present as a Clinical expert and much of the debate hinged upon interpretation of the variable quality data available to guide both EAG and NICE committee. As a consequence, we are in danger of failing this patient group once again. By failing to acknowledge the disease severity and impact we will be failing to provide a low risk, effective cure for those most severely affected. As a clinician with over 30 years of experience caring for patients with sickle cell disease, I have witnessed the physical and psychological toll of the disease first hand.  Normal life expectancy in the UK is around 80 years of age and, although studies of life expectancy give differing results there is no argument that individuals with sickle cell disease have a life expectancy that is around two to three decades less than the general population. Quality of life studies such as PISCES (McClish DK, doi:10.1186/1477-7525-3-50) and SWAY highlight the severe restrictions associated with sickle cell disease. I therefore do not see any grounds to continue to debate the severity of this disease. 

For decades sickle cell disease services have been under funded/provided and research funding minimal. This has severely affected access to the kind of high-quality data that we are used to for haematological malignancy or inherited haemorrhagic diatheses. Much of the data we have to work with does not fully clarify the clinical severity, the mortality and morbidity risk or the impact on patients’ quality of life and equality of opportunity. 

As an example of the problems we face, despite small improvements in sickle care within the NHS, good epidemiological data remains hard to come by. The inadequate funding for sickle services and data input into the National haemoglobinopathy registry leaves us with an incomplete picture. In Europe the French have experienced similar issues (Haematologica 2023 Sep 1;108(9):2476-2486). 

## **Are the summaries of clinical and cost effectiveness reasonable interpretations of the evidence?** 

I am not qualified to comment on the economic and cost effectiveness modelling so will concentrate this response on the effects of sickle cell disease from the perspective of survival, severity, quality of life and the benefits of exacel. 

Survival and severity: 

There are numerous reports highlighting the severity and early mortality of this disease (Udeze C. British Journal of Haematology 2023, Piel FB, Blood Cells Mol Dis. 2021;89:102567, Di Mauro M, Am J Hematol. 2023;98(11):E341-e4., Brousse V, Haematologica. 2023;108(9):2476-86. Jiao B, Blood Adv. 2023;7(13):3276-83.). Similar survival rates are seen in the Jamaican 



<!-- page 185 -->

cohort study, a case controlled study established in the 1970s which shows 55% of the population alive at the age of 40 years 

(https://doi.org/10.1371%2Fjournal.pone.0192710). 

The frequency of organ specific chronic organ dysfunction is likely to be high but data is limited and this aspect of the disease an evolving story. Definitions of chronic organ dysfunction in sickle cell disease are unclear, partly because many organs eg kidney, liver, heart, lung show evidence of altered function early in life. What is certain is that the process of HbS polymerisation is lifelong and attritional to the microvascular circulation and hence organ function. Hydroxycarbamide does not reverse this process. 

Pain remains the most frequent symptom and, despite the difficulty of using this subjective symptom as a measure of disease severity, remains the most commonly used marker of severity. Pain diary studies document that most pain is experienced outside the healthcare setting with almost a third of patients reporting pain every day (https://doi.org/10.7326/0003-4819-148-2-200801150-00004). This must be recognised when evaluating both severity and response to treatment. Failing to do so undermines the meaningful evaluation of any new treatment. 

## Quality of life: 

The SWAY study clearly articulates the challenges faced by those with sickle cell disease across all aspects of their life. Studies consistently demonstrate that individuals with SCD experience lower HRQOL compared to the general population. Moreover, comparisons with other chronic diseases such as cystic fibrosis and asthma reveal similar or even lower HRQOL scores among patients SCD patients. Further study from the Comprehensive sickle centres in the US documents the substantial impairment of HRQOL in adults with SCD suggesting that more effective treatments of persistent pain and depression would provide the largest HRQOL benefit. 

## Benefits of exacel: 

The CLIMB 121 trial evidence suggests an effective cure. This is unsurprising considering the very high levels of HbF achieved, the pancellular nature of the distribution and the effect this will have on polymerisation of HbS (https://doi.org/10.1182/blood-2013-09-528067).  That a trial patient had an episode of pain post treatment has raised questions of the effectiveness of the treatment. However, pain is a complex and subjective phenomenon. Experience suggests that in those rare patients with frequent acute or chronic pain, with a history of high or frequent opioid analgesic use, develop central sensitisation or opioid hyperalgesia. This maybe further complicated by the knowledge that pain similar to sickle cell can occur on reduction of opioids particular if this is done too quickly. In such patients it would be wrong to assume all pain is vaso-occlusion driven. Once again this highlights the difficulty of severity markers in sickle, there being no clear measurable biological marker of disease activity. The phenomenon of pain post treatment is also seen in patients post stem cell transplant (Br J Haematol. 2019;184(4):690-3). 



<!-- page 186 -->

). 

There is also the debate regarding eligibility for the 1.5% discounted rate. I would strongly suggest that this case does meet the criteria as set out below: 

_1) Without treatment people would die or have a severely impacted life:_ Please see previous section on survival and severity. _2) Treatment will restore full or near full health_ The trial data show an increase in total haemoglobin accompanied by a reduction in markers of red cell breakdown, prevention of further sickle complications and improved quality of life. Whether the treatment will reverse all aspects of chronic organ damage present before conditioning is uncertain but seems unlikely. In younger patients the risk of significantly disordered organ function is much lower. 

_3) Benefit likely to be sustained_ Thus far trial participants have shown consistent and stable high levels of the edited gene, and as a consequence very high levels of HbF at a level that will prevent the key pathogenetic event; the intracellular polymerisation of HbS (ref). There is no biological reason to believe that transcription levels will decline appreciably with longer follow up. Re-reading the NHSE commissioning documents on sibling stem cell transplantation - - - (https://www.england.nhs.uk/wp content/uploads/2020/02/clinical commissioning policy-allogeneic-haematopoietic-stem-cell-transplantation.pdf) it is clear that, using similar evidence of disease severity, this expensive treatment was approved risk on the basis of it being a _potential cure_ despite a significant risk of early and late graft failure, graft versus host disease and no analysis of cost effectiveness. Whilst I understand the NICE processes maybe more detailed, it would seem we are adopting different standards to the approval of curative treatments for use in the same setting. This is confusing and inconsistent. 

## **Are there any aspects of the recommendations that need particular consideration to ensure we avoid unlawful discrimination against any group of people on the grounds of age, disability, gender reassignment, pregnancy and maternity, race, religion or belief, sex or sexual orientation?** 

It seems to me that the difficulties experienced with the assessment of exacel relate to the lack of high-quality evidence on the natural history of the disease and the absence of a highly reliable marker of severe disease. Uncertainty with respect to the paucity of high-quality evidence of severity, impaired QOL or impaired survival must not be confused with absence of early death, impaired QOL for this disease group. The effect is particularly marked for those who have frequent complications who are unlikely to survive much beyond their fifth decade (https://doi.org/10.1002%2Fajh.23683). 

The issues around evidence described are themselves a result of discrimination and inequality within the NHS, society and research funding prioritisation. A recent publication in the US highlighted the 10-fold financial disparity per patient between national research funding on sickle cell versus cystic fibrosis. (J Clin Transl Sci. 2023; 7(1): e65).  My point being that NICE have reached their conclusion based on an inadequacy of good evidence which is, in itself, a result of longstanding inequality in 



<!-- page 187 -->

service provision and research. The “no” decision therefore risks amplifying this discrimination. That we are still debating the severity of the disease is an example of such discrimination. Whilst the published report comments that patients may be less likely to engage with research and correctly stresses the effects of deprivation, less emphasis has been placed on adverse effects on health of the decades of limited research funding. Using the example of cystic fibrosis once again to highlight the impact of poor funding; the last decade or so has seen major changes in the understanding of the disease, developments of new classes of therapies and multiple clinical trials and consequent changes to prognosis and survival. In comparison during that period Sickle cell patients saw a small handful of new drugs reach phase 2-3 trials (excluding exacel) most of which have proved to have a limited or inadequate effect. None have had ongoing NICE approval. 

I am not qualified to comment on the DCEA models used but feel I need to highlight the hidden effects of discrimination, not just in healthcare provision but also in research funding.

## **Are the recommendations sound and a suitable basis for guidance to the NHS?** 

As above, we feel that the severity of living with sickle cell and therefore the potential benefits in terms of quality of life as well as impact on life expectancy is not addressed. The NHS is currently managing the consequences of a lack of curative and effective treatments for those living with sickle cell disease. This includes the inpatient burden for those requiring frequent admissions, as well as the consequence of managing complex co-morbidities due to the long term organ damage that can occur. Wider society is also impacted; the impact of loss of earning potential not just for those directly affected but also for those in caring roles is also important to consider. 

**Are the summaries of clinical and cost effectiveness reasonable interpretations of the evidence?** 

The clinical effectiveness is not reasonable if you fail to interpret the clinical severity of living with sickle cell disease. 

**Are there any aspects of the recommendations that need particular consideration to ensure we avoid unlawful discrimination against any group of people on the grounds of age, disability, gender reassignment, pregnancy and maternity, race, religion or belief, sex or sexual orientation?** 

It is well recognised that those who live with sickle cell are more likely to be from a black and minority ethnic group. This can make those living with the condition feel that when such decisions are taken, it is a reflection of their race and not a reflection of the evidence being presented. It is important that this is recognised.

## **Has all of the relevant evidence been taken into account?** 

No. There is a fundamental misunderstanding about how the debilitating symptoms of SC manifest differently and their impact on day to day life for those living with the disease and it’s far reaching physical, social and mental effects. 

I also do not think that the long term organ damage is fully appreciated. The physical manifestation of Sickle Cell exists on a spectrum, whilst some patients may not experience regular crises, blood transfusions, pain etc, this is not be say their organs are not being damaged with each day and the legacy this causes for their long term health. What doesn’t affect people today, affects them tomorrow. They are also unable to participate in normal physical activities, which can leave them on the fringes of society. 

The earlier the gene therapy is offered the less the long-term damage will be experienced both mentally and physically. 

The detrimental effect on the mental health of SC patients has not been fully appreciated, particularly for Black males who have a high incidence on untreated mental health challenges. 

Furthermore, the existing social & health inequalities experienced by the African Caribbean communities have not been considered. Coupled with SC, those living with the disease are often experiencing poverty which makes managing the disease challenging and difficult to manage. Treatment for SC disease is not consistent and there is still a huge lack of knowledge and understanding within medical settings outside of the major cities i.e. London/Birmingham. This leads to further exacerbation of health inequalities. 

## **Are the recommendations sound and a suitable basis for guidance to the NHS?** 

I don’t believe that they are. Without gene therapy, patients are left with therapeutics that alleviate symptoms somewhat, however their quality of life is still impacted. 

There is a lack of accessible cures for SC that do not require donors, which bring their own challenges when trying to acquire a suitable match. 

## **Are the summaries of clinical and cost effectiveness reasonable interpretations of the evidence?** 

Whilst the cost of treatment is challenging at present, the impact on people’s lives will be revolutionary. The cost of managing the disease must be considered- hospital stays, transfusions, drugs, support services. As mentioned, the long term implications of SC on organs, creates further pressure on the NHS as they have to be treated. 



<!-- page 197 -->

**Are there any aspects of the recommendations that need particular consideration to ensure we avoid unlawful discrimination against any group of people on the grounds of age, disability, gender reassignment, pregnancy and maternity, race, religion or belief, sex or sexual orientation?** 

Within the Afro Caribbean community, there is a huge stigma of having sickle cell disease. Whereby people are dissuaded from reproducing with someone who has the disease/trait. This has a profound effect on those living with the disease who are sometimes viewed as social pariahs. This has a profound effect on their mental health how people negotiate their adult life, how they see themselves and their understanding and acceptance within their community. 

Together with the existing health inequalities experience by Afro Caribbean societies, and the impact of SC disease on daily life and mental health, SC serves to push those living with the disease further onto the fringes of society, with little hope. As a parent of a child with SC, this is something already at the forefront of my mind, even though my child is only in primary school. 

A cure for SC would be freeing for so many and give them an opportunity to live a life free of debilitating pain, hospital stays and constant fear of when their next crisis will happen.

I wish to submit a comment in response to the overall draft recommendation, covering two main points and a summary of additional thoughts set out by the subheadings below. 

1. The negative impact that severe sickle cell has on the day to day life of people living with the condition 

Sickle Cell is systemic and can affect all parts of the body, there is currently no one-treatment-for-all. This can lead to daily complications such as the ability to walk, work, be in school and wash and care for oneself. There is often significant financial costs such as equipment for disability adjustments, medicine due to not automatically entitled to the Med-Ex card, reduce in assets to qualify for certain disability allowances, missed days off work, and many more examples). There is also a cost a physical and mental cost of the daily upkeep in health for sickle cell patients. 

The negative impact does not begin and end in the event of a VOC, many suffer symptoms leading up to a crises such pain, nausea and chronic fatigue; and are often left with a weaken body which must take time to heal once the crisis is over. For example, I had a crisis in my leg which had me admitted into hospital for only under a day but left me be unable to walk properly for almost four months after being discharged. 

The negative impact of SCD would be significantly lifted with the introduction of Casgevy. Eliminating VOCs from the lives of SCD patients would lead to less hospitalisations, less time off sick and less costs to mitigate the debilitating effects of pain crises (before, during and after). Quality of life would improve greatly due to no longer worrying of the uncertainty of tomorrow which SCD often brings. 

2. The worsening impact that sickle cell has over time 

It is well documented the worsening impact SCD has with age. As aging often brings its own set of health complications, these can be aggravated by SCD. Often is the case of older SCD patients having to take early retirement due to the illness becoming debilitating to work despite being decade(s) away from the actually retirement age, and often not even in the financial position to do so. 

However, this does not only occur when reaching middle-age or becoming elderly. For example, my Sickle Cell was more severe during childhood, improved in my teenage years and has started to get worse again in my later teens to early adulthood, all under the age of 25 years old. Therefore the progression of SCD (or better put, the regression of the health of the SCD patient) must be taken into account to build a more accurate picture of the severity of the disease and its worsening impact over time. 

Casgevy can make things better by allowing us to age more steadily and - gracefully. I would not want my future children become early care givers. 



<!-- page 202 -->

Life won’t feel like a ticking time-bomb, and we can have a future to look forward to with hope. 

## 3. Additional Thoughts: 

Innovation: This is the first time as a lay person hearing innovation be an inhibitor. I believe the innovative aspect should highlight the milestone is research, and excite new possibilities of curable chronic diseases. Mainly highlighting the uncertainty seems a slight pessimistic read of this aspect. Treatments have been known the breed treatments, as seen in hydroxyurea’s origins as a drug for cancer patients now also used for Sickle Cell. The possibility of a domino-effect of funding this treatment leading to other possible cures could be considered instead. 

Discrimination: Sickle Cell is one of the most common genetic disorders in the country. Another common genetic disorder, Cystic Fibrosis has a population of 11,000 patience and 511 treatments available, Sickle Cell’s population is at almost 17,000 with currently only three treatments. Why is there such disparity between the treatments available for one condition over the other? It cannot be ignored a main difference between the average patient of CF and SCD which is race. I implore the committee to ensure that this decision be made completely unbiased, free of prejudice and of fair and sound judgement. Often we as patients have had our voices ignored, despite being the ones to experience the disorder ourselves. This experience, as seen the case of Tyrone Airey has been known in be fatal. I implore the committee to not make another fatal mistake in judgement today. 

Thank you for taking into consideration our comments, and we hope NICE are able to come to the correction decision by recommending the NHS funding of this vital, life-changing and life-saving treatment.

genome editing would not be as beneficial as where they are conferred by inherited genetic polymorphism. Finally, I acknowledge that exa-cel treatment is an intensive procedure with all of the risks we usually associate with myeloablative busulphan chemotherapy. Therefore, if available as a treatment option, it would be reserved for those with the most severe disease which is not adequately controlled by hydroxycarbamide treatment. There would be a rigorous and systematic assessment and review process for any patient in whom exa-cel therapy would be considered, such as there is currently for sibling bone marrow transplantation for adults, for which all potential cases are discussed by the National Haemoglobinopathy Panel with numbers of patients proceeding with that treatment option in practice being low. Based on my experience of considering other novel or intensive therapies with patients, such as crizanlizumab (when available) or allogeneic stem cell transplant for adults, I anticipate a low take-up of the option of exa-cel even in eligible patients, were it to be made available. This is due to a number of anxieties many patients hold regarding less well established treatments, as well as their personal priorities which often include maintenance of fertility. 

In practice, therefore, numbers receiving this therapy would be only a small fraction of the total percentage of patients with sickle cell disease. However, there is a significant minority of patients with very severe disease and frequent crises, for whom current treatment options are inadequate or inaccessible, and who have an intolerable level of suffering, for whom exacel now represents their only chance of long-term amelioration of disease. It is on behalf of this minority of patients, who have no other option and a high burden of unmet need, that I write to request reconsideration of the committee's initial decision and that this therapeutic option might be made available to them.

## **Comments on consultation:** 

Dear NICE, 

As a member of the African and Caribbean community, I am writing to express my deep concern and disappointment regarding the recent decision by the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) to potentially stop the availability of gene therapy for sickle cell patients in the United Kingdom. 

This decision is a devastating blow to our community, which has long faced significant health inequalities, especially when it comes to sickle cell disease. 

Sickle cell disease is a genetic blood disease that predominantly affects individuals of African and Caribbean descent. 

In the UK, it is estimated that 1 in every 2,000 babies born are affected by sickle cell disease, with the majority being of Black African or Black Caribbean heritage. Making this disorder one of the most (if not the most) common genetic disorder in England. 

This chronic condition causes immense pain, organ damage, and a significantly reduced life expectancy. Shockingly, the average life expectancy for someone with sickle cell disease in the UK is just 40-60 years, compared to the national average of 81 years. 



<!-- page 206 -->

The impact of sickle cell disease on the Black community is staggering. In England, Black people are over 80 times more likely to have sickle cell disease compared to White people. 

Furthermore, the mortality rate for sickle cell patients in the UK is alarmingly high, with an estimated 1 in 16 individuals with sickle cell disease dying before the age of 18. 

These statistics highlight the urgent need for effective treatments like the CRISPR gene editing therapy to be made available to the African and Caribbean community. 

The health inequalities faced by the African and Caribbean community in the UK are well-documented. 

Black people are more likely to experience poverty, discrimination, and barriers to accessing quality healthcare. 

A report by the NHS Race and Health Observatory found that Black people in the UK have a life expectancy that is up to four years shorter than their White counterparts. 

Furthermore, Black people are more likely to experience poor health outcomes across a range of conditions, including sickle cell disease. 

Gene therapy offers a revolutionary approach to treating sickle cell disease by addressing the root cause of the condition. 

By modifying the patient’s own stem cells to produce healthy red blood cells, gene therapy has the potential to alleviate the painful symptoms and complications associated with sickle cell disease. 

This innovative treatment can greatly improve the quality of life for those affected and reduce the burden on the healthcare system in the long run. 

It is crucial that NICE reconsiders its decision and ensures that gene editing therapy remains available to sickle cell patients in the UK, particularly those from the African and Caribbean community who are disproportionately affected by this condition. 

Denying access to this potentially transformative treatment would be a significant setback in the fight against health inequalities and would leave our community without hope for a better future. Such health inequalities tragically highlighted by the covid pandemic now urgently needs to be addressed. 

Moreover, the decision to stop the availability of gene editing therapy for sickle cell patients sends a troubling message about the priorities of our healthcare system. 



<!-- page 207 -->

It suggests that the lives and well-being of those affected by this condition, who are predominantly from the African and Caribbean community, are not valued as highly as they should be. 

This is unacceptable and goes against the principles of equality and fairness that should underpin our society. 

I urge NICE to reverse its decision and work towards making gene therapy for sickle cell disease more widely accessible. 

The African and Caribbean community in the UK deserves the same opportunities for improved health outcomes as any other group. 

By investing in and supporting this innovative treatment, we can take a significant step towards addressing the glaring health inequalities that have persisted for far too long. 

Thank you for your attention to this critical matter. 

I sincerely hope that NICE will reconsider its position and prioritise the health and well-being of the African and Caribbean community in the UK, especially those affected by sickle cell disease.

**Are the recommendations sound and a suitable basis for guidance to the NHS?** 

No, after reading the review of an individual who had undergone this treatment, the benefits of this new treatment option were highlighted whilst also understanding the physical and psychological impacts of this treatment, it was concluded to be a beneficial treatment and improved energy levels, feeling of control and quality of life. I believe that further research should be undertaken and that this treatment option should not be ruled out. 

**Are the summaries of clinical and cost effectiveness reasonable interpretations of the evidence?** 

Whilst it is important to consider the cost effectiveness of this treatment, it is also important to consider the impact this treatment could have on many individuals and families quality of life. Whilst currently individuals who experience sickle cell crisis present to A&E for treatment have repeat infections and admissions to hospital as a result of this disease, which costs the NHS, the treatment could help to reduce these admissions and patients quality of care and trust in the NHS after years of reporting poor quality care for sickle cell disease. 

**Are there any aspects of the recommendations that need particular consideration to ensure we avoid unlawful discrimination against any group of people on the grounds of age, disability, gender reassignment, pregnancy and maternity, race, religion or belief, sex or sexual orientation?** 

Socioeconomic factors should be considered within this study as this correlates to poorer health outcomes. It is important to consider the current health inequalities which impact an individuals health and wellbeing. Care for sickle cell disease has been reported as being poor and individuals have stated feeling judged and stigmatised when requesting pain relief, it is important to consider how this currently impact individuals mental health when accessing services in vulnerable circumstances.

## **Comment on section 1 (recommendations):** 

This is extremely disappointing that with such a major break through in curing sickle cell; a most debilitating condition to live with, can now not be offered to sickle cell patients in the UK. Given the lack of treatments available for people with sickle cell, compared to a genetic condition like cystic fibrosis (CF) this would have brought some hope to us. There are 511 treatments available to the 10,500 people with CF who are mainly white people, compared to 3 treatments available to the 18,000 people living with sickle cell, who are mainly black people. Additionally, 2 major treatments were made available voxelotor and crizanlizumab for sickle cell, and then latterly withdrawn.  As a sickle cell patient myself, it is very discouraging to know this decision is a finance one, when infact it can be life changing for many of us. 

Whilst it is a finance one, the huge health inequalities, stigmatisation and prejudice for a condition that mainly affects the African and Caribbean community is vast. This would help to start redress some of that balance and enable us to live a better lives. 

Treatments must be fair and equitable.

Do sickle cell lives matter more in the USA, than the UK?

## **Are the recommendations sound and a suitable basis for guidance to the NHS?** 

I would argue that this treatment should be offered to some patients with SCD given the severity of the condition and the impact on patients and the limited treatment options available. 

SCD is a severe condition with patients subjected to hospitalisation, risk of life threatening conditions and reduced quality of life. 

This condition is likely to have long lasting / life long benefits at reducing sickling and crises. With the expectation that patients will be able to achieve a near normal life (particularly if treatment accessed before long term organ complications develop) - it is difficult to describe return to normality as this is a life long condition and patients living with SCD will never have had what is often considered a normal life. 

## **Are the summaries of clinical and cost effectiveness reasonable interpretations of the evidence?** 

The benefit of this condition will offer long term improvement - and benefits will be accumulated over time. The treatment will reduce long term complications that would otherwise increase medical requirements and decrease quality of life

|Dear NICE,<br>As a member of the African and Caribbean community, I am writing to<br>express my deep concern and disappointment regarding the recent decision||





<!-- page 226 -->

by the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) to potentially stop the availability of gene therapy for sickle cell patients in the United Kingdom. 

This decision is a devastating blow to our community, which has long faced significant health inequalities, especially when it comes to sickle cell disease. 

Sickle cell disease is a genetic blood disease that predominantly affects individuals of African and Caribbean descent. 

In the UK, it is estimated that 1 in every 2,000 babies born are affected by sickle cell disease, with the majority being of Black African or Black Caribbean heritage. 

This chronic condition causes immense pain, organ damage, and a significantly reduced life expectancy. Shockingly, the average life expectancy for someone with sickle cell disease in the UK is just 40-60 years, compared to the national average of 81 years. 

The impact of sickle cell disease on the Black community is staggering. In England, Black people are over 80 times more likely to have sickle cell disease compared to White people. 

Furthermore, the mortality rate for sickle cell patients in the UK is alarmingly high, with an estimated 1 in 16 individuals with sickle cell disease dying before the age of 18. 

These statistics highlight the urgent need for effective treatments like the CRISPR gene editing therapy to be made available to the African and Caribbean community. 

The health inequalities faced by the African and Caribbean community in the UK are well-documented. 

Black people are more likely to experience poverty, discrimination, and barriers to accessing quality healthcare. 

A report by the NHS Race and Health Observatory found that Black people in the UK have a life expectancy that is up to four years shorter than their White counterparts. 

Furthermore, Black people are more likely to experience poor health outcomes across a range of conditions, including sickle cell disease. 

Gene therapy offers a revolutionary approach to treating sickle cell disease by addressing the root cause of the condition. 



<!-- page 227 -->

By modifying the patient’s own stem cells to produce healthy red blood cells, gene therapy has the potential to alleviate the painful symptoms and complications associated with sickle cell disease. 

This innovative treatment can greatly improve the quality of life for those affected and reduce the burden on the healthcare system in the long run. 

It is crucial that NICE reconsiders its decision and ensures that gene editing therapy remains available to sickle cell patients in the UK, particularly those from the African and Caribbean community who are disproportionately affected by this condition. 

Denying access to this potentially transformative treatment would be a significant setback in the fight against health inequalities and would leave our community without hope for a better future. 

Moreover, the decision to stop the availability of gene editing therapy for sickle cell patients sends a troubling message about the priorities of our healthcare system. 

It suggests that the lives and well-being of those affected by this condition, who are predominantly from the African and Caribbean community, are not valued as highly as they should be. 

This is unacceptable and goes against the principles of equality and fairness that should underpin our society. 

I urge NICE to reverse its decision and work towards making gene therapy for sickle cell disease more widely accessible. 

The African and Caribbean community in the UK deserves the same opportunities for improved health outcomes as any other group. 

By investing in and supporting this innovative treatment, we can take a significant step towards addressing the glaring health inequalities that have persisted for far too long. 

Thank you for your attention to this critical matter. 

I sincerely hope that NICE will reconsider its position and prioritise the health and well-being of the African and Caribbean community in the UK, especially those affected by sickle cell disease. 

Yours sincerely, 

Full Name

## **Has all of the relevant evidence been taken into account?** 

I do not think so.  I do not think that this consultation takes into account the severity of sickle cell or the magnitude of the long-term benefits to patients of exa-cel. 



<!-- page 231 -->

## **Are the recommendations sound and a suitable basis for guidance to the NHS?** 

Again, no - I would question the level of knowledge, and perspective taken from Sickle Cell sufferers, when making this decision, and would urge a rethink. In particular, I would ask the following is considered: 

The negative impact that severe sickle cell has on the day to day life of people living with the condition The worsening impact that sickle cell has over time The impact of sickle cell on life expectancy and the risk of mortality 

## **Are the summaries of clinical and cost effectiveness reasonable interpretations of the evidence?** 

Absolutely not. In terms of clinical effectiveness, based on studies from the US, there is a valid case for the use of exa-cel.  In terms of cost effectiveness, I would suggest that benchmarking the use of this treatment should be considered in comparision to other diseases that are equated to Sickle Cell in terms of clinical treatment - for example, severe Sickle Cell crises and related issues are generally treated in the same way as severe cancer patients, in Oncology wards. This should be what is used when looking at the cost effectiveness of the treatment. How much were radiology and chemotherapy treatments initially? 

**Are there any aspects of the recommendations that need particular consideration to ensure we avoid unlawful discrimination against any group of people on the grounds of age, disability, gender reassignment, pregnancy and maternity, race, religion or belief, sex or sexual orientation?** 

Absolutely. Sickle Cell is a disease that mainly affects people of African origin, and this has created a massive stigma in the way that it is treated, perceived and taken seriously as an illness, despite the fact that there are numerous case studies on how cripplingly severe it can be.  If cost effectiveness is the reason given for not going ahead with exa-cel treatment, this needs to be fully and transparently compared with similarly debilitating diseases that primarily affect people of European ancestry, and the initial cost of treatments for these - otherwise there is a clear racial bias at play.

|**Has all of the relevant evidence been taken into account?**|





<!-- page 232 -->

As a lay person, the evidence detailed in this initial consultation seems very detailed and contains detailed medical explanations and reasoning behind why the treatment should not be considered at this time. However, have any links between other treatments of this kind (for other genetic diseases) and small trials of this kind been investigated and the results been looked into? are there similar, trials that could be studied and conclusions made. 

## **Are the recommendations sound and a suitable basis for guidance to the NHS?** 

I’m sure the detailed analysis is sound and is trying to protect patients interests. But it has been pointed out  that Sickle Cell Disease has many negative socioeconomic factors and despite this treatment only having a small number of trials- if proved successful this treatment could have a massive impact on the QoL outcomes for the people it affects and would also reduce the medical needs and impact on services by these people in the long term. 

So although the recommendations are sound, some strategic consideration needs to be given to how more trials and feedback can be conducted -so that the limited trails so far can be extended and also longer term feedback from patients who’ve already received the treatment can be analysed and used to determine which patients would benefit from the treatment in the future. 

## **Are the summaries of clinical and cost effectiveness reasonable interpretations of the evidence?** 

As it’s a small sample the summaries are initial interpretations and these would need to be reviewed over a much longer term with more patients in the sample before a definitive cost could be assigned to the treatment. 

**Are there any aspects of the recommendations that need particular consideration to ensure we avoid unlawful discrimination against any group of people on the grounds of age, disability, gender reassignment, pregnancy and maternity, race, religion or belief, sex or sexual orientation?** 

The main aspect that needs to be taken into consideration is that as the report mentions, SCD mainly affects ethnic minorities disproportionately. It then compounds the socioeconomic disadvantages of many of these people. Any potential treatment that could reduce the severity and life long impact of the SCD needs larger trials in this country, before recommendations against the treatment should be made. 

No treatment will ever have 100% successful, but in this day and age advances in technology mean that any gene therapy should be considered as a potential treatment. No links to other ground breaking gene therapy treatments have been mentioned in the report - could some parallels be made, or at the very least lessons be learned?

By modifying the patient’s own stem cells to produce healthy red blood cells, gene therapy has the potential to alleviate the painful symptoms and complications associated with sickle cell disease. 

This innovative treatment can greatly improve the quality of life for those affected and reduce the burden on the healthcare system in the long run. 

It is crucial that NICE reconsiders its decision and ensures that gene editing therapy remains available to sickle cell patients in the UK, particularly those from the African and Caribbean community who are disproportionately affected by this condition. 

Denying access to this potentially transformative treatment would be a significant setback in the fight against health inequalities and would leave our community without hope for a better future. 

Moreover, the decision to stop the availability of gene editing therapy for sickle cell patients sends a troubling message about the priorities of our healthcare system. 



<!-- page 239 -->

It suggests that the lives and well-being of those affected by this condition, who are predominantly from the African and Caribbean community, are not valued as highly as they should be. 

This is unacceptable and goes against the principles of equality and fairness that should underpin our society. 

I urge NICE to reverse its decision and work towards making gene therapy for sickle cell disease more widely accessible. 

The African and Caribbean community in the UK deserves the same opportunities for improved health outcomes as any other group. 

By investing in and supporting this innovative treatment, we can take a significant step towards addressing the glaring health inequalities that have persisted for far too long. 

Thank you for your attention to this critical matter. 

I sincerely hope that NICE will reconsider its position and prioritise the health and well-being of the African and Caribbean community in the UK, especially those affected by sickle cell disease. 

Yours sincerely,

This context of inadequate care provision should influence the recommendation **Are the summaries of clinical and cost effectiveness reasonable interpretations of the evidence?** 

In the UK, 15,000 people are affected by sickle cell disease (SCD) and more than 300 babies are born with the condition each year. It affects a lot of different races and the two largest populations in the world are in Africa & India. SCD is the UK’s largest genetically inherited disorder and fastest growing. Around five years ago the UK needed 150 donors per day to treat patients with SCD. Now the need is around 250 donors per day. It is a life-long chronic condition which causes multi-morbidity, disability and premature death - It is characterised by: - repeated unpredictable sickle-cell crises which require emergency medical treatment in A&E, the most inefficient, costly way to manage chronic conditions - long stay admissions costing the NHS hundreds of thousands of pounds each time - chronic excruciating pain experienced at multiple sites around the body, often simultaneously - inability to either get a job or keep a job due to frequent sickness absence - stigma, loss of self worth, impaired mental health impacting social / family life 

**Are there any aspects of the recommendations that need particular consideration to ensure we avoid unlawful discrimination against any group of people on the grounds of age, disability, gender reassignment, pregnancy and maternity, race, religion or belief, sex or sexual orientation?** 

Discrimination on the grounds of race - The quality of care for non-white people, living with sickle-cell anaemia as a chronic condition, typically does not meet requirements in terms of the 6 domains of quality - safe, effective, patientcentred, timely, efficient, equitable. Statistics highlight annually preventable and premature deaths in people living with sickle-cell anaemia. 



<!-- page 242 -->

There is unacceptable variation in service provision and deterioration in standards across the board continue to occur as budgetary cuts deepen. Treatment options are extremely limited compared to other inherited conditions such as cystic fibrosis. The above is an outline of the devastating impact of sickle-cell anaemia on an individual and their loved ones in the current context of access to services, care and outcomes. It is unacceptable that although we have known about this condition for more than a century so little has been done to radically transform the quality of life and life expectancy for the significant population who live with this condition (see the AllParty Parliamentary Group (APPG) on Sickle Cell and Thalassaemia’s Report, No One’s Listening, 2022). ‘Reducing inequalities’ is repeatedly set out as a key priority for integrated health and care systems - Given that Casgevy results in 100% success for those who can complete the treatment and it has been use since 2019 in the USA, the evidence is surely overwhelming and the time is now, for a step-change in care. NICE must reconsider and rule in favour of Casgevy to make it available on the NHS forthwith.

As a mother with a daughter with sickle cell. I am writing to express my deep concern and disappointment regarding the recent decision by the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) to potentially stop the availability of gene therapy for sickle cell patients in the United Kingdom. This decision is a blow to my daughter and to our community, which has long faced significant health inequalities, especially when it comes to sickle cell disease. 



<!-- page 245 -->

The impact of sickle cell disease on the Black community is staggering. In England, Black people are over 80 times more likely to have sickle cell disease compared to White people. 

Furthermore, the mortality rate for sickle cell patients in the UK is alarmingly high, with an estimated 1 in 16 individuals with sickle cell disease dying before the age of 18. These statistics highlight the urgent need for effective treatments like the CRISPR gene editing therapy to be made available to the African and Caribbean community. The health inequalities faced by the African and Caribbean community in the UK are well-documented. 

A report by the NHS Race and Health Observatory found that Black people in the UK have a life expectancy that is up to four years shorter than their White counterparts. 

Furthermore, Black people are more likely to experience poor health outcomes across a range of conditions, including sickle cell disease. Gene therapy offers a revolutionary approach to treating sickle cell disease by addressing the root cause of the condition. 

By modifying the patient’s own stem cells to produce healthy red blood cells, gene therapy has the potential to alleviate the painful symptoms and complications associated with sickle cell disease. 

This innovative treatment can greatly improve the quality of life for those affected and reduce the burden on the healthcare system in the long run. It is crucial that NICE reconsiders its decision and ensures that gene editing therapy remains available to sickle cell patients in the UK, particularly those from the African and Caribbean community who are disproportionately affected by this condition. 

Denying access to this potentially transformative treatment would be a significant setback in the fight against health inequalities and would leave our community without hope for a better future. 

The decision to stop the availability of gene editing therapy for sickle cell patients sends a troubling message about the priorities of our healthcare system. 

It suggests that the lives and well-being of those affected by this condition, who are predominantly from the African and Caribbean community, are not valued as highly as they should be. 

This is unacceptable and goes against the principles of equality and fairness that should underpin our society. 

I urge NICE to reverse its decision and work towards making gene therapy for sickle cell disease more widely accessible. 

The African and Caribbean community in the UK deserves the same opportunities for improved health outcomes as any other group.  There are about 11 thousand suffers of Cystic Fibrosis in the UK and over 33 treatments available to them. Compared to 17 thousand suffers of Sickle Cell with less than 5 treatments available to them. 

I hope that NICE will reconsider its position and prioritise the health and well-being of the African and Caribbean community in the UK, especially those affected by sickle cell disease.
