## **Comment on draft guidance consultation:** 

•The negative impact that severe sickle cell has on the day to day life of the condition 

Sickle Cell Disease (HbSS) is an inherited disorder present from birth.  The sickle haemoglobin becomes rigid and sticks together causing the long premature breakdown of the red blood cells resulting in low blood count (haemolytic anaemia) and 2) vaso-occlusion which is the sticking of red blood cells in small blood cells resulting in down-stream lack of oxygen to the tissues and therefore damage to the organs affected. Information around sickle cell has not fully been grasped therefore information needed to help the patients are suppressed. For instance the severity of our blood cells imploding rapidly in our bodies and releasing haem (can be seen as poison in the blood stream) which has severe impact on our day to day lives. 

Sickle cell severely impacts our activities of daily living. Such as cooking, cleaning, remembering to take medication, laundry, shopping, managing our personal finances, communication and taking transport. Because patients have learnt to cope with their daily lives because of the lack of education and knowledge surrounding the illness due systemic racism, we’ve adapted to being unsupported. Not only is the physical impact of sickle cell crushing, the emotional and mental challenges are worse. The emotional and mental impact of sickle cell is what is medically ignored the most because of lack of funding that goes into adequate teaching and global recognition. Therefore this means the day to day challenges of sickle patients is intensified because the challenges are ignored and suppressed by the medical industry. Sickle cell patients are relied on to teach, be volunteers for the medical industry while also being gaslighted about the condition. This means sickle cell patients are most likely to be discriminated against. 

•The worsening impact that sickle cell has over time 



<!-- page 255 -->

The mental and emotional turmoil developed over time by realising that we are scape goats in the medical industry and no one truly cares despite the performative activism we are constantly exposed to. The damage to our organs from being exposed constantly to a sickle cell crisis that is severely under managed by health professionals we are meant to trust and be grateful for. Sickle cell patients are constantly abused and discriminated against which leads to severe emotional damage that can lead to severe depression or worse,suicide. 

The worse impact is realising nobody is really coming to help or save us and the performative helo is nothing but politics. The fact that pharmaceutical companies are willing to invest millions in research for medication but not thousands for proper training and education speaks volumes to the sickle cell community. Sickle cell receives low and unfair equity as opposed to cystic fibrosis that receives up to 9 times more funding and education. The exposure to racism and discrimination is directly linked to poor health management as you realise we are the sole authors of our care and health. 

•The impact of sickle cell on life expectancy and risk of mortality 

The risk of mortality is extremely high in the sickle cell community because of the exposure to systemic racism, discrimination and ignorance. Because of the lack of equity and funding that goes into sickle cell patients, we are more exposed to premature deaths when we visit Accident & Emergency department. The lack of resources and education given at university stage for medical students perpetuates the ignorance shown in hospital. Our life expectancy has direct links to being exposed to sickle cell abuse and poor treatment. If that if combined with inadequate funding, that then becomes the perfect cocktail for a shorted life expectancy and a high rate of mortality.

It is inconsistent to acknowledge both the absence of alternative options and the urgent necessity for additional treatment avenues to enhance the quality and longevity of life for those afflicted by this disease, yet dismiss the handful of promising healthcare advancements. Upon reviewing the consultation and considering the shortened lifespan of individuals with severe Sickle Cell, it becomes apparent that the lifetime cost of treatment may actually be less than that of a cure due to the shorter life expectancy associated with the condition. Therefore, the summaries of clinical and cost effectiveness may not offer reasonable interpretations of the evidence in this particular scenario. I urge NICE to revisit their approach, engaging with and researching a broader spectrum of sufferers to gain a more comprehensive understanding of why it is imperative to provide a cure for those who have no alternative options. **Are there any aspects of the recommendations that need particular consideration to ensure we avoid unlawful discrimination against any group of people on the grounds of age, disability, gender reassignment, pregnancy and maternity, race, religion or belief, sex or sexual orientation?** 

The consultation rightly acknowledges the challenges faced by Sickle Cell sufferers in accessing adequate management and treatment, whether due to intentional barriers or lack of awareness. However, the rejection of this curative method risks perpetuating the same injustices faced by those whose lives and struggles are deemed unworthy of available treatments. Whether intentional or not, this recommendation inadvertently discriminates against Sickle Cell sufferers, denying them access to a cure that is available to others worldwide. It's imperative to ensure equitable access to treatments for all individuals, regardless of their demographic background, and to prevent any form of unlawful discrimination. We must not only acknowledge instances where this equity is lacking, such as in the 'No One's Listening' report, but also take proactive steps to provide access to cures, as demonstrated by this curative method now available in the UK.

## **Comment on draft guidance consultation:** 

As a mother of a two-year-old living with Sickle Cell, I am deeply disheartened by the apparent lack of understanding from NICE regarding the profound challenges faced by those born with this condition. My son was born just weeks after 'Crizanlizumab' was greenlit for NHS use. By 10 months old, he had already undergone three blood transfusions and was placed on hydroxycarbamide to manage his condition. 

Both sufferers and healthcare professionals assured me that the landscape was changing, offering hope for a more manageable life. Gene therapy is now here as a potential cure. Yet, in just two short years, it's become painfully clear that progress has not matched expectations. While progress is being made in other countries, the availability of treatments for the Sickle Cell community in the UK seems to be falling behind. Despite the availability of treatments and potential cures, there's a glaring disparity in access and understanding, even within our own healthcare system. 

The fact that treatments exist to alleviate pain and prolong life isn't reason enough for approval here, despite their adoption in other countries. The NHS should set the gold standard for care, yet reports like 'No One's Listening' and tragic cases like Evan Nathan Smith's death underscore the urgent need for a reevaluation of our stance on making these curative methods accessible. 

I urge you to reconsider your position and make these curative methods available to those who desperately need them. Additionally, measures should be taken to streamline access to existing treatments for those fortunate enough to have HLA-matched donors. I am more than willing to provide further insights if needed.

## **Are the recommendations sound and a suitable basis for guidance to the NHS?** 

The recommendations are not a sound or suitable basis for NHS guidance in a rare disease, such as such as sickle-cell disease - an inherited chronic debilitating life, shortening disorder, 

A more collaborative and flexible approach should be employed, including consensus, building methodologies, such as Delphi studies, which were favoured by the EU, which funded considerable research into their use in public health matters in the 1990s. In addition consensus methodology is acceptable for the generation of SIGN guidelines 

## **Are the summaries of clinical and cost effectiveness reasonable interpretations of the evidence?** 

The methodology which the NICE process routinely follows is not appropriate for assessing drugs or treatments for use in rare diseases because of the issue of sample size which indeed dogs research in rare diseases. 

The patient numbers which are typically achievable in studies of novel treatments for rare diseases such as sickle cell are small. When sample sizes are small confidence intervals are bound to be wide. As a result, uncertainty becomes the inevitable outcome of health, economic evaluations based on clinical trials of new treatments for rare diseases. Unfortunately evidence based medicine, judges treatments, whose effectiveness is surrounded by economic uncertainty, unsuitable for routine use. 

This in turn means that for methodological  reasons, new treatments are not recommended, even though as in the case for casgevy the one study so far showed clinically interesting results with a 93.5% reduction in the endpoint of veno occlusive  episodes 

As stated previously NICE perhaps needs to adapt the methodology, it is using me to assess drugs such as Casgevy  to match the clinical settings in which drugs for rare diseases are researched and could be used to change lives

## **Are the summaries of clinical and cost effectiveness reasonable interpretations of the evidence?** 

Sickle-cell anaemia is by far the most common inherited condition in the UK and the numbers are rising. 

It begins to have a significant impact on physical health within the first year of life It is a life-long chronic condition which causes multi-morbidity, - disability and premature death It is characterised by: 



<!-- page 263 -->

- repeated unpredictable sickle-cell crises which require emergency medical treatment in A&E, the most inefficient, costly way to manage chronic conditions 

- long stay admissions costing the NHS hundreds of thousands of pounds each time 

- chronic excruciating pain experienced at multiple sites around the body, often simultaneously 

- inability to either get a job or keep a job due to frequent sickness absence - stigma, loss of self worth, impaired mental health impacting social / family life 

Each time a person has an acute sickle-cell crisis they risk complications of infection, damage to any internal organ of the body - lung, brain, liver, kidney, skin, eye, gallbladder, spleen, bowel - and most frightening of all for the individual, a significant risk of death during each hospital admission 

After each sickle-cell crisis, physical and mental health deteriorate, increasing a person’s morbidity, resulting in a poorer quality of life . I don't think sufficient predictive costings have been made over life course for the number of people living with sickle including the social and societal cost. This then needs to be compared with the costs of treatment and figures around proportion who will experience a 100% cure if treatment is completed and no longer need care for acute relapsing illness

While evidence was considered, it does not appear to have been fully comprehensive. It's important to recognise that living with sickle cell disease (SCD) can be incredibly challenging. Black individuals are disproportionately affected by this disease, and there's extensive research showing that they often face difficulties in articulating their pain and health challenges. This is largely due to systemic racism, lack of trust in healthcare systems that are still structurally biased, and inadequate health literacy. 

Having worked in health sector, I've witnessed firsthand how SCD tragically impacts many young lives, often preventing them from working or maintaining personal relationships or healthy mental well-being. The excruciating pain associated with SCD affects the entire body, permeating through the blood and impacting all organs of those affected. Therefore, it's clear that not all pertinent evidence has been taken into account.

No, the recommendations should support the approval of funding. Diseases that disproportionately affect Black communities are often under-researched and under-funded. It's time to change this pattern and prioritize funding for treatments like this within the NHS. Let's take a step towards closing the gap in health inequalities.

1. Audit transplant related consultations in patients 1 years post-BMT: A key issue in the assessment of efficacy is whether a 12-month assessment is an appropriate and representative time-point to assess the long-term effects of a myeloablative therapy. To address this, Dania El Tabech & Josu de la Fuente audited the relationship of allogeneic transplantation for sickle cell disease to long-term outcomes in 65 consecutive transplants at St Mary’s Hospital, Imperial College Healthcare. This can be treated as a representative cohort, not only because over two thirds of all allogenic transplant in the UK have been conducted in this centre, but also because approximately 50% of the allogeneic transplants with complete data in the European Society for Blood & Marrow Transplantation (EBMT) come from this centre. Six transplants were excluded due to not having reached a minimum 12 months follow-up and five due to transplant related mortality. The transplant procedures included a combination of related, unrelated and haploidentical stem cell sources, and both myeloablative and reduced intensity approaches, avoiding the outcomes to be skewed by a particular approach. With a median follow up of 3 years (range 1-8 years) 54 consecutive transplants with a minimum 12 months follow-up were audited with a median age of 15.24 years. No patient with successful engraftment had sickle related complications at 12 months. One patient had a subsequent secondary graft failure at 3 years. None of the 54 patients without sickle related events at 12 months went on to develop a sickle related event at subsequent follow up, indicating that the 12 months assessment is an appropriate and sufficient time point to assess efficacy. 2. The NHP was established in 2019 to provide a team of experts in the management of sickle cell disease SCD and dedicated experts in cellular therapy (bone marrow transplantation and gene therapy) to assess and screen complex patients presented by specialist centres across the country, including discussion and selection of cases to be referred for bone marrow transplantation. The monthly video MDT started in April 2020 and by March 2024 total of 109 cases had been discussed. Following discussion by experts, 76 cases an average of 20 cases per year) were approved for referral for BMT. However, following an audit of those approved to proceed to BMT, 75.5% are proceeding with the recommendation for stem cell transplantation and 22.45% declined to proceed with transplantation for various reasons. This shows that sickle cell patients given adequate information and enabled to participate in shared decision making are able to choose an option must suited to their individual situation. The recommendation should reflect the fact cases that are considered for gene therapy are those who despite the severe phenotype do not have another option to receive proper care. The recommendation should carefully offer those patients with severe VOCs that are not eligible to for bone marrow transplantation and may not be amenable to other high-risk therapies. Gene therapy uses endogenous graft and therefore free of graft versus host disease complication.

**Are the summaries of clinical and cost effectiveness reasonable interpretations of the evidence?** 

Sickle Cell Disease – Burden and Quality of Life 

Research indicates that individuals with Sickle Cell Disease (SCD) face significant challenges that impact their quality of life across various domains. A systematic review focussing on the effects of hematopoietic stem cell transplant (HSCT) and gene therapy on health-related quality of life (HRQOL) in patients with SCD and thalassemia revealed that these therapies are associated with positive effects across most HRQOL domains for SCD. Notably, in SCD, HSCT was linked with large positive effects in all HRQOL domains, suggesting improvements in HRQOL outcomes following gene therapy in addition. 

Reference: 

Sherif M. et al. A systematic review of quality of life in sickle cell disease and thalassemia after stem cell transplant or gene therapy. Blood Adv 2021; 5 (2): 570–583. 

https://doi.org/10.1182/bloodadvances.2020002948 

Pain is a hallmark symptom of SCD and has a profound impact on the HRQOL of affected individuals. A recent global study emphasised this profound impact of SCD on HRQOL, particularly among adults with recurrent vaso-occlusive crises (VOCs). It was found that these individuals experience significant disruptions to daily life due to recurrent pain crises and chronic pain, leading to substantial impairments in their ability to work and overall HRQOL. The study, which included surveys and interviews, reported lower than average scores in several HRQOL domains, including - physical and emotional well being, compared to the general population. A 



<!-- page 270 -->

notable percentage of respondents also reported experiencing pain, discomfort, anxiety, depression, and mobility impairment. 

## Reference: 

Jennifer Drahos, et al Blood 2022; 140 (Supplement 1): 1387–1388. https://doi.org/10.1182/blood-2022-157818 

Furthermore, chronic pain, acute pain crises and hospitalisations significantly reduce physical functioning, emotional well-being, and social activities, leading to a deterioration in overall HRQOL and decreased QALYs. 

## References: 

Anie KA, et al (2012).  Patient self-assessment of hospital pain, mood and health-related quality of life in adults with sickle cell disease. BMJ Open, 2, e001274. doi:10.1136/bmjopen-2012-001274. 

McClish DK, Penberthy LT, Bovbjerg VE, et al. Health related quality of life in sickle cell patients: The PiSCES project. Health Qual Life Outcomes. 2005;3:50. doi:10.1186/1477-7525-3-50. 

Smith WR, Penberthy LT, Bovbjerg VE, et al. Daily assessment of pain in adults with sickle cell disease. Ann Intern Med. 2008;148(2):94-101. doi:10.7326/0003-4819-148-2-200801150-00004. 

Comparison with General Population and Other Chronic Diseases Studies consistently demonstrate that individuals with SCD experience lower HRQOL compared to the general population. Moreover, comparisons with other chronic diseases such as cystic fibrosis and asthma reveal similar or even lower HRQOL scores among patients SCD patients. 

## Reference: 

McClish DK, Penberthy LT, Bovbjerg VE, Roberts JD, Aisiku IP, Levenson JL, Roseff SD, Smith WR. Health related quality of life in sickle cell patients: the PiSCES project. Health Qual Life Outcomes. 2005; 29; 3:50. doi: 10.1186/1477-7525-3-50. 

**Are there any aspects of the recommendations that need particular consideration to ensure we avoid unlawful discrimination against any group of people on the grounds of age, disability, gender reassignment, pregnancy and maternity, race, religion or belief, sex or sexual orientation?** 

SCD is a chronic, life-limiting, and debilitating condition that causes significant morbidity and mortality. In patients with severe SCD (with frequent vaso-occlusive episodes) mortality and morbidity are increased even further. SCD is characterised by haemolytic anaemia, widespread organ damage, unpredictable episodes of severe pain called VOC (‘vaso occlusive crisis’) and shortened life expectancy SCD has significant negative emotional, social and quality-of-life (QoL) effects on patients, and also their families on a daily basis. 



<!-- page 271 -->

The committee asked for additional data on mortality and QoL: British Journal of Haem VOLUME 189 SUPPLEMENT 1 (Baba Inusa, John James et al, 2020) shows that patients with SCD are affected by a myriad of complications and associated chronic multi-organ comorbidities. There is extensive recent literature (including studies from the UK) that consistently demonstrates that SCD patients have a significantly reduced life expectancy which is further reduced for patients with severe SCD/recurrent VOCs. 

These figures are consistent across cultures and over time with a lack of significant improvement over the last few decades even if optimal treatment is available see summary from SWAY study. In light this, it is clear that a whole population of patients is being gravely underserved. 

The main aim of treatment is to achieve cure but there is currently no such therapy available and therefore the main therapy is to prevent infection by using penicillin prophylaxis, vitamin supplementation using folic acid and the only disease modifying therapy is hydroxyurea which has been in use for over 35years. Current therapies offer only palliation but do not eliminate the symptoms and even though treatment improves the quality of life in many, not all patients respond to treatment. 

While in 2017 L-Glutamine, and 2019 both Crizanlizumab and Voxelotor were FDA approved, neither L-Glutamine, Voxelotor nor Crizanlizumab have been supported by NICE.

In England, we are over 80 times more likely to have sickle cell<br>disease compared to White people.<br>Furthermore, the mortality rate for sickle cell patients in the UK is alarmingly<br>high, with an estimated 1 in 16 individuals with sickle cell disease dying<br>before the age of 18.<br>These statistics highlight the urgent need for effective treatments like the<br>CRISPR gene editing therapy to be made available to the African and<br>Caribbean community.<br>The health inequalities faced by the African and Caribbean community in<br>the UK are well-documented.||





<!-- page 281 -->

We are more likely to experience poverty, discrimination, and barriers to accessing quality healthcare. 

A report by the NHS Race and Health Observatory found that Black people in the UK have a life expectancy that is up to four years shorter than their White counterparts. 

Furthermore, we are more likely to experience poor health outcomes across a range of conditions, including sickle cell disorder. 

Gene therapy offers a revolutionary approach to treating sickle cell disease by addressing the root cause of the condition. 

By modifying the patient’s own stem cells to produce healthy red blood cells, gene therapy has the potential to alleviate the painful symptoms and complications associated with sickle cell disease. 

This innovative treatment can greatly improve the quality of life for those affected and reduce the burden on the healthcare system in the long run. 

It is crucial that NICE reconsiders its decision and ensures that gene editing therapy remains available to sickle cell patients in the UK, particularly those from the African and Caribbean community who are disproportionately affected by this condition. 

Denying access to this potentially transformative treatment would be a significant setback in the fight against health inequalities and would leave our community without hope for a better future. 

Moreover, the decision to stop the availability of gene editing therapy for sickle cell patients sends a troubling message about the priorities of our healthcare system. 

It suggests that the lives and well-being of those affected by this condition, who are predominantly from the African and Caribbean community, are not valued as highly as they should be. 

This is unacceptable and goes against the principles of equality and fairness that should underpin our society. 

I urge NICE to reverse its decision and work towards making gene therapy for sickle cell disease more widely accessible. 

The African and Caribbean community in the UK deserves the same opportunities for improved health outcomes as any other group. 

By investing in and supporting this innovative treatment, we can take a significant step towards addressing the glaring health inequalities that have persisted for far too long. 



<!-- page 282 -->

Thank you for your attention to this critical matter. 

Yours sincerely,

of Medicine. The efficacy results are beyond expectation and it is hard to see how any trial could produce more positive results. ## **Are the summaries of clinical and cost effectiveness reasonable interpretations of the evidence?** 

The negative opinion is influenced by uncertainty about mortality rates and complication rates, but the committee has an acceptable body of evidence to make these estimates. In my opinion, the mortality and chronic morbidity seen with standard care for SCD would be completely prevented if Exa-cel is offered to  young patients who have not yet developed irreversible complications. 

I have commented in the document on the application of the 3.5% discount rate, which I think is unfair. For this kind of one-off curative treatment, where costs are incurred up front, the discount rate has a particular negative effect. The three criteria for a discount rate of 1.5% are met, and if the discount is to be applied, it  should be at  this rate. 

I also don't understand why SCD would not qualify for the highest severity modifier. The life expectancy is estimated at 

50 for the whole population, and lower for severely affected patients. This is at least 20 years less than the general population. This alone would account for >17 QALYS before even considering morbidities associated with reduced QOL 

## **Are there any aspects of the recommendations that need particular consideration to ensure we avoid unlawful discrimination against any group of people on the grounds of age, disability, gender reassignment, pregnancy and maternity, race, religion or belief, sex or sexual orientation?** 

I am concerned that the committee's negative opinion is influenced by uncertainties about disease outcomes with standard care. The deficiencies in data on long-term outcomes in the UK SCD population may be difficult to address where there is inadequate funding and resources to undertake the necessary studies. This was highlighted as an aspect of inequality in the APPG 'No one's Listening' report. 

**Comment on section 3.2 (Treatment options), “Regular blood transfusions may be required, which also means iron chelation therapy may also be considered”:** 

The committee should also be aware that 10- 20% of patients cannot be transfused because they have developed red cell antibodies which limit the availability of compatible blood or have severe haemolytic reactions when transfused with apparently compatible blood. 



<!-- page 287 -->

**Comment on section 3.2 (Treatment options), “Clinical experts noted that exa** ‑ **cel could offer a chance at disease-free survival, improved organ function, reduced symptoms such as VOCs and reduced healthcare use. But, they noted that people with mild SCD and few VOCs are less likely to derive benefit from exa** ‑ **cel and the treatment risks may outweigh any benefit”:** 

I agree with these comments from the clinical experts, but would add that many of the younger patients who would be eligible for exa-cel could be treated before they develop any significant organ dysfunction, and would therefore have normal rather than improved organ function after treatment. Also, it is difficult to predict the long-term health outcome for patients who are apparently mildly affected with few VOC's in adolescence and early adulthood. A significant proportion of patients who do not have frequent VOC's have evidence of severe haemolytic anaemia and may develop chronic complications such as pulmonary hypertension and renal impairment in their 4th or 5th decade, as documented in studies referenced in this guidance document. The natural history of these complications is not yet sufficiently clarified, and require results from long-term cohort studies which are not yet mature. 

**Comment on section 3.5 (Clinical trial evidence), “It also noted that more data collection to establish the long-term effectiveness of exa** ‑ **cel would reduce the uncertainties around durability of the treatment effect.”:** 

The committee should also consider the supportive data on long-term cure from numerous publications on  allogeneic stem cell transplantation in children and adults with SCD. Exa-cel treatment is expected to produce the same or better outcomes. It involves  the same procedure: use of harvested stem cells which are infused into recipient after myeloablation with chemotherapy. The long-term persistence and safety is expected to be superior, because exa-cel uses autologous rather than allogeneic stem cells, so there is no risk of graft versus host disease and less risk of rejection. 

## **Comment on section 3.14 (Non-reference case discount rate):** 

I question the  application of a reference case discount rate, although apparently standard practice in NICE assessments. My understanding is that this is based on the premise that the public prefers not to pay the full cost of treatment up-front, when the health benefits are achieved over a lifetime. Has this been verified by public consultation in the case of curative therapy for a life - shortening, debilitating disease, affecting a minority population, and where a novel gene therapy technology is concerned? It seems fairer to make a balanced health economic assessment where the full life-time costs of standard care, and the full additional social costs associated with lost productivity and QOL for patient and carers are taken 



<!-- page 288 -->

into account, without discounting. If the discounting is to be done, it seems clear to me that the 1.5% conditions are met for SCD 

**Comment on section 3.15 (Non-reference case discount rate), “The committee considered the third criterion was not met, concluding that** ‑ **it may be plausible that exa cel benefits were sustained over a long period. But it noted that this was highly uncertain given the limited follow up of clinical evidence. So it would like to see this explored with further data collection (see section 3.23).”:** 

The effects of exa-cel are highly likely to be sustained. Evidence from alloHSCT can be extrapolated. The durability is likely to be improved compared to allo-HSCT given that the risks of rejection are minimal and the risks of GVHD are zero 

**Comment on section 3.15 (Non-reference case discount rate), “When considering the second criterion, the committee noted considerable** ‑ **uncertainty with the likelihood of exa cel returning people to full or near-full health. It understood from experts that exa** ‑ **cel would reduce the risk of complications, but it was not clear whether persistent damage from complications and comorbidities would be reversed. The committee considered the second criterion was not met, concluding that it may be plausible that exa-cel returns people to full or near fullhealth. But, it noted the uncertainty was compounded by the shortterm follow up of the clinical-effectiveness evidence and that further data could allow the committee to consider if this criterion was met”:** 

As commented above, the evidence on returning people to full or nearly full health can be extrapolated from experience with allogeneic HSCT. It is clear from the CLIMB study data that patients are cured, with reversal of anaemia, haemolysis and absence of true vaso-occlusive events.   For subjects meeting criteria for treatment who have not yet developed any significant chronic complications, there would be no risk of subsequently developing chronic complications of SCD. A query of data in  the East London Sickle Cohort study ( patients with SCD diagnosed at birth from 1983 to the present and followed in NHS hospitals) 39 of 267 patients with HbSS met the inclusion criteria for Exa cel treatment, 33 of them between the age 12 and 18. Of these only one had a chronic complication (AVN hip). This younger population, if treated before age 18 would be cured by Exa-cel without any long-term complication developing 

**Comment on section 3.15 (Non-reference case discount rate), “The committee concluded that the first criterion for using a 1.5% discount rate was not met because there was insufficient evidence to show that people would otherwise die or have a severely impaired life.”:** 

I don't understand how the committee can come to this conclusion. Evidence from the literature has been presented that the mean life expectancy for the treated population with standard care is 53 years at the most optimistic estimate. This is more than 20 years less than a normal 



<!-- page 289 -->

population. Furthermore, there can be no question that repeated episodes of pain requiring hosptial admission, chronic pain and fatigue, and the increasing risk of morbidities such as renal impairment, pulmonary hypertension, impaired mobility due to avascular necrosis of hips, spine, visual impairment, and other morbdities etc, must severely impair life. The committee has heard testimonies from patients and clinicians and there is a very substantial literature documenting these effects 

**Comment on section 3.8 (Standard care mortality modelling), “It considered that the company's SMRs were more representative of the severe SCD population, but concluded that further validation is needed about the most accurate life expectancy for people having standard care.”:** 

These estimates of survival with standard care are reasonable and it is difficult to see what additional evidence can feasibly by provided. The cooperative study of sickle cell disease (CSSD) estimate of survival from a large population in USA followed carefully over >10 years gave an estimated median survival of 42 years for men and 48 for women. VOC was a significant predictor of worse survival. (Platt et al, NEJM 1994). More recent estimates based on less robust data quality do reflect improved care and availability of hydroxycarbamide, both of which have probably improved survival. The committee is aware of the more recent papers, and have selected the paper of Jiao et al (2023) which is based on USA patients covered by state health care schemes. The estimated survival of 53 years would be a most optimistic estimate, and does not account for the negative effect of frequent VOC's which are a feature of the population to be treated with. Exa-cel. I am CI for the E London Newborn Cohort study which is following patients followed from birth in the NHS and treated in E London (Telfer et al, Haematologica 2007 and subsequent abstracts at ASH and EHA). There are currently about 420 patients in the cohort, the oldest 40 years of age.  it is not yet possible to estimate median survival, but we have observed a significant increase in mortality rate in young adults between 15 and 25 years of age, and this has also been observed in the Dallas newborn cohort study (Quinn et al, Blood. 2010;115(17):3447-3452). 

I think it is unreasonable to make a negative judgement based on the uncertainty of the survival estimate, when the model has a reasonable estimate based on the most optimistic assumptions. In my view, the mean standard-care survival estimate for the eligible population is certainly less than 53 years. 

**Comment on section 3.9 (Long term treatment effects), “The company and clinical experts explained that VOCs are often seen after allogeneic HSCTs and people may still have pain events, particularly for the first year after the HSCT.”:** 

The evidence of outcomes after sibling allogeneic stem cell transplantation for SCD is very relevant here. Adults who go into transplantation with a past history of frequent VOC's may continue to have pain episodes for several years after the procedure, but are functionally cured. The reason for the 



<!-- page 290 -->

continued pain is that these patients have developed a complex pain syndrome (chronic pain) which is not directly related to Vaso-occlusion from sickled red cells. It is highly likely that this phenomenon will be observed in adults receiving Exa-cel, but less likely if the therapy is prioritised for teenagers and young adults who are less likely to have developed a chronic pain syndrome. 

**Comment on section 3.11 (Complication rates), “The committee concluded that directly estimating complications from the Brousse et al. (2023) severe population was most appropriate but that there was uncertainty associated with the estimated frequency of SCD complications.”:** 

Please see comment about the publication of Piel et al, which may provide more certainty of estimate 

**Comment on section 3.11 (Complication rates), “. The EAG assessed the effect on the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER) of using different complication rates, including directly modelling those from the literature (including Brousse et al. 2023, Shah et al. 2019 and the company's BOI study). It found that the ICER was sensitive to how complications were modelled. Clinical experts reviewed the complications from the literature and said that they were plausible. But they noted that there were some significant complications missing from the model, such as priapism and acute multi-organ failure”:** 

The study of Piel et al (Blood Cells, Molecules and Diseases 89 (2021)) assesses mortality and co-morbidities in a UK population using HES data over the period 2009-2018 and may be more representative than a French or US population 

**Comment on section 3.16 (Severity), “It noted that the condition disproportionately affects people from areas with higher levels of deprivation and considered how this could bias the estimates.”:** 

I believe that the absence of sufficiently convincing data, for instance on survival estimates, disease severity and quality of life, are examples of inequity. The All Party Parliamentary Group report 'No one's listening' and other reports highlight the inequality in health care provision for SCD compared to other long-term conditions in the NHS, and also highlight the paucity of research in SCD outcomes and treatments, which is another aspect of inequality. The difficulty for the committee in estimating important outcomes in SCD, including mortality rates and quality of life, reflect the reduced resources and funding available for these studies. As Chief investigator for the East London Sickle Cell Newborn Cohort Study, I can confirm that it is extremely difficult to obtain funding to sustain a long-term study into the natural history of this condition for NHS patients, which would help to answer some of these questions where uncertainty persists. There is - a risk of the situation becoming self fulfilling, where evidence cannot be 



<!-- page 291 -->

produced to satisfy regulatory committees and funders because of scarcity of funding opportunities and resources 

**Comment on section 3.16 (Severity), “The committee took into account the quantitative estimates and any possible changes to these estimates due to uncaptured benefits and uncertainties. It did not consider that the threshold for a severity modifier was met but noted the uncertainty in modelled mortality and complications.”:** 

I do not understand how SCD would not be treated as a high level severe condition. The following section is copied and pasted from the NICE reference document on severity modifiers: 

Severity is to be calculated as “Absolute Shortfall” (AS) and “Proportional Shortfall” (PS). Both express the difference between Quality Adjusted Life Years (QALYs) over remaining life expectancy for the general population compared to those with the health condition, conditional on age and sex. AS expresses this difference in absolute QALYs. PS expresses this as the ratio of general population QALYs / QALYs for those with the condition. Weights should be applied to incremental QALYs. 

The weight that is to apply is specified in Table 6.1 of the manual and reproduced below. The definition that provides the highest weight is the one that should be used. 

Table 1: QALY weightings for severity QALY weight 

Absolute QALY shortfall 1  Less than 12 

x1.2  12 to 18 

x1.7  At least 18 

If the committee use a mean survival of 53 years,  would this not amount to at least a 20 year loss of life (ie 20 QALY'S) compared to the general population? Within the 53 years of life, would not the reduced quality of life also add to the absolute loss of QALY'S  compared to the general population?

I have concerns in this area. The committee appears to be aware that sickle cell is a very severe and disabling disorder, which has impact on both patients and their families. ## **Are the summaries of clinical and cost effectiveness reasonable interpretations of the evidence?** 

I would challenge whether the quoted cost per QALY has considered the cost of not treating patients with a treatment with as high an efficacy as Exacel. Patients are not only unable to work, but often use substantial hospital resources when unwell (repeated, prolonged admissions; transfusions; medications), and their family members (even if not themselves unwell) are often themselves unable to work to be care givers. The cost per QALY would be far more favourable if this was accurately considered.

**Are the summaries of clinical and cost effectiveness reasonable interpretations of the evidence?** 

No. It is more costly in the long run to continue to treat sickle cell patients as is the case now, than a one off cure. 

**Are there any aspects of the recommendations that need particular consideration to ensure we avoid unlawful discrimination against any group of people on the grounds of age, disability, gender reassignment, pregnancy and maternity, race, religion or belief, sex or sexual orientation?** 

Yes. Sickle cell is a minority illness, so the vast majority of people will see it as discrimination against the minority groups who suffer the disease. 

## **Comment on draft guidance consultation:** 

Sickle cell has limited options of treatment and it is only in the last few years that a change is occurring. As a carer to sickle cell adults, it is a consistent cycle of pain, hospital admissions and low quality of life. The options available do not give a cure and are laden with side effects that not every one with sickle cell can tolerate. A one time cure will save the constant uncertainty, multiple hospital visits and admissions, costly medicament regimes, and a lack of ability to work that plagues those living with sickle cell. This new treatment brings hope to many who are unable to get a donor for bone marrow transplant. There is no fear of rejection as it is the persons own stem cells unlike bone marrow transplant. Also, lifelong drug regimes are difficult to keep to, and over time becomes ineffective. When more people are given a drug regime that cures, it naturally brings the cost down as more people are subscribed to it. Gene therapy has been used in cancer treatments and some other diseases and it has been found to be effective. I have no doubt in my mind that sickle cell cannot be an exception to effectiveness as a cure. It is pertinent to note that this particular CRISPR technology is directed first for treatment of sickle cell because it is easier to implement as there is only one gene responsible for the disorder unlike other diseases.

|Exacel has been taken into account, however the evidence in relation to||
|clinical consequences and mortality for sickle cell disease has been too||
|broad. The committee discussion references the effects of sickle cell||
|disease but does not focus adequately on the effects of severe sickle cell||





<!-- page 306 -->

disease which is the group of patients this therapy would be used for, and indeed was the population included in the trials to date. This is as opposed to living with pain that may occur in milder forms of the disease, which although significant may not result in hospitalisation for vaso-occlusive crisis (VOC). For example a recent large French study (Arlet et al, Landet Reg Health Eur Apr 2024) focussing on the population of sickle cell patients hospitalised for VOC showed an increased hazard ration for death of up to 3.7 in patients with VOC compared to non-VOC patients. The median age of death of death on patients who died was 49.8 which is significantly lower than the normal population. Of the 8018 patients in the study the overall VOC rate was 30%. We are concerned that the committee discussion did not adequately focus on the relative small proportion of patients with severe sickle cell disease and the relevant clinical and cost effectiveness modelling has therefore not been taken into account. 

In considering the impact of gene therapy it is particularly important to consider gains in quality of life (QoL). A number of transplant studies (most recently Aljaafri et al Onc Stem Cell Ther 2023, Bawdawy et al Blood Advances 2021) demonstrate improved quality of life post-transplant in the context of cure. It is likely these QoL gains would be even greater in the context of gene therapy as unlike stem cell transplant there is no risk of GVHD which is a major factor adversely impacting QoL. 

## **Are the recommendations sound and a suitable basis for guidance to the NHS?** 

We do not believe the recommendations are sound given the wrong assumptions have been used in relation to sickle cell severity as noted above. 

Additionally concerns in relation to the ability to extrapolate a 12 month effect size were thought speculative by the EAG. We note that the committee considered results to be potentially life-changing and our clinical experience would be consistent with this as detailed below. 

A key issue in the assessment of efficacy and cost effectiveness is whether a month 12 assessment is an appropriate and representative time-point to assess the long-term effects of a myeloablative therapy. To address this, Dania El Tabech & Josu de la Fuente audited the relationship of allogeneic transplantation for sickle cell disease to long-term outcomes in 65 consecutive transplants at St Mary’s Hospital, Imperial College Healthcare. This can be treated as a representative cohort, not only because over two thirds of all allogenic transplant in the UK have been conducted in this centre, but also because approximately 50% of the allogeneic transplants with complete data in the European Society for Blood & Marrow Transplantation (EBMT) come from this centre. Six transplants were excluded due to not having reached a minimum 12 months follow-up and five due to transplant related mortality. The transplant procedures included a combination of related, unrelated and haploidentical stem cell sources, and both myeloablative and reduced intensity approaches, avoiding the outcomes to be eschewed by a particular approach. 



<!-- page 307 -->

With a median follow up of 3 years (range 1-8 years) 54 consecutive transplants with a minimum 12 months follow-up were audited with a median age of 15.24 years. No patient with successful engraftment had sickle related complications at 12 months. One patient had a subsequent secondary graft failure at 3 years. None of the 54 patients without sickle related events at 12 months went onto develop a sickle related event at subsequent follow up indicating that the 12 months assessment is an appropriate and sufficient time point to assess efficacy. 

A potential way to address committee uncertainties would be via a managed access programme and we would be supportive of this approach to allow access to potentially curative therapy for sickle cell disease. 

## **Are the summaries of clinical and cost effectiveness reasonable interpretations of the evidence?** 

Again as the data taken by the committee were at the level of the whole sickle patient population rather than the group studied for this therapy- i.e those with a severe phenotype we do not believe this interpretation is adequately balanced. The threshold of returning patients to full health is incredibly high, and above that of a generally accepted gold standard of curative treatment in most disease therapies. 

The discussion notes that a cure is usually assumed after five years in other disease areas. This is normally the case for malignant disease but this concept should not be applied to a non-malignant disorder such as sickle cell disease. In the absence of any known biological mechanism that would reverse gene editing it would not be expected that a non-malignant disease would not recur/relapse. This is in contrast to cancer where evolution of the malignant clone, tumour escape and other immunological mechanisms contribute to relapse. 

## **Are there any aspects of the recommendations that need particular consideration to ensure we avoid unlawful discrimination against any group of people on the grounds of age, disability, gender reassignment, pregnancy and maternity, race, religion or belief, sex or sexual orientation?** 

We note that the committee has discussed the disproportionate health inequality experience in the ethnic population that suffer from sickle cell disease. We think it is critical to note that this population has suffered from a significant lack of investment in relation to research and approved effective therapy available on the NHS. As noted by Lee et al (Pub Health Rep, Dec 2019) this is in significant contrast to patients who are affected by cystic fibrosis, also a genetically inherited disorder but one that is present in white/Caucasian individuals. A decision to fund Exacel would be a major advance in addressing inequities in care that have occurred across decades as noted in the the Sickle Cell and Thalassaemia All-Party Parliamentary Group’s ‘No one’s listening’ report. 



<!-- page 308 -->

Adults with sickle cell disease also suffer from age inequity in that haploidentical transplant which may offer a potential cure is also not funded by the NHS where it is funded in children. There is limited scientific rationale for this decision. This population is also more likely to have related donors that disadvantaged making their ability to donate less certain, increasing further still the attractiveness of an autologous therapy.

A person living with Sickle Cell disease in the UK lives, on average, to 67 years of age, over a decade less than the national average for those without the disease. 

Exa-cel is a new treatment which is licensed by the MHRA to treat severe sickle cell in people aged 12 and over who do not have a matched sibling donor for stem cell transplant, but who would have been well enough to tolerate a transplant. If successful, treatment with exa-cel effectively provides a cure for sickle cell, meaning no more suffering for those who have the disease. It would be the first gene therapy available to treat sickle cell in the UK. 

Whilst I understand NICE draft recommendation that exa-cel should not receive NHS funding as it is not considered cost-effective, I would urge the board to seriously consider the quality of life benefits, as well as extension to life, that this treatment will have for those who suffer from this disease.

|As a member of the African and Caribbean community, I am writing to|

|by the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) to|

<!-- page 311 -->

In the UK, it is estimated that 1 in every 2,000 babies born are affected by sickle cell disease, with the majority being of Black African or Black Caribbean heritage. 

This chronic condition causes immense pain, organ damage, and a significantly reduced life expectancy. Shockingly, the average life expectancy for someone with sickle cell disease in the UK is just 40-60 years, compared to the national average of 81 years. 

The impact of sickle cell disease on the Black community is staggering. In England, Black people are over 80 times more likely to have sickle cell disease compared to White people. 

Furthermore, the mortality rate for sickle cell patients in the UK is alarmingly high, with an estimated 1 in 16 individuals with sickle cell disease dying before the age of 18. 

These statistics highlight the urgent need for effective treatments like the CRISPR gene editing therapy to be made available to the African and Caribbean community. 

The health inequalities faced by the African and Caribbean community in the UK are well-documented. 

Black people are more likely to experience poverty, discrimination, and barriers to accessing quality healthcare. 

A report by the NHS Race and Health Observatory found that Black people in the UK have a life expectancy that is up to four years shorter than their White counterparts. 

Furthermore, Black people are more likely to experience poor health outcomes across a range of conditions, including sickle cell disease. 

Gene therapy offers a revolutionary approach to treating sickle cell disease by addressing the root cause of the condition. 

By modifying the patient’s own stem cells to produce healthy red blood cells, gene therapy has the potential to alleviate the painful symptoms and complications associated with sickle cell disease. 

This innovative treatment can greatly improve the quality of life for those affected and reduce the burden on the healthcare system in the long run. 

It is crucial that NICE reconsiders its decision and ensures that gene editing therapy remains available to sickle cell patients in the UK, particularly those from the African and Caribbean community who are disproportionately affected by this condition. 



<!-- page 312 -->

Denying access to this potentially transformative treatment would be a significant setback in the fight against health inequalities and would leave our community without hope for a better future. 

Moreover, the decision to stop the availability of gene editing therapy for sickle cell patients sends a troubling message about the priorities of our healthcare system. 

It suggests that the lives and well-being of those affected by this condition, who are predominantly from the African and Caribbean community, are not valued as highly as they should be. 

This is unacceptable and goes against the principles of equality and fairness that should underpin our society. 

I urge NICE to reverse its decision and work towards making gene therapy for sickle cell disease more widely accessible. 

The African and Caribbean community in the UK deserves the same opportunities for improved health outcomes as any other group. 

By investing in and supporting this innovative treatment, we can take a significant step towards addressing the glaring health inequalities that have persisted for far too long. 

Thank you for your attention to this critical matter. 

I sincerely hope that NICE will reconsider its position and prioritise the health and well-being of the African and Caribbean community in the UK, especially those affected by sickle cell disease. 

Yours sincerely, 

XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX Civil Servant

This chronic condition causes me immense pain, I have children, but get regularly hospitalised. The pain come on fast for me and leaves me screaming in agony. Pain relief often fails, this is exacerbated by delays in complying with pain relief commissioning requirements, poor care, conflict and confrontation Sickle Cell Warriors experience at the hands of the NHS. We so wish we had access to a cure, removing us from the pain we suffer, the abuse of poor care, the stigma foisted upon us by medical professionals refusing us medication, accusing us of pretending to be ill, drug addiction, fecklessness, needing too much NHS resources. SC is a medical Emergency like a stroke and heart attack, yet people with these conditions are treated perfectly well and receive great healthcare at the point of need. Despite our widely reported burdens as a SC community as stated in your 250 page long Committee report, the associated aspects of anaemia, organ damage, bone and tissue damage, a significantly reduced life expectancy, medical practitioners and Society at large accuse us of faking illness. We so wish there was a cure available to us. The Lancet acclaimed book The Sickle Cell Guide, is meticulously referenced and has an encyclopaedic knowledge of SC.  The understanding of the condition that the book delivers would greatly enable NICE decision makers to appreciate the scope, scale, issues and impacts of the condition across the whole SC medico-social ecosystem. 

Shockingly, the average life expectancy for someone with sickle cell disease in the UK is just 40-60 years, compared to the national average of 81 years. Relationships with benefit departments, and indeed social services can also be traumatic and triggering, plus our deprivation can results in difficulty paying for prescription drugs; and the rationing and going without that results becomes a huge detriment to patient safety. Peer conditions get their treatments and prescriptions free. 

We have seen people cured of sickle cell relieved of the burdens and saving health services millions per person as US studies have found. Being frank the way we are treated in all parts of the sickle cell ecosystem, the failure to enforce makes such policies a waste of time.

**I live with Sickle Cell Disorder** (SCD), **XXXXXXX the award-winning UK Sickle Cell Society for a decade** , and have been a member of multiple NICE steering Committees, as well as NHS Boards and Groups evaluating and approving medicines, pathways, specifications, assurance etc, across different medical conditions, but including SCD, and other rare diseases. I have written articles published from the **Guardian** to **Elsevier** . Please note rejecting treatments with great efficacy for any condition de-incentivises funders, pharmaceutical companies, researchers, and the whole medical ecosystem from investing. 

I am the longest serving member of the SC and Thalassaemia All Party Parliamentary Group and Chaired the same when needed. Please accept my deep concern and disappointment regarding NICE’s decision on the 14[th] March 2024, to reject Exagamglogene (Casgevy). This is a devastating blow to my community of fellow sickle cell Warriors and their families across the UK, **a community that remains long suffering, and continues to face extreme health inequality.** 

XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX **‘The Sickle Cell Guide’** which was reviewed and highly acclaimed by the **Lancet** Medical Journal who say it is **essential reading for medical professionals** , **I wonder how many on the NICE Committee have read this book?** (‘The Sickle Cell Guide’ is available at Amazon **https://www.amazon.co.uk/dp/B0BJ84YHGY** Lancet Review April edition of the Lancet Medical Journal Hematology **https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S2352302623000 704 ).** In December 2023 the FDA Approved the world’s first CRISPR gene editing drug. 

XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX In the UK **structural and systemic inequality** has contributed to little, to no change in sickle cell care, because no one in the NHS with any power cares, resulting in the utter stagnation we see today.  Of course, we would welcome the opportunity to debate this, but even that offer gets rejected and dismissed with impunity. 

My reports highlighting the **testimonies of many patients and their complaints are ignored.** Government and other reports on sickle cell disorder (SC) are ignored, **Black, Achison, Marmot** , etc are ignored. Other peer conditions race miles ahead in the care and treatments they receive. 

The disparity occurs in plain sight, complaints are ignored, and patients are abused with impunity. Nearly **50% of patients, fearing to go to hospital** , because of the abuse and harm they experience, ref **SWAY** and ‘The Sickle ’ ‘ Cell Guide ! In their Vaso-Occlusive Crisis; which is a **Medical** 



<!-- page 319 -->

**Emergency** ’, the majority of patients say, they prefer to suffer at home, than suffer conflict with white authority!!!!! 

The above is important, there is so much I could do to save the NHS money, but it just does not care! People living with the condition know it, have voiced it for decades, and have little trust in the NHS and its clinical professionals at every level. This breaks my heart, and I think it would break anyone’s heart if they really cared.  They would understand that human beings in a civilised country should not be having totally avoidable, harmful, unsafe, distressing experiences, at a greater rate, and higher severity than their white counterparts. 

As a public for good I have tirelessly encourage my SC community to engage in the consultation https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=E20-z3qOeio if only the NHS and its associates demonstrated such leadership, ethics, and sincerity. The link sets out the flaws on the decision including the abject lack of choice and failure to develop healthcare, decade upon decade for people living with SC. The pain of a VOC likened to being repeatedly hammered or axed, indeed mothers from around the world report child-birth hurts less than a sickle cell crisis. 

I and the majority of people living with this life limiting, unpredictable, multisystem disorder; experience accumulative organ, tissue, bone, blood damage and complications including stroke, priapism, splenic sequestration, osteonecrosis, renal failure, pulmonary hypertension, liver disease, bone damage, limited growth, increased susceptibility to infections, fatigue, and progressive cognitive decline, meningitis, skin ulcers, complications in pregnancy functional asplenia, splenic infarction, splenic sequestration, septicaemia; sepsis, avascular necrosis, osteomyelitis, retinopathy, posthyphema glaucoma, retinal infarction (tissue death), avascular necrosis, cardiomegaly, diastolic heart failure, ACS, Pulmonary hypertension, oedema, pulmonary embolisms, hyperbilirubinanaemia, gallstones, sickle hepatopathy, erectile dysfunction, albuminuria, isosthenuria, substantial kidney injury, acute renal failure, clinically extremely vulnerable susceptible to virus’s and infections).  We experience **stigma** , **misogynoir** , and behaviours that arise out of racism and prejudice in plain sight, its an oft written about phenomenon yet patients and their families are reporting **things are getting worse** . In addition, there is poor **mental health** generated by all these triggers. Poor pain management services causing Drug dependency risks.  This is compounded by the **deprivation** , vulnerability, discrimination, and the economic and social disadvantage people with SCD experience in both the **health ecosystem** , and wider societal ecosystems. These issues result in greater illness and hospitalisation for those living with SCD. **NICE seem, as usual to ignore Principle 9 of NICE’s Charter for health inequalities.** Having a cure reduces and removes the clinical, social, and economic **burdens** of living with an invisible fluctuating illness that no one; including patients and

medical practitioners, understand. Nobody should have to live with all these chronic and acute burdens, as well as constant and acute pain!

Page 24 of NICE company evidence Committee Papers, ID4016, says 14,200 patients, when the latest used by the NHS is **17,500 patients** . It suggests some significant flaws in the reported information!!!!!! 

I honestly believe it is a scandal the way the SC community is treated! At every turn despite help being available, we are left to suffer, forced to endure abuses, and can die without any medical staff being held to account for complaints or serious harm and death. This treatment could be a gamechanger, but like my book; ‘The Sickle Cell Guide’, anything good in sickle cell appears to get blocked and denied, as such the plight of people living with the condition will continue to worsen. 

I and probably 100% of patients as a goal, would ask for zero hospitalisation and better quality of life. Guess what that is what Casgevy is proposed to deliver!!! And would clearly save the health services huge sums of money as an **IRR (Internal Rate of Return)** , and a huge saving in the social costs of carers, as well as the multi-disciplinary medical teams, ambulance services, GP’s, Doctors, Nurses, Consultants, and the 4 Psychologist we have; joke, yes it is a joke; and its one that results in suffering! 

If I were given the treatment, Casgevy would also enable me to enjoy, no symptoms of SCD, halt bodily deterioration and enable repair where possible, no VOC’s, no chronic or acute pain, longer life expectancy, reduced need for medications and analgesia (pain relief), improved mood, confidence, work productivity, increased family and social participation, time with the children, ability to swim, ski, travel, reduced expenditure on medicines, recover lost education, ability to do day to day tasks including look after the house, be less vulnerable, suffer less **stigma,** better sleep, better emotional regulation, support my partner and children, increase and improve employment options, reduce isolation, less anxiety, stress, and depression, etc etc. 

Many of those at NICE and ordinary folk without SC take these things for granted and have no idea people without SC reading this have no idea of the burdens we face, or how other limit our humanity. Doctors and Nurses have no idea, the see us for a fraction of a fraction of their life, are not invested in the condition, and the vast majority have received no training in the condition; have not even read my Lancet reviewed book, where the most prestigious medical journal in the world advocate the book is an essential read for any medical professional or student. 



<!-- page 321 -->

Just a glance at the hundreds of pages that are part of this consultation indicate there is nothing in the pipeline of treatments, guidelines on care, pathways coming down the line, the landscape looks positively barren including the actual recent removal of treatments like Crizanlizumab, and Voxelotor under dubious rational. SC has 3 approved treatments, cystic fibrosis 511, this disparity is in plan sight, I gaslighting and denial that goes on and block progress often leaves me worrying that I appear to be the only person that can see the emperor has no cloths on! And those that do know the emperor is naked, are unwilling to listen to and support basic solutions to level-up. 

As a patient I would prefer the option of a Cell and Gene Therapy because this is quicker safer, treatment only involves my own screened stem cell genetic material, less chemotherapy, can avoid GvHD, and higher rates of success. I would encourage patients to store sperms and eggs prior to the treatment. 

I, and people living with SCD report and complain that NICE commissioning guideline CG143 is routinely not enforced to the harm and detriment of the SC community, not in A&E, or on the ward; even in HCC’s (Specialist Sickle Cell Hospitals – Haemoglobinopathy Coordination Centres), and the NHP, CQC, hospital leaders themselves stand there letting it happen! If these behaviours regularly occurred with, stroke, heart attack patient’s; both these, as SCD, are ranked as ‘Medical Emergencies’, the NHS would not tolerate it!  If you consider this scenario bad allow me to expand, I have highlighted many times the existence of the **36 Quality Indicators in section 4.2 pages 10 to 12 Quality Indicators** ; Standards NHS England Service Specification No 170126S Specialist Haemoglobinopathy Services (All Ages) Specialist Haemoglobinopathy Teams - - https://www.england.nhs.uk/wp content/uploads/2019/07/Specialist Haemoglobinopathy-Teams-Service-Specification.pdf The 250 page consultation report does not mention it in its table of national SC guidelines at page 50.  This 2019 specification, developed carefully at great expense by the NHS, is all but ignored; and no one listens to those that raise it, epitomising the sentiments and concerns in the Parliamentary report “No One’s Listening”. 

The concern of the SC community is that we keep asking, and keep getting ignored, promises made are reneged on. MHRA Authorised the treatment to great plaudits and adoration for the UK Life Sciences, across mainstream media, in November 2023, only to see it fall apart like a cheap suit within weeks with this NICE rejection.  The studies and trials; **CLIMB SD-121** and 131 evidence ‘high’ clinical safety and efficacy, and 96.6% all participants VOC free, **100% hospitalisation free** . In America the FDA have approved the treatment, whilst in the UK we drag our heels. 

I sincerely urge NICE to reverse its decision and start to prioritise the health and well-being of those affected by Sickle Cell. NICE should recognise the disparity surrounding SC, Cystic Fibrosis, HIV, Haemophilia, etc and

position a plan to level up. The inequality experienced by SC Warriors has persisted far too long.

Fetal haemoglobin is maintained at around 40% in a pancellular distribution. This would be expected to prevent the process of vaso-occlusion and prevent progression of existing organ damage and development of new organ damage. This is evidenced by outcomes in compound hereditary persistence of fetal haemoglobin (HbS+HPFH) in which affected individuals do not suffer the pain and organ complications seen in sickle cell disease and have normal life expectancy. ## **Content of this report** 

In this document, we provide the EAG responses to Vertex draft guidance comment form, with further details included in the appendices. We then provide a validation or replication of the company’s base-case results and scenario analyses. Finally, we present EAG analyses, which considers the company’s preferred assumptions/preferences following the first appraisal committee meeting.

When presenting the new set of revised results, the company appears to have incorporated only a selected subset of committee’s preferences. 

Base case ICER before ACM1: *******, using discount rate at 1.5% per annum. 

Company’s base case after ACM1:********, using discount rate at 1.5% and severity modifier of 1.7. 

Because the company stripped or overwrote some EAG’s functionality and data out of the model and because some EAG’s base case data were deleted, it is not possible for the EAG to reconstruct or appraise the changes between the previous base case ICER and the base case ICER submitted by the company after ACM1. 

The company’s base-case is described as the ICER reflecting the Committee’s preferences. However, there are several preferences that have not been incorporated in the company’s base case. 

1. The company’s base case ICER uses a 1.5% discount and a severity modifier of 1.7. 

2. The base-case does not reflect the utility value after exa-cel preferred by the Committee. 

3. VOC rates are not reflecting hospitalisations VOCs (2.6 annualised rate). 

4. The company added unusable functionality to incorporate the costs and outcomes for people who fail apheresis and for people who did not receive exa-cel because of insufficient doses, substantially reduced drop-out rates and assumed no costs for exa-cel; 

5. The base-case uses two sets of evidence for acute and chronic complications, rather than the one preferred by the Committee. The company introduces a ‘co-base-case’ using rates from the Vertex BOI study (UK, unpublished) and various data retrieved from the literature, including data from Brousse, called ‘Literature’. 

**Issue 1** : The EAG generated results based on the 3.5% reference case discount and using no severity modifier. 

**Issue 2** : The utility value has been updated to reflect the preferred utility value 

**Issue 3** : The EAG updated the results to reflect the preferred rate of VOCs at baseline 

**Issue 4** : For the costs and outcomes of treatment failures after apheresis, the EAG reinstated the functionality overwritten by the company to return the corresponding ICER.

## **1.8** _**EAG’s critique of company’s analyses and results**_ 

**Issue 1** : Costs and outcomes associated with ACS should be excluded from the model as they constitute to double counting. 

**Issue 2** : In the opinion of the EAG, the Committee’s preference is to apply a utility value of 0.88 for cured SCD. 

**Issue 3** : The EAG believes that complication rates extrapolated in the model are obtained from studies with a more severe population than the one in the model decision problem. Specifically with reference to the absence of mortality data for older people, the company’s argument that there are no data because there are no deaths is disproven by Jiao et al., who include Medicare datasets, which include people with SCD in the age groups with mean age equal to 70 and 50. The absence of records for older people with SCD is not because there are none, but because the databases where these cases are recorded have not been included. 

However, given that the company has accepted the Committee’s preferred model structure, using mortality rates selected by the company, there are no material implications regarding mortality rates. 

The EAG has added specific study details to provide the evidence regarding 50 years being the lower bound for a reasonably justified life expectancy for this decision problem. 

**Issue 4** : The company base-case complication rates from Udeze et al 2023 should be replaced by the Udeze 2023 rates for the subgroup aged 12-35, more in line with the population of the decision problem. The EAG believes that the complication rates in the company base-case may be from a more severe population than that in the decision problem population and that in the CLIMB SCD-121 study. 

67 



<!-- page 392 -->

**==> picture [452 x 317] intentionally omitted <==**

## **Figure 2 :Acute complications by subgroup** 

**Issue 5** : The Udeze all-sample data may lack predictive validity with respect to the decision problem population, as they may come from a sicker population than data used in the decision problem for this appraisal. During ACM1, it was discussed that exa-cel would be used preferentially in people with low rates or no history of SCD complications. In the Udeze study, people with one type of event at baseline contributed data for the calculation of another complication. It is legitimate to assume that the risk of new complications would be higher in people that have a history of other SCD complications, probably conflating the overall risk of complications with respect to the decision problem population.  The population group aged 12-35 years old is in line with inclusion criteria from CLIMB SCD-121 although it does have a much higher rate of VOCs at baseline (6.37 vs 2.6 hospitalisations or 4.2 all VOCs). 

**Issue 6** : The company provides a co-base-case using literature-derived data for acute and chronic complications (see Table 29). 

Literature studies are far from providing accurate data to allow the EAG to identify best matching rates to the decision population. 

68 



<!-- page 393 -->

Overall, rates from the literature are lower than those reported in the Vertex UK BOI study, despite similar inclusion criteria used for restricting results to severe populations. 

The company obtained the majority of complication rates from Brousse et al. This study reports the number of VOCs in the more severe population, 166.9 per 100-person-years, equivalent to 1.7 per year, based on number of hospitalisations. This number if more in line with the decision population of this appraisal. The study by Brousse et al also does not provide a rates breakdown by age for most outcomes; however, the study does provide age subgroups for some outcomes; it is unclear whether the company has adjusted the relevant rates in the study to match the age restrictions in the decision problem in this appraisal. 

The ‘literature’ co-base-case also includes one complication rate (chronic liver disease) derived from Udeze 2023.
