## **2.1** _**Further details**_ 

In this section, we present further details to support our critique of the company’s response to the draft consultation document. 

**Issue 4** : For the costs and outcomes of treatment failures after apheresis, the EAG reinstated the functionality overwritten by the company to return the corresponding ICER. 

The reasons for dropouts in the CLIMB SCD-121 study do not pertain to access inequalities, as stated by the company, but to technical reasons. All patients in the study did provide quantities of biological material as per the CLIMB SCD-121 protocol. Based on the biological material provided, some patients were not returned with sufficient exa-cel for reimplantation. The relationship between technical production and inequalities is hard to see. 

Removing the outcomes would violate a basic principle of health technology assessment (HTA), that of using ITT efficacy in the appraisal. 

Whilst the company states that their base-case includes the costs of failed exa-cel implants, the company’s base case assumes that no costs are imputed for exa-cel for people whose biological samples are sent for manufacture. 

The company added alternative functionality to the model that overwrote the previously active EAG functionality. 

**==> picture [452 x 61] intentionally omitted <==**

The company’s functionality assumes that there are no tangible consequences to people that withdraw from the process, but the costs of care are set to the costs of SoC. When activating the functionality, the selection of the “cost of withdrawn patients” menu decreases the ICER slightly, reflecting lower costs of care and lower QALYs, and setting the cost of exa-cel to zero for all dropouts; the application of exa-cel cost to withdrawn patients’ menu as per company’s functionality has no effect on the ICER. 

The company also changed the number of people who drop out from the process in their base-case, assigning a probability of drop out of ****, instead that that calculated from the CLIMB SCD-121 trial as in the ACM1 model ( _see_ Table 30) 

80 



<!-- page 405 -->

**Table 30: Proportion of safety analysis set that discontinues CLIMB SCD-121** 

**==> picture [398 x 120] intentionally omitted <==**

The company provides no justification why the rate is reduced. The company’s rate is locked, in that any change in the rate does not seem to propagate through the model. 

********************************************************************************************************* 

**************************************** – regardless of the reason why the manufactured biological materials not reimplanted. The key is that exa-cel cannot be given to another patient, it has to be discarded entirely and as such, it is wasted, regardless of the reason why implantation does not occur, including insufficient yield or patient preferences. The EAG proceed to reinstate the overwritten functionality, as per Committee’s preferences. 

## **2.1.1 Critique** 

The original submission suffered from the lack of validation of both mortality and complication rates in the model. Some papers were used as references, however there was no attempt to provide a review (systematic or otherwise) of model input and outputs, neither to justify the use of certain values as inputs, a serious deviation from the process of appraisals using the NICE methodology. 

In the response after ACM1, the applied in the model, the company has provided somehow more detailed data to populate the model, for both mortality and complication rates although data from none of the mortality studies, and data from only two complications studies are incorporated in the model for the Committee to be able to see the impact of assumptions. 

## **Issue 1: Costs and outcomes for ACSs should be excluded from the model as they constitute double count** 

The EAG ‘s found that the definition of VOCs includes ACS rates in most of the studies included as data sources for this appraisal (Udeze 2023; Brousse 2023) Consequently, the EAG argues that costs and outcomes for this endpoint are already captured in the model. Cost and outcomes of ACSs constitute a double count and should be set to zero in the model. 

81 



<!-- page 406 -->

## **Issue 2: Utilities with exa-cel** 

The first issue affecting utilities calculation in the company’s model was that genera- 

population utilities and utilities with exa-cel were applied in the model in an additive manner 

82 



<!-- page 407 -->

causing a spike in utilities up to **** in the exa-cel model. The EAG is satisfied that the calculation has been corrected using a multiplicative approach, therefore this issue is resolved. 

The second issue concerns the Committee’s preference for utility with exa-cel after transplant, to use the utility value calculated from CLIMB SCD-121 at 12 months. This was because the increment calculated for people who had data at 24 months suffered from selection bias, in that patients who had not hit the 24 months follow up had higher utility values at baseline compared with those included in the 24 months utility analysis, suggesting missingness not at random. 

The company provided a post-hoc analysis of utility values that excludes people with utility of 1 at baseline (perfect health). It is unclear what this data has to offer in terms of evidence, since the bias in the utility gain provided by this new analysis is larger than the original bias it meant to resolve. 

Further, the company provides a break-down distribution of utilities at baseline for 31 people in the FAS and argues that a lower baseline value should be applied, with a larger gain after exa-cel. 

The problem with this approach is that it creates inconsistency between efficacy rates, that remain those for the entire sample of patients in CLIMB SCD-121, and utility values, selected to reflect the (relatively) most severe people. The rate of VOCs at baseline is also likely to differ between the whole sample and the selected sub-sample. 

The company argues that the presence of high utility values at baseline should be interpreted as the evidence of a ceiling effect in the measurement of utility values.  Hover the company does not consider the alternative explanation, pointing to another limitation of the trial, that of selecting a potentially relatively healthier population than the general SCD severe population. There are other indications that suggest a potential misalignment between the clinical trial population and the decision problem population, specifically regarding the prognostic data applied in the model, mortality data and complication data. The EAG’s base-case retains the utility value preferred by the Committee, 0.88.

## **Issue 4: The company base case complication rates from Udeze et al 2023 should be replaced by the Udeze 2023 rates for the subgroup aged 12-35, in line with the population of the decision problem.** 

The EAG’s solution should be intended as a convenience solution. These complication rates remain a source of uncertainty in the model because this subgroup may still be more severe than people in the CLIMB SCD-121 study. As a result, the burden of disease averted with exa-cel may be overestimated. Complication data from Udeze et al. should be matched by age and average VOC rates at baseline, to the CLIMB SCD-121 study population and to the model population. 

## **Detailed explanation and evidence base** 

The Vertex burden of disease study (Udeze et al 2023) is an unpublished observational study using administrative data from primary care records (Clinical Research Practice Database [CPRD]) linked with secondary care data sources (Hospital Episode Statistics [HES]) in England. The study population has no age limitations.  The data were analysed separately for a cohort of people defined as ‘severe SCD population (Udeze, 2023: p.22), i.e., cases that met the following definition: 

   - Patients must have a primary or secondary diagnosis of SCD on or prior to index date. 

   - Patients must have ≥ 2 VOCs* per year in at least 2 consecutive years 

   - Patients must be registered within CPRD at index date. 

   - Patients must be eligible for HES linkage. 

- Patients must have a minimum of 1 year follow-up data available from their index date. 

- VOCs were defined as any of the following: 

   - Record of primary or secondary diagnosis of SCD with crisis 

   - Record of primary or secondary diagnosis of priapism

## **2.1.1.1 Detailed explanation and evidence base** 

Data in the Udeze study may lack comparability to the CLIMB SCD-121 data with respect to baseline comorbidities. 

The model population included in the company’s base-case assumes no comorbidity at baseline, other than 14% retinopathy and 3% neurocognitive impairment. 

The Udeze report provides baseline data for the sample of n=1,117. These data are reported in Figure 5. First, the Udeze study is affected by a problem in classification of baseline complications, lacking clarity regarding how these numbers were derived: the definition of study variables states that, “ _In HES APC, primary diagnosis (reason for admission) and secondary diagnoses were used to report health conditions that need secondary care.”_ [Udeze, 2023, Section 7.4.2 page 27] 

In data tabulations however the expression” any record” as opposed to “no record” is used; it is unclear whether ‘any record’ means that there is a mention of comorbidity for each case, or whether it refers to data missingness. 

If the expression refers to mentions of comorbidity, then the burden of comorbidity in the Udeze sample is far higher than baseline comorbidities in the model (that are derived from CLIMB SCD-121). Alternatively, the expression may mean that there is no information regarding history of comorbidities at baseline. 

**==> picture [346 x 309] intentionally omitted <==**

90 



<!-- page 415 -->

## **Figure 5: From Udeze, Table 6 Baseline demographics characteristics for the severe SCD cohort and for the matched general population, page 44** 

The entire table of comorbidity at baseline is reproduced in Appendix 0. 

Further, the definition and measurement of event rates in the Udeze et al study is reported in the text below, directly quoted from the Udeze study report (Udeze 2023, page 32). 

- For treatment use, HCRU and acute complications […] each patient can experience the event of interest multiple times. […] the number of events per patient per year (PPPY) was calculated as the total number of events per patient during follow-up, divided by the total number of years observed from index date until censor date.  […] specifically for strokes and cerebral vasculopathy [based on medical advice], an upper limit of 3 events per patient was applied. _Prevalence for acute complications was calculated based on the follow-up data only, by dividing the number of patients with the acute complication during follow up by the total number of patients._ 

- For mortality and chronic complications […] each patient could only experience the event of interest once. The rate was the total number of patients with the event, divided by the total number of person-years observed _for all patients_ from their index date until the date of the event of interest (or censor date in case of no event), inclusive of both dates. _Rates were reported as events per 100 person-years. [….]_ patients were not included in the rate calculation if they had a record of the event of interest at baseline. _Prevalence (for chronic complications) was calculated as the total number of patients with the relevant event at either baseline or during follow-up, divided by the total number of patients in the cohort._ 

This approach provides the rate of one particular chronic complication event in people who did not have such event at baseline. As such, the rate represents new cases of one particular chronic state. 

The approach however is still likely to overestimate rates for chronic complications because, for each complication, rates include events for people who reported another complication at baseline, therefore at higher risk than the population in the decision problem and CLIMB SCD-121. Similar limitations apply to the definition of acute complication rates. 

91 



<!-- page 416 -->

## ID4016 – Update to proposed source for complications in the model 

## Background and implication of EAG proposed assumption on complication rates 

During the second committee meeting (ACM2), there was a discussion on the appropriate source of complications rates for the standard of care arm in the model. The EAG, in its response to the Vertex ACD response, expressed a preference for a sub-group of patients reported in the Udeze et al. (2023) study, which limited complications rates to those experienced by the 12-35 age range, on the basis that it aligned with the decision problem. 

Vertex disagreed with this at ACM2 and suggested that using the entire severe cohort from Udeze et al. (2023) was more appropriate, on the basis that capturing complications across all ages was important to better represent the disease progression of severe sickle cell disease (SCD) in the model. Vertex made the case that using all ages (from 2 years of age) from the severe SCD cohort from Udeze et al. (2023) was generalisable to the UK severe SCD population, on the basis that it captures the natural progression of the disease and the increase in the risk of complications as patients age. 

Patients in the CLIMB SCD-121 clinical trial included those in the 12-35 age group, and the license indication for exa-cel includes _all_ patients 12 years and older. For modelling purposes, and in line with the decision problem, the aim is to look at the entirety of the disease progression of patients with severe SCD. Patients in the model have a starting age of 22 years (taken from the baseline characteristics reported in the CLIMB SCD-121 clinical trial) and their disease progression and onset of complications is modelled until death (lifetime horizon). 

The literature shows clear evidence for reduced life expectancy, severely impaired quality of life and accumulation of complications and co-morbidities with age. At ACM2 the clinical experts commented that complications beyond the clinical trial upper age limit are relevant to lifelong disease-related morbidity; they further expressed a strong preference for using higher literature estimates of complications based on their clinical experience and the often underestimation of complication rates they see documented in the literature. This was supported by online consultation comments submitted by patients, carers and clinicians who gave evidence on the progressive nature of the condition. 

Vertex wrote to NICE following ACM2 to further clarify that applying the complication rates of a younger group of patients (12-35 years old) in the model, to all patients 12 years and over significantly underestimates the severity of SCD over a patient's entire lifetime. This is a particularly inaccurate reflection of the disease progression when the estimated median age of death for patients on standard of care (SoC) in the model is 52 years of age. 

This submission provides further analysis addressing both the committee’s and EAG’s request for a source for complications rates that is aligned with the decision problem, and which also does **All** not artificially limit the complications accrued by patients over their lifetime in the model.

## Impact in the model 

If one implements complications rates as the EAG has in the 12-35 scenario, the rates of complications don’t change over the lifetime horizon in the model – and the impact of using the average rates from the 12-35 age group over the lifetime horizon is artificially misconstruing disease progression, with an overall underestimation of disease severity. 

- Hence, when patients turn 35+ years in the model, as the time horizon elapses, they are developing complications at a much lower rate than they would otherwise develop as seen in the evidence, hence their overall QoL at the end of the time horizon (median age of survival 52 years of age) is heavily underestimated; as well as the cost of treating these patients. 

- As seen in Udeze, rates of complications are higher in older patients as their disease progresses. E.g. Complication rates in the paediatric population are lower than in adulthood. 

Vertex’s ACM2 base case included risks of complications from all ages (including paediatric patients) in a conservative fashion, this is due to the fact that Udeze only presents ALL, or age subgroups but no 12+ group. 

**In response to the committee’s concerns during ACM2, we have derived specific risks of complications for the 12+ population from Udeze (using a weighted approach) and as expected, the outcomes show negligible impact when compared to our initial approach.** 

## EAG implementation of 12-35 cohort in the model 

Vertex has identified some misalignment between the complications reported in the literature and the EAG’s update of the model to reflect the 12-35 population. The implementation of the 1235 cohort by the EAG is uncertain, as the EAG has hardcoded the values without explanation or formulae, but it appears the EAG is making additional assumptions on the risk values for developing complications. For example, from the data table in the model, that is copied from the Udeze et al study, 0% of patients 12-35 had heart failure (which we know is a significant complication that patients with severe SCD experience later in life). However, the EAG’s version of the model states the rate for this complication is greater than 0%, but does not reference this figure. Of course, the risk of developing heart failure is an important consideration, and the value should not be 0% for the whole SoC arm - and the fact this is reported in the 12-35 population is evidence of the fact that using this age restricted band leads to inaccurate model results. 

We believe deriving the risks of complications from a uniform cohort (Udeze) is the preferred option to address uncertainty instead of mixing derivation of risk from multiple sources that are based on different cohort characteristics. 

**This issue and other underestimated complications are addressed in the updated Vertex scenario below. All other committee preferred and optimistic assumptions are kept constant - the only update is the complications rates which are all derived from the Udeze.**

## Calculation of complication rates 

The acute complication rates were calculated by taking a weighted average (using overall patient counts in each age group) of each age group’s reported mean rate. For example, there were 898 patients in the combined cohort – 649 in the 12-35 age group and 249 in the 36+ age group. Thus, to calculate the weighted average rate for pulmonary embolism, the reported rate for patients aged 12-35 (0.003) was multiplied by 649/898 and the reported rate for patients 36+ (0.18) was multiplied by 249/898. These numbers were then added together to produce the weighted average annual acute complication rate. Lastly, this value is converted into a monthly rate in the model, in column D of the Raw_complication_risks sheet. 

The risks for developing chronic complications were calculated by combining the person-years and event counts for both age groups and calculating the new rate by summing the total events by total patient-years; which is then converted into a risk in the model. For example, for pulmonary hypertension, the number of events in both cohorts (25 in ages 36+ and 25 in ages 1235) are summed, as are the person years (977.93 and 2737.47, respectively). The summed number of events (50) is then divided by the summed person-years (3715.4) to calculate a rate per patient-year, which is multiplied by 100 to produce a rate per 100 patient-years, which is the reported outcome from the study. This is converted into a monthly risk in the model, in column D of the Raw_complication_risks sheet.

- _‘The efficacy in the company’s model is based not on the ITT population (all of those who started the treatment pathway), but only those who go on to have exa-cel i.e., does not include 20% withdrawn and begins at the point of exa-cel being infused. This is our interpretation, but we would just like to double check.’_ 

We confirm this. All the exa-cel cohort is treated with exa-cel and has 96.6% efficacy of exacel (to account for the proportion in CLIMB SCD-121 that fail the primary endpoint). Approximately 18.9% dropouts (***% who fail apheresis) and ****% who successfully pass apheresis but do not receive exa-cel are not part of the cohort, a cost ‘uplift’ is added to total cost of care to account for the cost of apheresis (approximately **£** 43k multiplied by 19%, **£** 8,990) although it is unclear how this is done because there is no formula in the model that does this. 

- _‘The cost of a VOC using the ‘all-event,_ 4.2 _’ rate, uses the appropriate costings. I think we heard in committee that 2.6 of these were inpatient hospitalisations, so, if possible, committee would like this proportion costs (the 2.6) as inpatient hospitalisations and the remaining proportion costed as day cases.’_ 

The company’s base case uses the _**National Schedule of NHS Cost (SA36A-C, SickleCell Anaemia with Crisis)**_ . 

The value applied in the model is **£** 1,567 (unclear why not **£** 1,587, probably a typo) (Table below, obtained from

## **Content of this report** 

In this document, we provide an EAG viewpoint on: 

- The new subgroup analysis of Udeze 12+, that it was implemented correctly 

- The appropriateness of this source vs Udeze full, 12-35, or literature. Please also provide a view on the EAG's preference (if any). For example. if Udeze 12+ or Udeze 12-35 is preferred over Brousse et al severe population - include comments on whether implementation of Brousse et al complications is correct 

During ACM2, the Committee preferred to use SCD complication rates for the subgroup 1235 years of age at study entry. This is because the model population, reflecting the CLIMB SCD-121 trial, is restricted to people between 12 and 35 years of age, and because clinical opinion heard during the meeting (as well as during ACM1) suggested that exa-cel would be limited to people in that age band, with no or little history of complications. 

The company did not accept this choice based on two arguments: 

1. The marketing authorisation for exa-cel is not restricted by age. 

2. The model covers the lifetime horizon. 

The company proceeded to recalculate complication rates from the Vertex BoD study using the entire sample, including people aged above 35 years. 

Complication rates for the two groups of age were combined as a weighted average, using weights proportional to the number of people in the respective age groups in the BoD study and generated corresponding ICERs. 

First, whilst the license is unrestricted, the CLIMB SCD-121 data are restricted to age at entry ≤35; there are no data in the submission to support the case for reimbursement in people older than 35. 

With regards to the claim that complication rates could be modelled as age-dependent, the EAG agrees that such approach is reasonable (in agreement with what is known about SCD), however, the data provided by the company is not fit for purpose to proceed because the company’s implementation reflects several methodological misconceptions; the application of the revised complication rates increase biases and uncertainties in the model 

5 



<!-- page 439 -->

rather than reducing them. The approach is affected by both misalignment in scope and several methodological errors. 

Specifically, the following methodological issues apply: 

1. The weights applied to complication rates should reflect the composition of the model population, in turn, reflecting the composition of CLIMB SCD-121. Specifically, the distribution of age in CLIMB SCD-121 and that in the Vertex BoD study are unmatched; rates applied to the model population are taken from a population (BoD) with a different age distribution. As age is a predictor of complication rates, the rates applied in the model are biased. 

2. The age distribution at baseline (both in the model and the BoD study) is cross-sectional in nature, a ‘photographic’ description of the ages of individuals at the point of entry into the study, whilst complication data – and the application in the model – is longitudinal, meaning that complications occur over time as patients’ age also increases.  The BoD rates are calculated over the time after the index date; follow-up is on average 4.69 years [and up to 10 years]. 

This has two implications: 

1. The company applied a constant rate in the model, recalculated for all ages 12+; this means that complication rates applied early in the model (starting at age 21 with max age =35 as per CLIMB SCD-121) are derived from an older population, including 28% of people older than 35, ranging up to 86 years old. As the model population is largest in early years, the bias may be potentially large. 

2. The application of the 12-35 and 35+ sets of rates separately for early model ages and for later model ages is methodologically flawed.  Because complication data are longitudinal, people aged 31 to 35 years at entry contribute complication data for the years of age 35-40; however, these rates are counted in the group 12-35; likewise, the 35+ age group includes complications for the years of age between 35+ and 41, overlapping, at least in part, the 12-35 years group. This means that applying two sets of rates in the model, using a cut-off (e.g., 35) will lead to double count of complications for the cycles corresponding to 35 to 40 of age. 

This overlap is methodological (i.e., it depends on the way the company has framed the analysis) and it would occur regardless of the cut-off chosen. Alternatively, it could be argued, should rates of the group 12-35 be applied until – perhaps 40 years of age - or until 

6 



<!-- page 440 -->

the effective recalculated mean age of that group at the end of follow-up. None of these solutions however are methodologically sound; the overlap between the two sets of complication rates cannot be resolved other than by a regression model that takes age at the time of the complication (not age at baseline) into account. 

3. The cross-sectional nature of the index age in the Vertex BoD study is such that data from people 12-35 and 35+ cannot be equated to data derived from one unique population starting at 12 years old and followed-up longitudinally until older than 35 (max 86). 

The two groups in the Vertex BoD are contemporary, with the older population showing a baseline VOC rate higher than that for the population in the model. The model does not include an estimation of VOCs over time - i.e., modelling SOC rates of VOCs over time [these data could be in the dataset, but no analysis has been made]. It is unknown whether the higher VOC rates are due to age or to some other uncontrollable factor, the direction of which cannot be assessed.  For example, the older subgroup may be subject to survivor bias – i.e., people that are alive beyond 35 may be healthier than those alive at 20 years, because the sickest people may have been deceased before 35 years old. There may be differences due to temporal evolution in the healthcare practice: younger people may have been diagnosed earlier, may have received better healthcare and better treatment compared with that received by the older cohort, when they were younger. These factors could have driven VOC rates at baseline in either direction. 

In general, it is not possible to exclude that younger and older people are 'different' groups for other reasons than just age and complication rates may be confounded. This means that stacking the two subgroups as if they were one longitudinal cohort, or mixing / weighting the two, may introduce uncontrollable biases and increase uncertainty in the model. Mixing and matching these two groups should be done in a way that controls for at least important differences between groups. 

Finally, the application of higher rates for older people does require that the reverse logic also applies to younger people. The model starts at 21 years and rates applied to the early cycles are those including people potentially as old as 40-45 years, so complication rates in the model are overestimated in the early cycles. Should the model become one that tracks complication rates by age, then lower complication rates should be applied early as well. 

7 



<!-- page 441 -->

We acknowledge that the extrapolation of 12-35 years rates to people older than 40-45 may conservatively underestimate complication rates. However, the model population is largest in early ages, and smallest at older ages. This means that the potential underestimation of complication rates at late cycles (smaller cohort, more discounted) in the model may be counterbalanced by the overestimation of complications in the early cycles (larger cohort, less discounted). Conversely, the 12+ entire population rates amplify overestimation in earlier cycles, and downplays underestimation in later cycles; therefore, the 12-35 population data remain preferable. The EAG advises against the application of two separates sets of complications before and after 35 years in the model because this approach is flawed. 

The methodological impasse could be resolved analytically, estimating an equation for complication rates based on longitudinal data, controlling for age, VOC rates and other factors that may differ between BoD age groups – perhaps year of diagnosis if available, or prior treatments. Longitudinal patient-level analyses have been used for decades in the analyses of observational data and are a well-known statistical approach to handling data such as complication rates from the BoD. Such analyses, at the same time, would allow for more appropriate matching between BoD and model population characteristics. 

Finally, a minor point regards the critique of the company to the EAG’s method of incorporating complication rates. The EAG’s modification was limited to changing the values for complications rates, using the values provided by the company as part of complication rates breakdowns by age groups at study index date (baseline). For anything else, the EAG used the company’s functionality (i.e., derivation of probabilities from rates, propagation of rates via model formulae etc..) with no modification. It is unclear what the company considers inappropriate in this implementation. 

8

## **Content of this report** 

In this document, we provide further details on the EAG viewpoint about: 

- The appropriateness of this source vs Udeze full, 12-35, or literature. Please also provide a view on the EAG's preference (if any). For example. if Udeze 12+ or Udeze 12-35 is preferred over Brousse et al severe population - include comments on whether implementation of Brousse et al complications is correct 

The submission still suffers from a major limitation in that no review of complication data/studies was conducted. The EAG's selection of the Brousse paper before ACM1 was to show that the model was highly reactive to complication rates assumed for SOC, contrary to the company's statements. Brousse was a plausible alternative - but not the only one - to the approach implemented by the company using data from Shah; Brousse had lower rates of complications, which suggested that the complication rates originally used in the model were certainly an overestimate, although by how much was a matter of selecting the best data source. Raw complication rates from Shah [reported in the paper but not considered by the company] were also tested by the EAG in the set of results submitted to ACM1 - however Shah suffered from a) limited range of complications and b) lack of definitions of the severe population. Therefore, Brousse was preferred in that instance. 

For ACM2, the EAG expressed concerns - impacting all sources of complication data - that literature studies identified severe populations that were in fact more severe than the population in CLIMB SCD-121. The EAG argued that matching external populations to the model population was essential to avoid substantial overestimation of benefits from exa-cel. Baseline data that showed mismatching were a) age; b) VOCs rates and c) history of complications prior to receiving exa-cel. 

The Vertex BOD study subgroup, at least, was matched to the model population [restricted to 12-35 despite unrestricted marketing authorisation] but the BOD population remained unmatched with respect to prior complications (much broader range and higher percentage) and definition of VOCs [whilst the model allows for non-hospitalisation VOCs, the BOD does not break down which VOCs were hospitalisations and which were not, in addition to having two definitions of VOCs - 'any VOCs' and 'SCD with crisis'  whilst all other sources use hospitalisations therefore the assessment of comparability of data to CLIMB SCD-121 and matching should still be done based on hospitalisation VOCs. 

The EAG's preference for the BOD study subgroup 12-35 relies on the fact that at least age is matched to that of the model starting cohort, i.e., at baseline [other sources do not specify 

5 



<!-- page 447 -->

a restriction by age of the starting cohort] but overestimation of SOC complication rates may still be driven by higher VOC rates at baseline and higher burden of disease of the BOD cohort at baseline. 

This approach is far from ideal - the EAG believes that overall, given the choice of sources operated by the company, matching could and should be conducted to align the severity of the model population to that of the model cohort [all sources allow matching, whether based on individual level patient data as the BOD or literature sources, matched on baseline averages].

## **1. BACKGROUND** 

The ongoing Single Technology Appraisal (STA) of exagamglogene autotemcel (exa-cel) for treating sickle cell disease (SCD) has identified that, after two Appraisal Committee meetings (ACMs), there remains uncertainty about the appropriate rates and implementation method for the inclusion of complications in the company’s economic model. The cost-effectiveness results for exa-cel and the appropriate severity decision modifier may be sensitive to these values. The current version of the company’s economic model includes seven acute complications and eight chronic complications. 

Following ACM1, the company submitted evidence from an unpublished burden of illness study (Udeze _et al._ , 2023[1] ) based on an analysis of data obtained from the UK Clinical Practice Research Datalink (CPRD) linked to Hospital Episode Statistics (HES). The overall population within this study includes a total of 1,117 patients aged 2 years (yrs) or over with a primary or secondary diagnosis of SCD who had at least two vaso-occlusive crises (VOCs) per year in the two consecutive years prior to the index date. Complication rates were calculated based on the number of events observed and the number of years of follow-up per patient from the index date to the event or censoring date. The analysis assumed that acute complications can recur, but chronic complications can occur only once. Within the full Udeze _et al._ study report, complication rates are presented according to broad age bands (0-11yrs, 12-35yrs and 36+yrs). The company and the External Assessment Group (EAG) have applied data on complication rates from Udeze _et al._[1] in the economic model in different ways, based on different age subgroups. The selected complication rates mostly impact on the QALYs and costs for the standard of care (SoC) group. There are concerns that there are significant differences between the populations in Udeze _et al._[1] and the CLIMB SCD-121 study[2] (which provides the main clinical evidence for exa-cel) and questions about which would be the appropriate population(s) from Udeze _et al._ for the economic modelling and the correct method to implement these complications. 

The DSU understands that following ACM2, the Appraisal Committee has accepted that Udeze _et al._[1] is an appropriate source of data to inform acute and chronic complication rates in the economic model. The EAG has stated a preference for the use of data on complication rates from the 12-35yrs subgroup of Udeze _et al._ at all ages in the economic model, as this reflects the age range specified in the inclusion criteria applied in CLIMB SCD-121.[2] Following ACM2, this approach was also included as part of the Appraisal Committee’s preferred model assumptions. Following ACM2, the company submitted an additional document which provides new analyses which use complication rate data for the age 12+ subgroup of Udeze _et al_ .,[1] based on the weighted mean of the rates in the 12-35yrs and 36+yrs subgroups.[3] The company has argued that this new scenario matches the decision problem (patients aged 12+yrs with severe SCD) and that it is a more accurate reflection of the lifetime disease-related morbidity experienced by people with SCD. 

4 



<!-- page 452 -->

In July 2024, NICE asked the DSU to undertake further work to address this issue. The DSU was asked 

to: 

- Provide an overview of the different analyses presented from Udeze _et al._[1] and an assessment of their suitability to the economic model 

- Assess the method of implementing complication rates used in the economic model, determine the most appropriate method to apply complications rates in the economic model and implement it for all analyses. 

- Consider any alternative analyses that may be preferred and, where these can be derived from the data already provided, implement these in the economic analysis. 

- Demonstrate the impact on both cost effectiveness and, separately, the severity modifier calculations. 

- Outline any additional analyses that may be undertaken using data from Udeze _et al._[1] to inform the economic model. 

This DSU report presents the results of a range of scenario analyses based on complication rate estimates reported by Udeze _et al._[1] These analyses include the scenarios preferred by the EAG, the Appraisal Committee and the company following ACM2, as well as additional analyses undertaken by the DSU which attempt to reflect some degree of age-dependence in the modelled complication rates. 

The report is structured as follows. Section 2 summarises the alternative approaches explored by the DSU and the DSU’s scenario analyses undertaken using the company’s economic model. Section 3 summarises the results of the DSU’s scenario analyses. Section 4 provides a summary of the limitations of the available options for incorporating complication rates in the economic model and provides recommendations for decision-making. 

## **2. DEFINITION OF THE PROBLEM AND APPROACHES EXPLORED BY THE DSU** 

## 2.1 Summary of approaches explored by the DSU 

The DSU examined the full study report describing the methods and results of the Udeze _et al._ study[1] and an accompanying Microsoft Excel spreadsheet which provided summary complication rate estimates for patients aged 0-11yrs, 12-17yrs, 18-35yrs, 36+yrs, and 12-35yrs at their baseline assessment date (described as their ‘index’ age). The spreadsheet also provides calculations for the weighted mean complication rates in patients aged 12+yrs, based on the 12-35yrs and 36+yrs subgroups (the company’s preferred analysis). The DSU also scrutinised the approach used to implement complication rates in the latest version of the company’s executable model; the DSU did not identify any computation errors in this part of the model. 

5 



<!-- page 453 -->

The DSU consulted the EAG to understand their views regarding the data reported by Udeze _et al._[1] and to better understand what their preferred analysis of these data might entail. The EAG raised concerns that applying the 12+ subgroup data from Udeze _et al._ may overestimate SCD complication rates over the patient’s lifetime, and they have stated that they would have preferred an analysis in which complications are predicted according to the age at which they occur. The EAG stated that they preferred the 12-35yrs subgroup because, in the absence of their proposed re-analysis of the Udeze _et al._ data, this was more conservative than other approaches proposed by the company. The mean age of patients within the 12-35 age band of Udeze _et al._ is 23.57 years, which is similar to the mean age of 21.2 years in CLIMB SCD-121, but will not reflect age as patients in the model get older. The EAG also raised concerns that the population in Udeze _et al._ is more severe than that in CLIMB SCD-121, evidenced for example by the higher baseline VOC rate (8.6 versus 4.2 per year). It is not clear to the DSU whether the relevant population for the decision problem in England is represented by CLIMB SCD-121 or the real-world CPRD-based evidence from Udeze _et al._ (or a subset of it). 

The company’s economic model tracks a cohort of patients with a start age of 21.2 years over their lifetime and estimates the proportions experiencing complications in each 1-month cycle. The relevance of Udeze _et al._ is in informing the estimates of these complication rates as the patient cohort ages. There is therefore a disparity between the reporting of “age at index date” in the Udeze _et al._ analysis rather than the age at which each complication was observed to occur. As suggested by the EAG, a more suitable analysis would provide estimates of complication rates by age of occurrence. In addition, the use of broad age categories for the reporting of complication rates may obscure the true relationship and risks introducing bias. For example, whilst the estimates from Udeze _et al._ are reported for the category of index age 36+yrs, there are approximately 82% of patients in the economic model SoC arm who survive beyond age 36 years (see Appendix, Figure 1). The ideal analysis would be based on a statistical model of the relationship between complications and age, but a more granular description of the data is first required to assess if this would be feasible. The DSU therefore asked the company (via NICE) whether the data from Udeze _et al._[1] could be broken down into narrower age bands, and reanalysed according to the patient’s age at which the complications occurred. This might then have provided some insight as to whether it would be possible to undertake further statistical analyses to predict complication rates according to each age, which could then be applied to each patient age in the economic model _._ However, in their response, the company stated that they do not have the granular level of data that the DSU requested, including age of occurrence of complications, as the study was not set up to collect this. 

As no further analyses of the Udeze complication rate data were available, the DSU’s analysis is therefore limited to additional analyses using the data previously provided by the company. 

6 



<!-- page 454 -->

## 2.2 Scenario analyses conducted by the DSU 

The DSU undertook scenario analyses using the most recently updated version of the company’s model (version 5, dated 4[th] June 2024) to further explore the impact of age-specific complication rates on the cost-effectiveness of exa-cel. All analyses were conducted using the deterministic version of the model, with separate analyses undertaken using discount rates of 3.5% and 1.5% both for health outcomes and costs. All scenarios undertaken include the EAG’s preferred assumptions about exa-cel treatment withdrawal (8.62% patients fail apheresis and 10.34% fail to receive exa-cel). In line with concerns about double-counting raised by the EAG, the rate of acute chest syndrome (ACS) was set equal to zero in all scenarios because these events are counted as VOCs elsewhere in the company’s economic model. 

The details of the additional scenario analyses are described below. The first four scenarios reflect analyses which have previously been presented by the company and/or the EAG. Whilst some of these scenarios (e.g., the company’s weighted average approach for the 12+yrs population) attempt to reflect increasing complication rates in older patients, all of these analyses apply constant acute and chronic complication rates in every model cycle. The DSU undertook four additional scenario analyses in which different complication rates for specific age bands in Udeze _et al._[1] are applied once patients reach a particular age in the model. Monthly rates of acute complications and monthly probabilities of chronic complications for each age band in the Udeze _et al._ data were calculated and implemented in the model by one member of the DSU (MMY). All analyses were then checked by another member of the DSU (PT). 

## **Scenario using complication rates from the literature** 

This analysis includes complication rates reported from Brousse _et al_ . 2023,[4] Yeruva _et al_ . 2016,[5] Shah _et al_ . 2019,[6] Singh _et al_ . 2016,[7] Cahil _et al_ . 2019[8] and the American Academy of Opthalmology.[9] The rate of chronic liver disease was not available from the literature and therefore, the weighted average chronic liver disease rate for people aged 12-35yrs and 36+yrs in Udeze _et al_ .[1] was applied in this scenario. This analysis reflects complication rates used in previous versions of the model and is presented here for information only. 

## **Scenario using the complication rates of overall cohort data (2+yrs)** 

This analysis applies complication rates for the 2+yrs population in Udeze _et al._[1] to all patients in every model cycle. This scenario corresponds to the company’s preferred analysis presented following ACM1. 

## **Scenario using complication rates for the 12-35yrs subgroup, EAG and Appraisal Committee’s** 

## **preferred approach** 

This analysis applies complication rates for the 12-35yrs subgroup from Udeze _et al._[1] to all patients in every model cycle. 

7 



<!-- page 455 -->

## **Scenario using the weighted average complication rates for the 12+yrs subgroup (12-35yrs and 36+yrs), company’s preferred approach at ACM2** 

This analysis applies the weighted average complication rates for patients aged 12+yrs in Udeze _et al._[1] to all patients in every model cycle. A weighting of 72.27% is applied to the 12-35yrs subgroup and a weighting of 27.73% is applied to the of 36+yrs subgroup, based on the number of patients in each age band in Udeze _et al._[1] (649 and 249 patients, respectively). This analysis is based on observed differences in complication rates by age, but then applies constant complication rates in every model cycle. 

## **DSU Scenario 1: Age-dependent complication rates for the 12-35yrs and 36+yrs subgroups** 

This analysis applies the complication rates for the 12-35yrs subgroup from Udeze _et al_ .[1] to modelled patients until they reach the age of 36 years, and then switches to the complication rates for the 36+yrs subgroup for all subsequent model cycles. 

## **DSU Scenario 2: Age-dependent complication rates for the 18-35yrs and 36+yrs subgroups** 

This analysis applies the complication rates for the 18-35yrs subgroup from Udeze _et al_ .[1] to modelled patients until they reach the age of 36 years, and then switches to the complication rates for the 36+yrs subgroup for all subsequent model cycles. 

## **DSU Scenario 3** : **Age-dependent complication rates for 12-17yrs, 18-35yrs and 36+yrs subgroups, including a lag to account for follow-up duration** 

The median follow-up period in Udeze _et al._[1] is 4.69 years. This analysis applies complication rates for each age band in the model including a 5-year lag to account for this follow-up time. This analysis applies the complication rates for the 12-17yrs subgroup for modelled patients aged <23 years, then switches to use complication rates for the 18-35yrs whilst modelled patients are aged 23-41 years, and then switches to use complication rates for the 36+yrs subgroup for all subsequent model cycles. In this way, the analysis attempts to align the age of patients in Udeze _et al._ with the appropriate time point in the modelled age. 

## **DSU Scenario 4: Age-dependent complication rates for 18-35yrs and 36+yrs subgroups, including a lag to account for follow-up duration** 

This analysis is the same as DSU Scenario 3, but applies the 18-35yrs subgroup data for all modelled patients until they reach the age of 41 years. Complication rates for the 36+yrs subgroup are applied for all subsequent model cycles. 

The rates of acute and chronic complication applied in these scenario analyses are summarised in Table 1.

## **3. RESULTS** 

The results of the DSU’s scenario analyses are summarised in Table 2 (3.5% discount rates) and Table 

3 (1.5% discount rates). Table 4 and Table 5 in the appendix present the mean number of acute complications and the number of life years with chronic complications predicted by each of the scenarios. 

The model results shown in Table 2 and Table 3 suggest that when the severity modifier is excluded from the analysis, the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER) for exa-cel is moderately sensitive to the choice of complication rates. Across all eight scenarios, when using the Reference Case discount rates of 3.5%, the ICER for exa-cel versus SoC ranges from £******* per quality-adjusted life year (QALY) gained (DSU Scenario 2 – age-dependent rates, 18-35yrs and 36+yrs subgroups) to £******* 

9 



<!-- page 457 -->

per QALY gained (EAG-preferred scenario – age-independent rates, 12-35yrs subgroup). Assuming non-Reference Case discount rates of 1.5% for both QALYs and costs suggests an ICER range of £****** to £****** per QALY gained. Assuming that the population has a mean age of 21.2 years and 44.2% of patients are female (based on CLIMB SCD-121), a QALY gain for the SoC group of 10.52 or less leads to a decision modifier of 1.2, whereas a QALY gain for the SoC group which is higher than this value leads to a decision modifier of 1.0. The decision modifier is 1.2 when complication rates are based on other literature, the whole Udeze cohort (2+yrs, age-independent), the Udeze 12+yrs subgroup (weighted average), DSU Scenario 1 (age-dependent, 12-35yrs and 36+yrs) and DSU Scenario 2 (agedependent, 18-35yrs and 36+yrs). The other scenarios suggest a decision modifier of 1.0, although the DSU notes that the SoC group QALYs are fairly close to 10.52 in all scenarios except for the EAG’s preferred Udeze 12-35yrs scenario.

## **4. DISCUSSION** 

None of the available options for incorporating complication rates in the company’s model are ideal. Given that the rates of several SCD complications are generally expected to increase as patients get older, the DSU’s preferred analysis would be to reflect this age-dependence in the complication rates applied in the economic model. The application of the 12-35yrs subgroup data of Udeze _et al._ ,[1] which is the currently preferred option by the EAG and the Appraisal Committee, does not account for this factor as constant rates are applied in every model cycle. The DSU also notes that the underlying 12-35yrs subgroup data may not be reflective of the complication risks for older patients ages in the model, as around 82% of SoC patients are predicted to survive beyond age 36 years (see Appendix, Figure 1). The company’s suggested approach of using a weighted average of the 12-35yrs and 36+yrs subgroup in Udeze _et al._ is similarly problematic in that the underlying rate data incorporate different effects by age, but these are applied as constant age-independent rates in the economic model. As noted in the EAG’s previous critique, this approach may inflate the complication risks for younger patients in the model. 

In the absence of further statistical modelling of the Udeze _et al._ data to predict complication risks by age, the DSU’s preferred approach is to apply age-band specific rates from Udeze _et al._[1] in line with the age of patients in the model. This approach allows for some degree of age-dependence to be included in the modelled rates, although this relies on very broad age categories which may mask some of the true age/complication rate relationship. However, given the relatively low frequency of events per annum, more detailed modelling of this relationship may not be feasible.  It may also be preferable to focus on the analyses which include a time lag for follow-up time to better reflect the age at which the complications occurred in the Udeze study, rather than the subject’s age at the index date. However, the precise age at which complications occurred cannot be estimated which likely leads to inaccuracy in the model predictions. The use of complication rates for age-bands in the model is also limited in that it reduces the number of patients and events at those specific model ages – this is a particular issue for DSU Scenario 3, whereby the 12-17yrs subgroup is informed by only 110 patients. Notwithstanding these limitations, the DSU’s preferred scenario is DSU Scenario 3. DSU Scenario 4 produces very similar results. 

As is typical for trial- and real-world derived evidence, there are differences between the Udeze _et al._ study population(s) and the population included in the CLIMB SCD-121 study. These differences have been previously noted by the EAG and presented to the Appraisal Committee. Specifically, there is evidence that the Udeze _et al._ population is more severe at baseline than the trial population in terms of the annual VOC rate (6.4 per year vs 4.2 years) and complications at baseline. Udeze _et al._ identified patients in England at the point when they first met the eligibility criteria i.e., patients with an SCD diagnosis and ≥2 VOCs in two consecutive years. Applying the observed rates of complications from this study population assumes that these patients are reflective of those eligible for exa-cel and that the treatment benefit observed in CLIMB SCD-121 is applicable to this more severe population. The degree of overlap between Udeze _et al._ and the 

15 



<!-- page 463 -->

clinical trial has not been reported and therefore it is not possible to address if some form of matching of patients to the trial population would be feasible, if this were considered to be a better reflection of the target population for England. 

16

## **Overview** 

## **Explanation** 

This page details the Managed Access Team's overall assessment on whether a medicine could be suitable for Managed Access and if data collection is feasible. The feasibility assessment does not provide any guidance on whether a medicine is a cost-effective, or plausibly cost-effective, use of NHS resources. This document should be read alongside other key documents, particularly the company's evidence submission and External Assessment Centre (EAC) report. Further detail for each consideration is available within the separate tabs. 

Whilst a rationale is provided, in general the ratings for each area: Green  - No key issues identified Amber - Either outstanding issues that the Managed Access team are working to resolve, or subjective judgements are required from committee / stakeholders (see key questions) 

Red - The managed access team does not consider this topic suitable for a managed access recommendation. 

The Managed Access Team may not assess other areas where its work has indicated that topic is not suitable for a managed access recommendation 

The feasibility assessment indicates whether the Managed Access team have scheduled to update this document, primarily based on whether it is undertaking actions to explore outstanding issues. There may be other circumstance when an update is required, for example when the expected key uncertainties change or a managed access proposal is substantially amended. In these cases an updated feasibility assessment should be requested from the Managed Access team.

## **Uncertainties** 

## **Explanation** 

This page details the Managed Access Team's assessment on whether data collection could sufficiently resolve key uncertainties through further data collection within managed access. The overall assessment is the key judgement from the Managed Access Team. The Managed Access Team will justify it decision, but broadly it is a matter of judgement on whether the further data collection could lead to a positive NICE decision at the point the technology exits managed access. For this reason individual uncertainties that have a higher impact on the ICER have a greater impact on the overall rating. Further detail is available on each uncertainty identified primarily informed from a company's managed access proposal, the External Assessment Group (EAG) report, judgements from the NICE Managed Access Team, and where available directly from NICE committee deliberations. The likelihood that data could sufficiently resolve each specific outcome is informed both by the expected primary data source in general (as detailed in the separate tab) and specifically whether the data collected is expected to sufficiently resolve that uncertainty.

|EAG6|The model does not<br>have the requisites for<br>a Markov structure|The model structure is not organised as a<br>Markov structure.<br>Deaths are calculated by applying each acute<br>complication a death rate specific to the event,<br>corrected by the proportion of alive<br>population. Although the (incremental)<br>death rates are applied to the “alive”<br>population, the “alive” population is<br>determined in a circular manner, subtracting<br>the number of total deaths in the model from<br>1. This circularity provides no guarantee that<br>the sum of deaths is less or equal to the total<br>number of people in the cohort.<br>The overall effect is that some people may “die<br>twice” at each cycle in the model, i.e., people<br>in the model are “double counted”.  Because<br>of the lack of face validity, rates of chronic<br>complications and mortality calculated in the<br>model may be biased.|Model rebuild using<br>standard practices<br>for Markov state-<br>transition models.|Unquantified|Model rebuild using standard<br>practices for Markov state-transition<br>models.|Committee<br>judgement required|No further data<br>collection possible /<br>proposed||

|EAG8|VOC rates as a<br>predictor in a risk<br>equation for acute and<br>chronic complications|The model extrapolates all longer-term events<br>from hazard ratios of each event, multiplied by<br>the rate of VOCs at each cycle. The rate of VOC<br>is applied in the model as mean number of<br>events per month; for each complication, this<br>rate is multiplied by a hazard ratio, as if the<br>number of VOCs were a term in a risk<br>equation. Yet the original study with all<br>likelihood did not use VOCs in this way; in any<br>case, the original risk equations are not<br>published. In addition, the original study did<br>not show that the risk of complications is zero<br>when patients report no VOCs, but only that<br>the risk is reduced. Therefore, applying the<br>“number of VOCs” as a significant independent<br>variable, associated with a specific coefficient<br>for the risk of acute and chronic complications<br>in the manner of the model originates from a<br>misinterpretation of the analysis in the original<br>study (Shah et al 2019). ## **Other issues** 

## **Explanation** 

This page details the Managed Access Team's assessment on whether there are any potential barriers to agreeing a managed access agreement and that any potential managed access agreement operates according to the policy framework developed for the Cancer Drugs Fund and Innovative Medicines Fund. 

The items included are informed by the relevant policy documentation, expert input from stakeholders including the Health Research Authority, and the Managed Access team's experience with developing, agreeing and operating managed access agreements. Additions or amendments may be made to these considerations as further experience is gained from Managed Access. 

The Managed Access Team will justify it decision, but broadly it is a matter of judgement on whether any issues identified, taken as a whole, are likely to lead to a barrier to a Managed Access Agreement being agreed, or operationalised in the NHS. No assessment is made whether a Commercial Access Agreement is likely to be reached between the company and NHS England, which could be a substantive barrier to managed access.
